abstract: We study the representation of static patterns and temporal associa(cid:173) tions in neural networks with a broad distribution of signal delays. For a certain class of such systems, a simple intuitive understanding of the spatia-temporal computation becomes possible with the help of a novel Lyapunov functional. It allows a quantitative study of the asymptotic network behavior through a statistical mechanical analysis. We present analytic calculations of both retrieval quality and storage capacity and compare them with simulation results.

paragraphs: The paper examines how neural networks represent both static patterns and associations across time when signals arrive with widely varying delays. This brings spatial pattern storage and temporal relationships into the same analysis. The distribution of delays is part of the system being studied, making timing central to its computational behavior.

For a particular class of these networks, the authors introduce a Lyapunov functional that makes the spatiotemporal computation easier to understand. This mathematical construction supports analysis of the network's long-run behavior. It provides a route from a system with delayed interactions to a quantitative description using statistical mechanics.

The authors derive analytical calculations for retrieval quality and storage capacity, then compare them with simulation results. These quantities address how successfully stored information can be recovered and how much the system can store. The contribution combines an explanatory mathematical tool with measurable properties of memory performance, within the class of delayed networks for which the functional applies.
summary.tldr: A Lyapunov functional enables statistical-mechanical analysis of retrieval and storage in neural networks with distributed signal delays.

title: Statistical Mechanics of Temporal Association in Neural Networks

abstract: Feedforward networks composed of units which compute a sigmoidal func(cid:173) tion of a weighted sum of their inputs have been much investigated. We tested the approximation and estimation capabilities of networks using functions more complex than sigmoids. Three classes of functions were tested: polynomials, rational functions, and flexible Fourier series. Un(cid:173) like sigmoids, these classes can fit non-monotonic functions. They were compared on three problems: prediction of Boston housing prices, the sunspot count, and robot arm inverse dynamics. The complex units at(cid:173) tained clearly superior performance on the robot arm problem, which is a highly non-monotonic, pure approximation problem. On the noisy and only mildly nonlinear Boston housing and sunspot problems, differences among the complex units were revealed; polynomials did poorly, whereas rationals and flexible Fourier series were comparable to sigmoids.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether neural networks benefit from units with more flexible response functions than the usual sigmoid. It tests polynomial, rational, and flexible Fourier functions. These alternatives can represent nonmonotonic responses, in which output can rise and fall as input changes, making the individual units more expressive.

The authors compare the alternatives on housing-price prediction, sunspot counts, and robot-arm inverse dynamics. The robot-arm task is described as a pure approximation problem with strongly nonmonotonic relationships. On that task, networks using the more complex units achieve clearly better performance, supporting their usefulness when the target function has that structure.

The pattern differs on the noisy, mildly nonlinear housing and sunspot tasks. Polynomial units perform poorly, while rational and flexible Fourier units perform comparably to sigmoids. The findings show that greater unit flexibility has task-dependent value: it helps on the strongly nonmonotonic approximation problem, but does not provide a consistent advantage on the two noisy prediction problems.
summary.tldr: More flexible unit responses improve robot-arm approximation, but their benefits vary on noisy prediction tasks.

title: Networks with Learned Unit Response Functions

abstract: Representations for semantic information about words are neces(cid:173) sary for many applications of neural networks in natural language processing. This paper describes an efficient, corpus-based method for inducing distributed semantic representations for a large num(cid:173) ber of words (50,000) from lexical coccurrence statistics by means of a large-scale linear regression. The representations are success(cid:173) fully applied to word sense disambiguation using a nearest neighbor method .

The representations are success(cid:173) fully applied to word sense disambiguation using a nearest neighbor method .

paragraphs: Many language-processing tasks need a representation of word meaning that can be learned for a large vocabulary. This paper derives distributed semantic vectors from how words co-occur in a corpus. The approach uses contextual statistics rather than requiring a manually specified semantic description for every word.

A large-scale linear-regression method induces representations for 50,000 words. The learned vectors encode semantic information in a shared distributed space, allowing relationships among words to be expressed through their positions in that representation. The emphasis is on an efficient corpus-based construction that can operate at substantial vocabulary size.

The representations are successfully applied to word-sense disambiguation with a nearest-neighbor method. That application tests whether the induced space supports a concrete semantic decision rather than only descriptive similarity. The contribution links large-scale distributional learning with a simple downstream procedure, illustrating the usefulness of reusable word representations beyond the statistics used to create them.
summary.tldr: Word Space learns distributed semantic vectors for 50,000 words from co-occurrence statistics and applies them to word-sense disambiguation.

title: Word Space

abstract: The following investigates the use of single-neuron learning algo(cid:173) rithms to improve the performance of text-retrieval systems that accept natural-language queries. A retrieval process is explained that transforms the natural-language query into the query syntax of a real retrieval system: the initial query is expanded using statis(cid:173) tical and learning techniques and is then used for document ranking and binary classification. The results of experiments suggest that Kivinen and Warmuth's Exponentiated Gradient Descent learning algorithm works significantly better than previous approaches.

paragraphs: A natural-language query must be converted into something a retrieval system can execute. This paper investigates how single-neuron learning algorithms can improve that process. The focus is the connection between a user's initial wording, the query submitted to an existing retrieval system, and the resulting treatment of documents.

The proposed retrieval process expands the initial query using statistical and learning techniques, then translates it into the target system's query syntax. The expanded query is used for document ranking and binary classification. These are related outputs: ranking orders documents, while binary classification assigns them to one of two categories. Learning therefore participates in a pipeline that supports both forms of retrieval decision.

Experiments suggest that Kivinen and Warmuth's Exponentiated Gradient Descent performs significantly better than previous approaches. The reported finding favors that learning algorithm within the investigated retrieval setting. The contribution is to show how a relatively simple learned component can improve the transformation and use of natural-language queries in a working text-retrieval process.
summary.tldr: A query-expansion and retrieval pipeline using Exponentiated Gradient Descent shows significantly better experimental performance than previous approaches.

title: Text-Based Information Retrieval Using Exponentiated Gradient Descent

abstract: Model learning combined with dynamic programming has been shown to be effective for learning control of continuous state dynamic systems. The simplest method assumes the learned model is correct and applies dynamic programming to it, but many approximators provide uncertainty estimates on the fit. How can they be exploited? This paper addresses the case where the system must be prevented from having catastrophic failures dur(cid:173) ing learning. We propose a new algorithm adapted from the dual control literature and use Bayesian locally weighted regression models with dy(cid:173) namic programming. A common reinforcement learning assumption is that aggressive exploration should be encouraged. This paper addresses the con(cid:173) verse case in which the system has to reign in exploration. The algorithm is illustrated on a 4 dimensional simulated control problem.

The algorithm is illustrated on a 4 dimensional simulated control problem.

paragraphs: A controller can learn a model of a changing system and use dynamic programming to choose actions. The simplest version treats the learned model as correct, even though its predictions may be uncertain. This paper asks how estimates of that uncertainty can help when catastrophic failures must be prevented during learning.

The proposed algorithm draws on dual control and combines Bayesian locally weighted regression models with dynamic programming. The regression models provide uncertainty estimates alongside their fitted behavior. Those estimates give the controller information about where its knowledge is weak, making uncertainty relevant to action selection rather than merely a description of model quality.

The problem deliberately calls for restrained exploration: trying unfamiliar actions can carry unacceptable consequences. The algorithm is illustrated on a simulated control task with four dimensions. Its contribution is an approach to using model uncertainty in the learning-and-control process when gathering experience must be balanced against avoiding failure, rather than assuming that aggressive exploration is always desirable.
summary.tldr: A control-learning algorithm uses Bayesian model uncertainty to restrain exploration when failures could be catastrophic.

title: Exploiting Model Uncertainty Estimates for Safe Dynamic Control Learning

paragraphs: The paper seeks a scalable way to construct Bayes point classifiers. The Bayes point is the center of mass of the version space: the set of linear classifiers consistent with the training data. It expresses the Bayesian idea of averaging across compatible classifiers, but an earlier sampling algorithm required memory and computation growing quadratically with training sample size.

The authors propose a method based on the simple perceptron learning algorithm to overcome that computational drawback. The method extends readily to multiple classes, and its computational effort can be adjusted through the number of posterior samples. This makes the amount of sampling a practical control over the work spent constructing the classifier.

Experiments on MNIST show performance competitive with support vector machines in the reported comparison. The paper also examines rejecting predictions using approximate posterior probabilities. It reports 0.1% generalization error at a 10% rejection rate. That figure describes selective prediction, where some test points are declined, and should be interpreted together with the fraction of cases rejected.
summary.tldr: A perceptron-based method scales Bayes point learning and achieves competitive MNIST performance, with further error reductions when uncertain predictions are rejected.

title: Large Scale Bayes Point Machines

abstract: We compare discriminative and generative learning as typified by logistic regression and naive Bayes. We show, contrary to a widely(cid:173) held belief that discriminative classifiers are almost always to be preferred, that there can often be two distinct regimes of per(cid:173) formance as the training set size is increased, one in which each algorithm does better. This stems from the observation- which is borne out in repeated experiments- that while discriminative learning has lower asymptotic error, a generative classifier may also approach its (higher) asymptotic error much faster.

We show, contrary to a widely(cid:173) held belief that discriminative classifiers are almost always to be preferred, that there can often be two distinct regimes of per(cid:173) formance as the training set size is increased, one in which each algorithm does better. This stems from the observation- which is borne out in repeated experiments- that while discriminative learning has lower asymptotic error, a generative classifier may also approach its (higher) asymptotic error much faster.

paragraphs: The paper compares discriminative and generative learning through logistic regression and naive Bayes. It challenges the widespread expectation that discriminative classifiers should almost always be preferred. The comparison focuses on how performance changes as more training examples become available, making sample size central to the question of which learning approach works better.

The key distinction is between eventual error and the speed of approaching it. In the comparison, discriminative learning has a lower asymptotic error, meaning a better error level with sufficiently much data. A generative classifier, however, may approach its higher limiting error much faster. A better eventual result therefore does not by itself determine which method performs better with the data currently available.

The authors show that there can often be two performance regimes, with each algorithm doing better over a different range of training-set sizes. Repeated experiments support the observation behind this explanation. The finding makes classifier preference depend on both the amount of data and the learning behavior, rather than on asymptotic performance alone.
summary.tldr: Naive Bayes may learn faster with limited data, while logistic regression can achieve lower error as training data grows.

title: On Discriminative vs. Generative Classifiers: A comparison of logistic regression and naive Bayes

abstract: We employ an efﬁcient method using Bayesian and linear classiﬁers for analyzing the dynamics of information in high-dimensional states of generic cortical microcircuit models. It is shown that such recurrent cir- cuits of spiking neurons have an inherent capability to carry out rapid computations on complex spike patterns, merging information contained in the order of spike arrival with previously acquired context information.
originalAbstract: We employ an efﬁcient method using Bayesian and linear classiﬁers for analyzing the dynamics of information in high-dimensional states of generic cortical microcircuit models. It is shown that such recurrent cir- cuits of spiking neurons have an inherent capability to carry out rapid computations on complex spike patterns, merging information contained in the order of spike arrival with previously acquired context information.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how information evolves within recurrent networks of spiking neurons. It examines generic cortical microcircuit models, whose internal states are high-dimensional, to ask what computations such circuits can perform on complex patterns of arriving spikes.

The authors use Bayesian and linear classifiers as an efficient way to analyze information in those states. This shifts the analysis toward what can be extracted from the network's activity as it changes. The relevant information includes the order in which spikes arrive and context acquired previously, so the question concerns both incoming events and the circuit's preceding experience.

The study shows that these modeled recurrent circuits have an inherent capacity for rapid computation that merges spike-order information with earlier context. The significance is that a circuit's current response can reflect the temporal organization of new input together with information already present in its state. The stated finding concerns the computational capabilities of the microcircuit models, linking recurrent spiking dynamics to contextual processing.
summary.tldr: Analysis of recurrent spiking microcircuit models shows rapid computations that combine spike arrival order with previously acquired context.

title: Information Dynamics and Emergent Computation in Recurrent Circuits of Spiking Neurons

abstract: In order to understand AdaBoost’s dynamics, especially its ability to maximize margins, we derive an associated simpliﬁed nonlinear iterated map and analyze its behavior in low-dimensional cases. We ﬁnd stable cycles for these cases, which can explicitly be used to solve for Ada- Boost’s output. By considering AdaBoost as a dynamical system, we are able to prove R¨atsch and Warmuth’s conjecture that AdaBoost may fail to converge to a maximal-margin combined classiﬁer when given a ‘non- optimal’ weak learning algorithm. AdaBoost is known to be a coordinate descent method, but other known algorithms that explicitly aim to max- imize the margin (such as AdaBoost⁄ and arc-gv) are not. We consider a differentiable function for which coordinate ascent will yield a maxi- mum margin solution. We then make a simple approximation to derive a new boosting algorithm whose updates are slightly more aggressive than those of arc-gv.

paragraphs: The paper examines AdaBoost as a dynamical system to understand how its repeated updates affect classification margins. The authors derive a simplified nonlinear iterated map and study low-dimensional cases. In these cases, they find stable cycles that can be used to solve explicitly for AdaBoost's output.

This analysis proves a conjecture that AdaBoost may fail to converge to a maximum-margin combined classifier when its weak learning algorithm is non-optimal. The conclusion identifies a possible failure under that condition; it does not say that AdaBoost always fails to maximize margins. Viewing the updates as a dynamical process makes this behavior accessible to direct mathematical analysis.

The authors also investigate how coordinate-based optimization could explicitly target maximum margin. Although AdaBoost is a coordinate-descent method, the cited margin-focused alternatives do not share that characterization. They identify a differentiable function whose coordinate ascent yields a maximum-margin solution, then approximate it to derive a new boosting algorithm with updates slightly more aggressive than those of arc-gv.
summary.tldr: A dynamical analysis proves that AdaBoost can miss maximum margin with a non-optimal weak learner and motivates a new boosting algorithm.

title: On the Dynamics of Boosting

abstract: The context in which a name appears in a caption provides powerful cues as to who is depicted in the associated image. We obtain 44,773 face im- ages, using a face detector, from approximately half a million captioned news images and automatically link names, obtained using a named en- tity recognizer, with these faces. A simple clustering method can pro- duce fair results. We improve these results significantly by combining the clustering process with a model of the probability that an individual is depicted given its context. Once the labeling procedure is over, we have an accurately labeled set of faces, an appearance model for each individual depicted, and a natural language model that can produce ac- curate results on captions in isolation.

paragraphs: This paper automatically connects faces in news photographs with names in their captions. It extracts 44,773 face images from approximately half a million captioned news images using a face detector, and obtains names through named entity recognition. The key challenge is deciding which named individuals are actually depicted.

A simple clustering method produces fair results, but the authors significantly improve it by incorporating the context surrounding each name. Their model estimates the probability that an individual appears in the image given that context. Combining this probability model with face clustering lets linguistic evidence contribute directly to the assignment of identities.

The completed procedure produces an accurately labeled collection of faces and an appearance model for each depicted individual. It also yields a language model that can make accurate predictions from captions alone. The contribution is a joint use of facial appearance and caption context that improves labeling while producing reusable models of both visual identity and textual evidence of depiction.
summary.tldr: Combining face clustering with caption-context probabilities significantly improves automatic identification of people in news images.

title: Who's In the Picture

abstract: We consider the problem of geometrical surface reconstruction from one or several images using learned shape models. While humans can effort- lessly retrieve 3D shape information, this inverse problem has turned out to be difficult to perform automatically. We introduce a framework based on level set surface reconstruction and shape models for achieving this goal. Through this merging, we obtain an efficient and robust method for reconstructing surfaces of an object category of interest. The shape model includes surface cues such as point, curve and silhou- ette features. Based on ideas from Active Shape Models, we show how both the geometry and the appearance of these features can be modelled consistently in a multi-view context. The complete surface is obtained by evolving a level set driven by a PDE, which tries to fit the surface to the inferred 3D features. In addition, an a priori 3D surface model is used to regularize the solution, in particular, where surface features are sparse. Experiments are demonstrated on a database of real face images.

paragraphs: The paper addresses reconstructing an object's three-dimensional surface from one or several images. It combines learned shape models with level-set surface reconstruction, using knowledge of an object category to guide the inverse problem. The authors describe the resulting method as efficient and robust for the category of interest.

The shape model incorporates point, curve, and silhouette cues. Drawing on Active Shape Models, the framework represents both the geometry and appearance of these features consistently across multiple views. These cues support the inference of three-dimensional features, which then guide reconstruction of a complete surface.

A partial differential equation evolves the level set to fit the inferred features. An additional prior model of the three-dimensional surface regularizes the result, especially where surface cues are sparse. This connects local image evidence with learned information about the overall shape. Experiments on real face images demonstrate the framework, illustrating how feature inference and a surface prior can work together in reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Learned shape models guide level-set surface reconstruction from image features, with a surface prior supporting regions where cues are sparse.

title: Surface Reconstruction using Learned Shape Models

abstract: A novel linear feature selection algorithm is presented based on the global minimization of a data-dependent generalization error bound. Feature selection and scaling algorithms often lead to non-convex opti- mization problems, which in many previous approaches were addressed through gradient descent procedures that can only guarantee convergence to a local minimum. We propose an alternative approach, whereby the global solution of the non-convex optimization problem is derived via an equivalent optimization problem. Moreover, the convex optimization task is reduced to a conic quadratic programming problem for which effi- cient solvers are available. Highly competitive numerical results on both artificial and real-world data sets are reported.

We propose an alternative approach, whereby the global solution of the non-convex optimization problem is derived via an equivalent optimization problem. Moreover, the convex optimization task is reduced to a conic quadratic programming problem for which effi- cient solvers are available. Highly competitive numerical results on both artificial and real-world data sets are reported.

paragraphs: This paper presents a linear feature selection method whose objective is a data-dependent bound on generalization error. Such a bound connects the available training data to performance on unseen examples. The method chooses features by optimizing that bound, making the stated error guarantee the organizing principle of feature selection.

The main difficulty is that feature selection and scaling can produce nonconvex optimization problems. Gradient descent approaches used in earlier work can guarantee only arrival at a local minimum. The authors instead derive the global solution to their nonconvex problem through an equivalent optimization problem, avoiding that particular limitation of local optimization.

They further reduce the convex formulation to conic quadratic programming, a problem class with efficient solvers. This connects the mathematical reformulation to a practical computational route. The paper reports highly competitive numerical results on artificial and real-world datasets. Its global optimality claim concerns the specified bound-based optimization problem; minimizing that objective should not be confused with directly guaranteeing the smallest possible error on unseen data.
summary.tldr: A feature selection method obtains a global solution to its nonconvex error-bound objective through an equivalent, efficiently solvable convex formulation.

title: A Feature Selection Algorithm Based on the Global Minimization of a Generalization Error Bound

abstract: This paper presents an algorithm for synthesis of human motion in specified styles. We use a theory of movement observation (Laban Movement Analysis) to describe movement styles as points in a multi-dimensional perceptual space. We cast the task of learning to synthesize desired movement styles as a regression problem: sequences generated via space-time interpolation of motion capture data are used to learn a nonlinear mapping between animation parameters and movement styles in perceptual space. We demonstrate that the learned model can apply a variety of motion styles to pre-recorded motion sequences and it can extrapolate styles not originally included in the training data.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for generating human motion in specified styles. It describes style through Laban Movement Analysis, a theory of movement observation, and represents styles as points in a multidimensional perceptual space. This supplies a structured way to describe how a movement is perceived and connect that description to animation.

The authors formulate learning as a regression problem. They generate motion sequences by interpolating motion-capture data in space and time, then use those sequences to learn a nonlinear relationship between animation parameters and positions in the perceptual style space. The model links adjustable animation quantities with the movement qualities the synthesis process is intended to produce.

The demonstrations show that the learned model can apply a variety of styles to prerecorded motion sequences. It can also extrapolate styles that were absent from the training data. These findings indicate that the learned relationship can support style control beyond reproducing the styles explicitly supplied during training, within the motion-synthesis setting demonstrated by the paper.
summary.tldr: A learned relationship between animation parameters and perceptual style enables varied motion synthesis, including demonstrated extrapolation to untrained styles.

title: Learning Motion Style Synthesis from Perceptual Observations

abstract: Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) are an effective tool for a variety of different data segmentation and labeling tasks including visual scene interpretation, which seeks to partition images into their constituent semantic-level regions and assign appropriate class labels to each region. For accurate labeling it is important to capture the global context of the image as well as local information. We in- troduce a CRF based scene labeling model that incorporates both local features and features aggregated over the whole image or large sections of it. Secondly, traditional CRF learning requires fully labeled datasets which can be costly and troublesome to produce. We introduce a method for learning CRFs from datasets with many unlabeled nodes by marginalizing out the unknown labels so that the log-likelihood of the known ones can be maximized by gradient ascent. Loopy Belief Propagation is used to approximate the marginals needed for the gradi- ent and log-likelihood calculations and the Bethe free-energy approximation to the log-likelihood is monitored to control the step size. Our experimental results show that effective models can be learned from fragmentary labelings and that incorporating top-down aggregate features signiﬁcantly improves the segmenta- tions. The resulting segmentations are compared to the state-of-the-art on three different image datasets.

paragraphs: Scene segmentation divides an image into meaningful regions and assigns each a class label. This paper develops a conditional random field model that combines local visual features with information aggregated across large image sections or the whole image. The aim is to let broader scene context contribute alongside evidence near each region.

The authors also address the cost of producing fully labeled training images. Their learning method permits many nodes to remain unlabeled by marginalizing over the unknown labels and maximizing the likelihood of the known ones through gradient ascent. Loopy belief propagation approximates the marginal quantities needed for these calculations.

A Bethe free-energy approximation to the log-likelihood is monitored to control the optimization step size. Experiments show that effective models can be learned from fragmentary annotations and that aggregate features significantly improve segmentation. Results are compared with leading methods on three image datasets. The two contributions work on different parts of the problem: richer contextual evidence improves labeling, while partial-label learning makes incomplete annotations usable for training.
summary.tldr: A CRF combines local and image-wide context while learning from incomplete annotations, with experiments showing effective training and improved segmentation.

title: Scene Segmentation with CRFs Learned from Partially Labeled Images

abstract: Metal binding is important for the structural and functional characterization of proteins. Previous prediction efforts have only focused on bonding state, i.e. deciding which protein residues act as metal ligands in some binding site. Identifying the geometry of metal-binding sites, i.e. deciding which residues are jointly involved in the coordination of a metal ion is a new prediction problem that has been never attempted before from protein sequence alone. In this paper, we formulate it in the framework of learning with structured outputs. Our solution relies on the fact that, from a graph theoretical perspective, metal binding has the algebraic properties of a matroid, enabling the application of greedy algorithms for learning structured outputs. On a data set of 199 non-redundant metalloproteins, we obtained precision/recall levels of 75\%/46\% correct ligand-ion assignments, which improves to 88\%/88\% in the setting where the metal binding state is known.

Here, binding-site geometry means determining joint ligand-ion assignments, extending prediction beyond the binding status of individual residues.

The authors formulate the task as learning with structured outputs, so the predicted answer describes relationships among residues and ions. summary.tldr: A matroid-based structured predictor groups protein residues by the metal ions they coordinate, using sequence information.

title: Predicting the Geometry of Metal Binding Sites from Protein Sequence

abstract: Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a useful technique for modeling dependencies between two (or more) sets of variables. Building upon the recently suggested probabilistic interpretation of CCA, we propose a nonparametric, fully Bayesian framework that can automatically select the number of correlation components, and effectively capture the sparsity underlying the projections. In addition, given (partially) labeled data, our algorithm can also be used as a (semi)supervised dimensionality reduction technique, and can be applied to learn useful predictive features in the context of learning a set of related tasks. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach for both CCA as a stand-alone problem, and when applied to multi-label prediction.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis models dependencies between two or more groups of variables. This paper builds on its probabilistic interpretation to develop a fully Bayesian, nonparametric version. The method addresses two modeling choices together: how many correlation components to use and which variables should contribute to the projections.

The framework can select the component count automatically while capturing sparsity in the projections. These features allow the shared representation to adapt in size and to concentrate its dependence on selected variables. With fully or partially labeled observations, the same algorithm can also serve as supervised or semi-supervised dimensionality reduction.

The authors connect this representation learning to predicting multiple labels and learning related tasks. A shared account of dependencies can supply useful predictive features across those tasks. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness both when canonical correlation analysis is the main problem and when the method supports multi-label prediction. The contribution is a unified Bayesian treatment of representation size, sparse projections, and predictive feature learning, with empirical support for both its dependency-modeling and prediction roles.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian sparse CCA model automatically chooses correlation components and learns features useful for multi-label prediction.

title: Multi-Label Prediction via Sparse Infinite CCA

abstract: While human listeners excel at selectively attending to a conversation in a cocktail party, machine performance is still far inferior by comparison. We show that the cocktail party problem, or the speech separation problem, can be effectively approached via structured prediction. To account for temporal dynamics in speech, we employ conditional random fields (CRFs) to classify speech dominance within each time-frequency unit for a sound mixture. To capture complex, nonlinear relationship between input and output, both state and transition feature functions in CRFs are learned by deep neural networks. The formulation of the problem as classification allows us to directly optimize a measure that is well correlated with human speech intelligibility. The proposed system substantially outperforms existing ones in a variety of noises.

paragraphs: The cocktail party problem asks how to separate speech from a mixture of competing sounds. This paper treats separation as a structured classification task. It divides the mixture into time-frequency units and predicts speech dominance within each unit. The decisions are connected through a conditional random field, allowing the system to account for the temporal dynamics of speech.

Deep neural networks learn both the state and transition feature functions used by the conditional random field. The state functions help relate the input to individual classification decisions, while the transition functions support relationships between decisions over time. Learning both kinds of functions gives the structured model a way to represent complex, nonlinear relationships between the sound mixture and its desired output.

The classification formulation also allows direct optimization of a measure that correlates well with human speech intelligibility. That connects the learning objective to how understandable separated speech is, although correlation does not make the measure identical to intelligibility. The authors report substantial improvements over existing systems across a variety of noises, supporting the combination of learned nonlinear features and temporal structure.
summary.tldr: Deep neural networks and conditional random fields jointly predict speech dominance, improving separation across a variety of noises.

title: Cocktail Party Processing via Structured Prediction

abstract: The problem of estimation of entropy functionals of probability densities has received much attention in the information theory, machine learning and statistics communities. Kernel density plug-in estimators are simple, easy to implement and widely used for estimation of entropy. However, kernel plug-in estimators suffer from the curse of dimensionality, wherein the MSE rate of convergence is glacially slow - of order $O(T^{-{\gamma}/{d}})$, where $T$ is the number of samples, and $\gamma>0$ is a rate parameter. In this paper, it is shown that for sufficiently smooth densities, an ensemble of kernel plug-in estimators can be combined via a weighted convex combination, such that the resulting weighted estimator has a superior parametric MSE rate of convergence of order $O(T^{-1})$. Furthermore, it is shown that these optimal weights can be determined by solving a convex optimization problem which does not require training data or knowledge of the underlying density, and therefore can be performed offline. This novel result is remarkable in that, while each of the individual kernel plug-in estimators belonging to the ensemble suffer from the curse of dimensionality, by appropriate ensemble averaging we can achieve parametric convergence rates.

paragraphs: Estimating entropy from data often begins by estimating a probability density and plugging that estimate into an entropy calculation. Kernel-based versions are simple and widely used, but their mean squared error can decrease very slowly as dimensionality grows. The paper asks whether combining several such estimators can improve this unfavorable rate.

For sufficiently smooth densities, the authors show that an appropriately weighted convex combination achieves mean squared error of order O(T^-1), where T is the number of samples. This is a parametric convergence rate. The individual estimators still suffer from dimension-dependent rates; the improved guarantee belongs to their carefully constructed combination.

The weights can be obtained by solving a convex optimization problem that requires neither training data nor knowledge of the underlying density. Weight selection can therefore happen offline. The result shows that useful statistical improvements can arise from how estimators are combined, even when their individual rates are poor. The density-smoothness condition is part of the guarantee and remains essential to interpreting its scope.
summary.tldr: For sufficiently smooth densities, carefully weighted kernel entropy estimators achieve O(T^-1) mean squared error with weights computable offline.

title: Ensemble weighted kernel estimators for multivariate entropy estimation

abstract: We investigate the relationship between three fundamental problems in machine learning: binary classification, bipartite ranking, and binary class probability estimation (CPE). It is known that a good binary CPE model can be used to obtain a good binary classification model (by thresholding at 0.5), and also to obtain a good bipartite ranking model (by using the CPE model directly as a ranking model); it is also known that a binary classification model does not necessarily yield a CPE model. However, not much is known about other directions. Formally, these relationships involve regret transfer bounds. In this paper, we introduce the notion of weak regret transfer bounds, where the mapping needed to transform a model from one problem to another depends on the underlying probability distribution (and in practice, must be estimated from data). We then show that, in this weaker sense, a good bipartite ranking model can be used to construct a good classification model (by thresholding at a suitable point), and more surprisingly, also to construct a good binary CPE model (by calibrating the scores of the ranking model).

paragraphs: Binary classification predicts a class, bipartite ranking orders examples, and class probability estimation assigns probabilities to classes. Good probability estimates can support both classification and ranking, but the reverse relationships are less immediate. This paper studies how predictive quality can transfer among these problems using bounds on regret, or excess error.

The authors introduce weak regret transfer bounds. Here, the transformation from a model for one problem to a model for another may depend on the underlying data distribution. This qualification expands the possible connections, but it also means that the required transformation must be estimated from data in practical use.

Within this weaker framework, a good ranking model can produce a good classifier by selecting a suitable score threshold. It can also produce good class probability estimates by calibrating its scores. The latter result gives a stronger role to ranking quality: with an appropriate distribution-dependent conversion, useful ordering information can support probability estimation as well as discrete class decisions.
summary.tldr: Distribution-dependent regret bounds show how good rankings can be converted into good classifiers and calibrated probability estimates.

title: On the Relationship Between Binary Classification, Bipartite Ranking, and Binary Class Probability Estimation

abstract: We combine the ideas behind trees and Gaussian graphical models to form a new nonparametric family of graphical models. Our approach is to attach nonparanormal blossoms", with arbitrary graphs, to a collection of nonparametric trees. The tree edges are chosen to connect variables that most violate joint Gaussianity. The non-tree edges are partitioned into disjoint groups, and assigned to tree nodes using a nonparametric partial correlation statistic. A nonparanormal blossom is then "grown" for each group using established methods based on the graphical lasso. The result is a factorization with respect to the union of the tree branches and blossoms, defining a high-dimensional joint density that can be efficiently estimated and evaluated on test points. Theoretical properties and experiments with simulated and real data demonstrate the effectiveness of blossom trees."
originalAbstract: We combine the ideas behind trees and Gaussian graphical models to form a new nonparametric family of graphical models. The non-tree edges are partitioned into disjoint groups, and assigned to tree nodes using a nonparametric partial correlation statistic. A nonparanormal blossom is then "grown" for each group using established methods based on the graphical lasso. The result is a factorization with respect to the union of the tree branches and blossoms, defining a high-dimensional joint density that can be efficiently estimated and evaluated on test points. Theoretical properties and experiments with simulated and real data demonstrate the effectiveness of blossom trees."

paragraphs: This paper introduces a family of graphical models that combines nonparametric trees with more richly connected components called blossoms. The goal is to describe a high-dimensional joint distribution while retaining efficient estimation and evaluation. The construction brings together the flexibility of nonparametric tree relationships and methods associated with Gaussian graphical models.

Tree edges are selected to connect variables whose relationships most strongly violate joint Gaussianity. The remaining edges are divided into disjoint groups and assigned to tree nodes using a nonparametric partial-correlation statistic. Each group then becomes a nonparanormal blossom, with an arbitrary graph learned using established graphical-lasso methods.

The final distribution factorizes according to the combined tree branches and blossoms. This arrangement gives the model a way to represent relationships beyond a tree while preserving a structured joint density that can be efficiently estimated and evaluated at test points. The paper supplies theoretical properties and experiments on simulated and real data supporting the effectiveness of the construction. Its central contribution is this combination of complementary forms of dependency modeling.
summary.tldr: Blossom trees combine nonparametric tree relationships with richer graphical components to efficiently model high-dimensional distributions.

title: Blossom Tree Graphical Models

abstract: Solving real world problems with embedded neural networks requires both training algorithms that achieve high performance and compatible hardware that runs in real time while remaining energy efficient. For the former, deep learning using backpropagation has recently achieved a string of successes across many domains and datasets. For the latter, neuromorphic chips that run spiking neural networks have recently achieved unprecedented energy efficiency. To bring these two advances together, we must first resolve the incompatibility between backpropagation, which uses continuous-output neurons and synaptic weights, and neuromorphic designs, which employ spiking neurons and discrete synapses. Our approach is to treat spikes and discrete synapses as continuous probabilities, which allows training the network using standard backpropagation. The trained network naturally maps to neuromorphic hardware by sampling the probabilities to create one or more networks, which are merged using ensemble averaging. To demonstrate, we trained a sparsely connected network that runs on the TrueNorth chip using the MNIST dataset. With a high performance network (ensemble of $64$), we achieve $99.42\%$ accuracy at $121 \mu$J per image, and with a high efficiency network (ensemble of $1$) we achieve $92.7\%$ accuracy at $0.408 \mu$J per image.

paragraphs: This paper connects two capabilities that do not naturally fit together: training neural networks with backpropagation and running them on energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. Backpropagation works with continuous quantities, whereas the hardware uses spikes and discrete synapses. That mismatch makes it difficult to transfer a conventionally trained network directly into the hardware's operating format.

The authors represent spikes and discrete synapses through continuous probabilities during training. This makes standard backpropagation available without requiring the deployed network to use continuous outputs or weights. After training, they sample those probabilities to produce one or more hardware-compatible networks. When multiple networks are produced, ensemble averaging combines their outputs.

A sparsely connected network on the TrueNorth chip demonstrates the approach using MNIST. An ensemble of 64 reaches 99.42% accuracy while consuming 121 microjoules per image. A single-network configuration reaches 92.7% at 0.408 microjoules per image. These two reported configurations illustrate a practical accuracy–energy trade-off: the probabilistic training method supports both a higher-performing ensemble and a much lower-energy individual network.
summary.tldr: Training with continuous probabilities lets backpropagation produce spiking networks that trade accuracy against energy use on neuromorphic hardware.

title: Backpropagation for Energy-Efficient Neuromorphic Computing

abstract: We propose efficient algorithms for simultaneous clustering and completion of incomplete high-dimensional data that lie in a union of low-dimensional subspaces. We cast the problem as finding a completion of the data matrix so that each point can be reconstructed as a linear or affine combination of a few data points. Since the problem is NP-hard, we propose a lifting framework and reformulate the problem as a group-sparse recovery of each incomplete data point in a dictionary built using incomplete data, subject to rank-one constraints. To solve the problem efficiently, we propose a rank pursuit algorithm and a convex relaxation. The solution of our algorithms recover missing entries and provides a similarity matrix for clustering. Our algorithms can deal with both low-rank and high-rank matrices, does not suffer from initialization, does not need to know dimensions of subspaces and can work with a small number of data points. By extensive experiments on synthetic data and real problems of video motion segmentation and completion of motion capture data, we show that when the data matrix is low-rank, our algorithm performs on par with or better than low-rank matrix completion methods, while for high-rank data matrices, our method significantly outperforms existing algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper tackles missing-data recovery and clustering together for high-dimensional observations lying in a union of low-dimensional subspaces. Its organizing idea is self-expression: complete the data so each point can be reconstructed from a small number of other points using linear or affine combinations. This structure can remain useful even when the entire data matrix has high rank.

Because the resulting problem is NP-hard, the authors introduce a lifting framework that turns it into group-sparse recovery with rank-one constraints. They propose both a rank-pursuit algorithm and a convex relaxation. The resulting solutions fill in missing entries and produce a similarity matrix that can be used for clustering.

The methods handle low- and high-rank matrices without requiring subspace dimensions in advance, and the authors report freedom from initialization problems and applicability with few observations. Experiments include synthetic data, video motion segmentation, and motion-capture completion. Performance matches or exceeds low-rank completion methods when the matrix is low rank and substantially exceeds existing algorithms on the evaluated high-rank data.
summary.tldr: Self-expressive subspace structure enables joint matrix completion and clustering even when the overall data matrix has high rank.

title: High-Rank Matrix Completion and Clustering under Self-Expressive Models

abstract: Determinantal Point Processes (DPPs) are probabilistic models over all subsets a ground set of N items. They have recently gained prominence in several applications that rely on diverse subsets. However, their applicability to large problems is still limited due to O(N^3) complexity of core tasks such as sampling and learning. We enable efficient sampling and learning for DPPs by introducing KronDPP, a DPP model whose kernel matrix decomposes as a tensor product of multiple smaller kernel matrices. This decomposition immediately enables fast exact sampling. But contrary to what one may expect, leveraging the Kronecker product structure for speeding up DPP learning turns out to be more difficult. We overcome this challenge, and derive batch and stochastic optimization algorithms for efficiently learning the parameters of a KronDPP.

They have recently gained prominence in several applications that rely on diverse subsets. However, their applicability to large problems is still limited due to O(N^3) complexity of core tasks such as sampling and learning. We enable efficient sampling and learning for DPPs by introducing KronDPP, a DPP model whose kernel matrix decomposes as a tensor product of multiple smaller kernel matrices. This decomposition immediately enables fast exact sampling. But contrary to what one may expect, leveraging the Kronecker product structure for speeding up DPP learning turns out to be more difficult. We overcome this challenge, and derive batch and stochastic optimization algorithms for efficiently learning the parameters of a KronDPP.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes assign probabilities to subsets and are useful when those subsets should be diverse. Their computational cost limits their use on large collections: the abstract identifies cubic complexity in the number of items for core tasks such as sampling and learning. This paper addresses that obstacle through a structured model called KronDPP.

KronDPP requires its kernel matrix to decompose into a tensor product of smaller kernel matrices. That structure immediately permits fast exact sampling. Exactness matters here because the sampling improvement comes from the chosen representation, rather than replacing samples from the model with an approximation to its distribution.

Learning the kernel parameters presents a separate challenge. The authors emphasize that the same decomposition does not automatically make learning efficient, and they derive both batch and stochastic optimization algorithms to address it. The contribution thus covers two distinct needs: drawing subsets and fitting the structured model. Its computational benefits are tied to kernels represented by the proposed tensor-product decomposition.
summary.tldr: KronDPP uses tensor-product kernels to enable fast exact sampling and efficient batch and stochastic parameter learning.

title: Kronecker Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Intrinsic decomposition from a single image is a highly challenging task, due to its inherent ambiguity and the scarcity of training data. In contrast to traditional fully supervised learning approaches, in this paper we propose learning intrinsic image decomposition by explaining the input image. Our model, the Rendered Intrinsics Network (RIN), joins together an image decomposition pipeline, which predicts reflectance, shape, and lighting conditions given a single image, with a recombination function, a learned shading model used to recompose the original input based off of intrinsic image predictions. Our network can then use unsupervised reconstruction error as an additional signal to improve its intermediate representations. This allows large-scale unlabeled data to be useful during training, and also enables transferring learned knowledge to images of unseen object categories, lighting conditions, and shapes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method performs well on both intrinsic image decomposition and knowledge transfer.

Our network can then use unsupervised reconstruction error as an additional signal to improve its intermediate representations. This allows large-scale unlabeled data to be useful during training, and also enables transferring learned knowledge to images of unseen object categories, lighting conditions, and shapes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method performs well on both intrinsic image decomposition and knowledge transfer.

paragraphs: A single image combines surface reflectance, object shape, and illumination into one observation. Separating those factors is ambiguous, and labeled training examples are scarce. This paper proposes learning the decomposition partly by requiring its predicted factors to explain the image from which they were obtained.

The Rendered Intrinsics Network joins a decomposition pipeline with a learned shading model. The first part predicts reflectance, shape, and lighting from an image; the second recombines those predictions to reconstruct it. Differences between the reconstruction and the input provide an additional training signal for the intermediate representations, without requiring labels for that reconstruction objective.

This design allows large collections of unlabeled images to contribute during training. It also enables transfer to images involving previously unseen object categories, lighting conditions, and shapes. Experiments show good performance on both intrinsic decomposition and knowledge transfer. The central contribution is the connection between predicting hidden image factors and checking their combined explanation of the observed image, making reconstruction useful alongside the other training information.
summary.tldr: Rendered Intrinsics Networks improve image decomposition by reconstructing inputs from predicted reflectance, shape, and lighting.

title: Self-Supervised Intrinsic Image Decomposition

abstract: We use surrogate losses to obtain several new regret bounds and new algorithms for contextual bandit learning. Using the ramp loss, we derive a new margin-based regret bound in terms of standard sequential complexity measures of a benchmark class of real-valued regression functions. Using the hinge loss, we derive an efficient algorithm with a $\sqrt{dT}$-type mistake bound against benchmark policies induced by $d$-dimensional regressors. Under realizability assumptions, our results also yield classical regret bounds.
originalAbstract: We use surrogate losses to obtain several new regret bounds and new algorithms for contextual bandit learning. Using the ramp loss, we derive a new margin-based regret bound in terms of standard sequential complexity measures of a benchmark class of real-valued regression functions. Using the hinge loss, we derive an efficient algorithm with a $\sqrt{dT}$-type mistake bound against benchmark policies induced by $d$-dimensional regressors. Under realizability assumptions, our results also yield classical regret bounds.

paragraphs: This paper develops contextual bandit algorithms and performance guarantees using surrogate losses. A surrogate loss supplies an alternative mathematical objective through which learning can be analyzed. The results connect bandit performance to benchmark classes of real-valued regression functions, providing a way to express guarantees in terms of the predictors used to define decisions.

The authors obtain two different types of result from two losses. With ramp loss, they derive a margin-based regret bound involving standard sequential complexity measures of the benchmark class. With hinge loss, they construct an efficient algorithm whose mistake bound has square-root-of-dT scaling against policies induced by d-dimensional regressors, where T denotes the learning horizon.

These contributions connect the choice of surrogate objective to both theoretical guarantees and an efficient learning procedure. The paper also recovers classical regret bounds under realizability assumptions, which restrict the relationship between the learning problem and the model class. That qualification is part of the result: the classical guarantees are stated for the realizable setting.
summary.tldr: Ramp and hinge surrogate losses yield new contextual bandit guarantees, including an efficient algorithm with square-root-of-dT-type mistake bounds.

title: Contextual bandits with surrogate losses: Margin bounds and efficient algorithms

abstract: We introduce a method which enables a recurrent dynamics model to be temporally abstract. Our approach, which we call Adaptive Skip Intervals (ASI), is based on the observation that in many sequential prediction tasks, the exact time at which events occur is irrelevant to the underlying objective. Moreover, in many situations, there exist prediction intervals which result in particularly easy-to-predict transitions. We show that there are prediction tasks for which we gain both computational efficiency and prediction accuracy by allowing the model to make predictions at a sampling rate which it can choose itself.
originalAbstract: We introduce a method which enables a recurrent dynamics model to be temporally abstract. Our approach, which we call Adaptive Skip Intervals (ASI), is based on the observation that in many sequential prediction tasks, the exact time at which events occur is irrelevant to the underlying objective. Moreover, in many situations, there exist prediction intervals which result in particularly easy-to-predict transitions. We show that there are prediction tasks for which we gain both computational efficiency and prediction accuracy by allowing the model to make predictions at a sampling rate which it can choose itself.

paragraphs: A recurrent dynamics model predicts how a sequence evolves. This paper asks whether the model must always predict at a fixed sampling rate. Its starting observation is that the exact timing of events does not matter for the underlying objective in many sequential prediction tasks. When that is true, the model has room to choose which temporal transitions to predict.

The proposed method, Adaptive Skip Intervals, lets the model select its own prediction intervals. The motivation is that some intervals connect states through transitions that are especially easy to predict. Choosing the interval therefore changes the prediction problem itself, allowing the model to work at a temporal resolution suited to the task.

The authors show that there are prediction tasks where this freedom improves both computational efficiency and prediction accuracy. The finding is conditional on the task: it establishes the usefulness of adaptive timing in suitable settings. Its significance is that temporal abstraction can help a model make better predictions while also reducing the computation those predictions require.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Skip Intervals lets recurrent models choose prediction timing, improving efficiency and accuracy on suitable tasks.

title: Adaptive Skip Intervals: Temporal Abstraction for Recurrent Dynamical Models

abstract: Early stopping of iterative algorithms is an algorithmic regularization method to avoid over-fitting in estimation and classification. In this paper, we show that early stopping can also be applied to obtain the minimax optimal testing in a general non-parametric setup. Specifically, a Wald-type test statistic is obtained based on an iterated estimate produced by functional gradient descent algorithms in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. A notable contribution is to establish a ``sharp'' stopping rule: when the number of iterations achieves an optimal order, testing optimality is achievable; otherwise, testing optimality becomes impossible. As a by-product, a similar sharpness result is also derived for minimax optimal estimation under early stopping. All obtained results hold for various kernel classes, including Sobolev smoothness classes and Gaussian kernel classes.

paragraphs: Stopping an iterative learning algorithm before it fully fits the data is a familiar way to control overfitting. This paper studies early stopping for a different statistical goal: hypothesis testing in a general nonparametric setting. The question is whether the number of optimization steps can be chosen to obtain the best possible testing performance in a minimax sense.

The authors construct a Wald-type test from an estimate produced by functional gradient descent in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Their central result gives a sharp rule for when to stop. Testing optimality is achievable when the iteration count has the required optimal order, and becomes impossible when that order is not met within the analyzed setting.

The stopping time therefore plays a fundamental statistical role, beyond saving computation or serving as a practical heuristic. The paper also derives a related sharpness result for optimal estimation under early stopping. The analysis covers multiple kernel classes, including Sobolev smoothness and Gaussian kernels, showing that the relationship between iteration count and statistical optimality extends across these function classes.
summary.tldr: A sharp early-stopping rule makes minimax-optimal nonparametric testing achievable and identifies iteration orders where optimality is impossible.

title: Early Stopping for Nonparametric Testing

abstract: Subsampling is a common and often effective method to deal with the computational challenges of large datasets. However, for most statistical models, there is no well-motivated approach for drawing a non-uniform subsample. We show that the concept of an asymptotically linear estimator and the associated influence function leads to asymptotically optimal sampling probabilities for a wide class of popular models. This is the only tight optimality result for subsampling we are aware of as other methods only provide probabilistic error bounds or optimal rates. Furthermore, for linear regression models, which have well-studied procedures for non-uniform subsampling, we empirically show our optimal influence function based method outperforms previous approaches even when using approximations to the optimal probabilities.

paragraphs: Subsampling reduces the computational burden of fitting statistical models to large datasets. Choosing observations with unequal probabilities can be useful, but many models lack a principled rule for deciding which observations deserve greater sampling probability. This paper derives such a rule using the estimator's influence function, which describes how individual observations affect the estimate.

The derivation applies to asymptotically linear estimators and yields asymptotically optimal sampling probabilities for a broad class of popular models. The authors distinguish this tight optimality result from guarantees that provide only probabilistic error bounds or optimal rates. The strength of the claim is asymptotic and tied to the estimator framework they analyze.

For linear regression, the paper also compares the method empirically with existing nonuniform subsampling procedures. It reports better performance even when using approximations to the optimal probabilities. This connects the theoretical sampling rule to a practical implementation: useful gains can remain when the ideal sampling probabilities are not calculated exactly.
summary.tldr: Influence functions yield asymptotically optimal subsampling probabilities, with empirical improvements for linear regression even using approximate probabilities.

title: Optimal Subsampling with Influence Functions

abstract: Learning to make decisions from observed data in dynamic environments remains a problem of fundamental importance in a numbers of fields, from artificial intelligence and robotics, to medicine and finance. This paper concerns the problem of learning control policies for unknown linear dynamical systems so as to maximize a quadratic reward function. We present a method to optimize the expected value of the reward over the posterior distribution of the unknown system parameters, given data. The algorithm involves sequential convex programing, and enjoys reliable local convergence and robust stability guarantees. Numerical simulations and stabilization of a real-world inverted pendulum are used to demonstrate the approach, with strong performance and robustness properties observed in both.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a control policy for a linear dynamical system whose parameters are unknown. The controller aims to maximize a quadratic reward, so its decisions are evaluated through a particular mathematical measure of performance. Observed data provide information about the system, but uncertainty about its parameters remains part of the problem.

The proposed method optimizes reward averaged over the posterior distribution of those unknown parameters. In other words, the objective accounts for a distribution of possible systems supported by the data. The algorithm uses sequential convex programming, organizing the optimization as a sequence of convex programs, and has reliable local convergence and robust stability guarantees.

The authors demonstrate the approach in numerical simulations and by stabilizing a real inverted pendulum. Both settings show strong performance and robustness in their reported results. The combination matters because the method addresses uncertainty in the control objective while also supplying stability guarantees. Its convergence claim is local, and the demonstrations provide practical evidence for the approach in the systems that were studied.
summary.tldr: Sequential convex programming learns linear-quadratic controllers that account for parameter uncertainty and provide local convergence and robust stability guarantees.

title: Learning convex bounds for linear quadratic control policy synthesis

abstract: Synaptic plasticity is widely accepted to be the mechanism behind learning in the brain’s neural networks. A central question is how synapses, with access to only local information about the network, can still organize collectively and perform circuit-wide learning in an efficient manner. In single-layered and all-to-all connected neural networks, local plasticity has been shown to implement gradient-based learning on a class of cost functions that contain a term that aligns the similarity of outputs to the similarity of inputs. Whether such cost functions exist for networks with other architectures is not known. In this paper, we introduce structured and deep similarity matching cost functions, and show how they can be optimized in a gradient-based manner by neural networks with local learning rules. These networks extend F\"oldiak’s Hebbian/Anti-Hebbian network to deep architectures and structured feedforward, lateral and feedback connections. Credit assignment problem is solved elegantly by a factorization of the dual learning objective to synapse specific local objectives. Simulations show that our networks learn meaningful features.

paragraphs: A central question in neural learning is how synapses using only local information can collectively optimize a network-wide objective. Previous results connected local plasticity with similarity matching in single-layer, fully connected networks. Similarity matching encourages relationships between outputs to reflect relationships between inputs, giving local updates a shared learning goal.

This paper introduces similarity-matching objectives for structured and deep networks and shows how local learning rules can optimize them through gradient-based learning. The resulting networks extend a Hebbian/anti-Hebbian architecture to multiple layers and structured feedforward, lateral, and feedback connections. This expands the architectures for which an explicit objective can be connected to local synaptic changes.

The key credit-assignment mechanism factors a dual learning objective into separate objectives associated with individual synapses. That factorization explains how local updates contribute to the broader optimization problem. Simulations show that the networks learn meaningful features. Together, the mathematical construction and simulations support the feasibility of objective-driven learning with local rules in the proposed structured and deep architectures.
summary.tldr: Structured similarity-matching objectives enable deep networks to learn meaningful features through local Hebbian and anti-Hebbian updates.

title: Structured and Deep Similarity Matching via Structured and Deep Hebbian Networks

abstract: We present a neural program synthesis approach integrating components which write, execute, and assess code to navigate the search space of possible programs. We equip the search process with an interpreter or a read-eval-print-loop (REPL), which immediately executes partially written programs, exposing their semantics. The REPL addresses a basic challenge of program synthesis: tiny changes in syntax can lead to huge changes in semantics. We train a pair of models, a policy that proposes the new piece of code to write, and a value function that assesses the prospects of the code written so-far. At test time we can combine these models with a Sequential Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply our approach to two domains: synthesizing text editing programs and inferring 2D and 3D graphics programs.

paragraphs: Program synthesis searches for code that performs a desired task. A central difficulty is that small changes in program text can cause large changes in behavior. This paper makes execution part of the search process, using an interpreter or read-eval-print loop to expose what partially written programs actually do.

The approach trains two models with complementary roles. A policy proposes the next piece of code, while a value function assesses the prospects of the partial program. Immediate execution gives the process access to program semantics as construction proceeds. At test time, the two models can be combined with a Sequential Monte Carlo search algorithm.

The authors apply the approach to synthesizing text-editing programs and inferring programs for two-dimensional and three-dimensional graphics. These applications demonstrate the proposed integration across distinct program domains. The core contribution is an architecture that connects writing, running, and assessing partial code, making intermediate behavior available to guide further search rather than relying solely on the appearance of the code written so far.
summary.tldr: A neural synthesis system executes partial programs and combines code proposals with value assessments to guide program search.

title: Write, Execute, Assess: Program Synthesis with a REPL

abstract: Recently, a spate of papers have provided positive theoretical results for training over-parameterized neural networks (where the network size is larger than what is needed to achieve low error). The key insight is that with sufficient over-parameterization, gradient-based methods will implicitly leave some components of the network relatively unchanged, so the optimization dynamics will behave as if those components are essentially fixed at their initial random values. In fact, fixing these \emph{explicitly} leads to the well-known approach of learning with random features (e.g. \citep{rahimi2008random,rahimi2009weighted}). In other words, these techniques imply that we can successfully learn with neural networks, whenever we can successfully learn with random features. In this paper, we formalize the link between existing results and random features, and argue that despite the impressive positive results, random feature approaches are also inherently limited in what they can explain. In particular, we prove that random features cannot be used to learn \emph{even a single ReLU neuron} (over standard Gaussian inputs in $\reals^d$ and $\text{poly}(d)$ weights), unless the network size (or magnitude of its weights) is exponentially large in $d$. Since a single neuron \emph{is} known to be learnable with gradient-based methods, we conclude that we are still far from a satisfying general explanation for the empirical success of neural networks. For completeness we also provide a simple self-contained proof, using a random features technique, that one-hidden-layer neural networks can learn low-degree polynomials.

paragraphs: Some guarantees for training oversized neural networks rely on parts of the network staying close to their random initialization. Random features explain some successful learning behavior, while the stated lower bound identifies behavior that calls for a broader explanation.
summary.tldr: Random features explain some neural-network guarantees but face exponential requirements for learning even one ReLU neuron in the studied setting.

title: On the Power and Limitations of Random Features for Understanding Neural Networks

abstract: Bayesian optimization has recently emerged as a popular method for the sample-efficient optimization of expensive black-box functions. However, the application to high-dimensional problems with several thousand observations remains challenging, and on difficult problems Bayesian optimization is often not competitive with other paradigms. In this paper we take the view that this is due to the implicit homogeneity of the global probabilistic models and an overemphasized exploration that results from global acquisition. This motivates the design of a local probabilistic approach for global optimization of large-scale high-dimensional problems. We propose the TuRBO algorithm that fits a collection of local models and performs a principled global allocation of samples across these models via an implicit bandit approach. A comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that TuRBO outperforms state-of-the-art methods from machine learning and operations research on problems spanning reinforcement learning, robotics, and the natural sciences.

paragraphs: The paper addresses expensive black-box optimization in high dimensions and with thousands of observations, where Bayesian optimization can struggle. The authors argue that global probabilistic models implicitly impose too much homogeneity and that global acquisition can overemphasize exploration. This diagnosis motivates a method built around local models.

TuRBO fits a collection of local probabilistic models while coordinating the overall search. An implicit bandit approach allocates samples across those models, providing a principled way to decide where evaluations should go. The method thus combines local descriptions of the objective with a global decision about distributing the evaluation effort.

A comprehensive evaluation shows TuRBO outperforming state-of-the-art methods from machine learning and operations research on problems in reinforcement learning, robotics, and natural sciences. These findings support the use of locally modeled regions for difficult large-scale optimization. The central idea is that pursuing a global optimization objective need not require one global probabilistic description: several local models can contribute through coordinated sampling.
summary.tldr: TuRBO coordinates multiple local probabilistic models to improve large-scale, high-dimensional black-box optimization.

title: Scalable Global Optimization via Local Bayesian Optimization

abstract: In this paper, we give a faster width-dependent algorithm for mixed packing-covering LPs. Mixed packing-covering LPs are fundamental to combinatorial optimization in computer science and operations research. Our algorithm finds a $1+\eps$ approximate solution in time $O(Nw/ \varepsilon)$, where $N$ is number of nonzero entries in the constraint matrix, and $w$ is the maximum number of nonzeros in any constraint. This algorithm is faster than Nesterov's smoothing algorithm which requires $O(N\sqrt{n}w/ \eps)$ time, where $n$ is the dimension of the problem. Our work utilizes the framework of area convexity introduced in [Sherman-FOCS'17] to obtain the best dependence on $\varepsilon$ while breaking the infamous $\ell_{\infty}$ barrier to eliminate the factor of $\sqrt{n}$. The current best width-independent algorithm for this problem runs in time $O(N/\eps^2)$ [Young-arXiv-14] and hence has worse running time dependence on $\varepsilon$. Many real life instances of mixed packing-covering problems exhibit small width and for such cases, our algorithm can report higher precision results when compared to width-independent algorithms. As a special case of our result, we report a $1+\varepsilon$ approximation algorithm for the densest subgraph problem which runs in time $O(md/ \varepsilon)$, where $m$ is the number of edges in the graph and $d$ is the maximum graph degree.
