summary.tldr: An area-convexity algorithm improves precision dependence for mixed packing-covering linear programs, with particular benefits when constraints have small width.

title: Faster width-dependent algorithm for mixed packing and covering LPs

abstract: We consider a novel stochastic multi-armed bandit setting, where playing an arm makes it unavailable for a fixed number of time slots thereafter. This models situations where reusing an arm too often is undesirable (e.g. making the same product recommendation repeatedly) or infeasible (e.g. compute job scheduling on machines). We show that with prior knowledge of the rewards and delays of all the arms, the problem of optimizing cumulative reward does not admit any pseudo-polynomial time algorithm (in the number of arms) unless randomized exponential time hypothesis is false, by mapping to the PINWHEEL scheduling problem. Subsequently, we show that a simple greedy algorithm that plays the available arm with the highest reward is asymptotically $(1-1/e)$ optimal. When the rewards are unknown, we design a UCB based algorithm which is shown to have $c \log T + o(\log T)$ cumulative regret against the greedy algorithm, leveraging the free exploration of arms due to the unavailability. Finally, when all the delays are equal the problem reduces to Combinatorial Semi-bandits providing us with a lower bound of $c' \log T+ \omega(\log T)$.

paragraphs: In this bandit problem, choosing an option temporarily makes it unavailable. Such delays can represent a recommendation that should not be repeated immediately or a machine occupied by a job. The learner must therefore consider both an option’s reward and how using it changes the choices available over subsequent time steps.

Even with known rewards and delays, optimizing total reward is computationally difficult. Through a connection to PINWHEEL scheduling, the authors rule out a pseudo-polynomial algorithm in the number of arms unless the randomized exponential time hypothesis fails. They nevertheless show that choosing the available arm with the highest reward achieves an asymptotic 1−1/e approximation.

For unknown rewards, the paper develops an algorithm based on upper confidence bounds, with regret c log T plus lower-order terms relative to that greedy policy. Temporary unavailability helps exploration by creating opportunities to try other arms. When all delays are equal, a reduction to combinatorial semi-bandits supplies a lower bound, giving additional perspective on the difficulty of learning in this setting.
summary.tldr: Blocking bandits model choices with reuse delays and admit an asymptotically approximate greedy policy plus a learning algorithm with logarithmic leading-order regret against it.

title: Blocking Bandits

abstract: SLOPE is a relatively new convex optimization procedure for high-dimensional linear regression via the sorted $\ell_1$ penalty: the larger the rank of the fitted coefficient, the larger the penalty. This non-separable penalty renders many existing techniques invalid or inconclusive in analyzing the SLOPE solution. In this paper, we develop an asymptotically exact characterization of the SLOPE solution under Gaussian random designs through solving the SLOPE problem using approximate message passing (AMP). This algorithmic approach allows us to approximate the SLOPE solution via the much more amenable AMP iterates. Explicitly, we characterize the asymptotic dynamics of the AMP iterates relying on a recently developed state evolution analysis for non-separable penalties, thereby overcoming the difficulty caused by the sorted $\ell_1$ penalty. Moreover, we prove that the AMP iterates converge to the SLOPE solution in an asymptotic sense, and numerical simulations show that the convergence is surprisingly fast. Our proof rests on a novel technique that specifically leverages the SLOPE problem. In contrast to prior literature, our work not only yields an asymptotically sharp analysis but also offers an algorithmic, flexible, and constructive approach to understanding the SLOPE problem.

paragraphs: SLOPE is a method for high-dimensional linear regression that penalizes fitted coefficients according to their ordering. This sorting couples the coefficients: the penalty on one coefficient depends on where it sits relative to others. That makes the solution difficult to analyze with techniques that treat coefficients separately, even though the optimization problem is convex.

The paper develops an approximate message passing algorithm, or AMP, whose successive estimates provide a more tractable route to understanding SLOPE. It uses state evolution for non-separable penalties to characterize how these estimates behave asymptotically. Under Gaussian random designs, this produces an asymptotically exact description of the SLOPE solution.

The authors also prove that AMP converges to the SLOPE solution in an asymptotic sense, using a proof technique tailored to this problem. Simulations show fast convergence. The contribution therefore combines a sharp theoretical characterization with a constructive algorithm for approximating the solution, while keeping the Gaussian-design and asymptotic qualifications central to its guarantees.
summary.tldr: Approximate message passing gives an asymptotically exact, constructive characterization of SLOPE regression under Gaussian random designs.

title: Algorithmic Analysis and Statistical Estimation of SLOPE via Approximate Message Passing

abstract: A fundamental result in differential privacy states that the privacy guarantees of a mechanism are preserved by any post-processing of its output. In this paper we investigate under what conditions stochastic post-processing can amplify the privacy of a mechanism. By interpreting post-processing as the application of a Markov operator, we first give a series of amplification results in terms of uniform mixing properties of the Markov process defined by said operator. Next we provide amplification bounds in terms of coupling arguments which can be applied in cases where uniform mixing is not available. Finally, we introduce a new family of mechanisms based on diffusion processes which are closed under post-processing, and analyze their privacy via a novel heat flow argument. On the applied side, we generalize the analysis of "privacy amplification by iteration" in Noisy SGD and show it admits an exponential improvement in the strongly convex case, and study a mechanism based on the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck diffusion process which contains the Gaussian mechanism with optimal post-processing on bounded inputs as a special case.

By interpreting post-processing as the application of a Markov operator, we first give a series of amplification results in terms of uniform mixing properties of the Markov process defined by said operator. Next we provide amplification bounds in terms of coupling arguments which can be applied in cases where uniform mixing is not available. Finally, we introduce a new family of mechanisms based on diffusion processes which are closed under post-processing, and analyze their privacy via a novel heat flow argument. On the applied side, we generalize the analysis of "privacy amplification by iteration" in Noisy SGD and show it admits an exponential improvement in the strongly convex case, and study a mechanism based on the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck diffusion process which contains the Gaussian mechanism with optimal post-processing on bounded inputs as a special case.

paragraphs: Differential privacy guarantees survive any post-processing of a mechanism's output. This paper asks a stronger question: under what conditions can randomized post-processing improve those guarantees? It represents post-processing as a Markov operator, connecting privacy amplification to the behavior of an associated stochastic process.

The authors first derive amplification results using uniform mixing properties. They then develop coupling-based bounds for cases where uniform mixing is unavailable. A further contribution is a family of diffusion-based mechanisms that remains closed under post-processing, with privacy analyzed through a heat-flow argument. These approaches provide different routes to establishing when amplification occurs.

For applications, the paper generalizes privacy-amplification-by-iteration analysis for Noisy SGD and obtains an exponential improvement in the strongly convex case. It also studies an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck diffusion mechanism containing the Gaussian mechanism with optimal post-processing on bounded inputs as a special case. The results make amplification conditional on mathematical properties of the process and problem, rather than claiming that every randomized transformation strengthens privacy.
summary.tldr: Mixing, coupling, and diffusion analysis establish conditions under which randomized post-processing strengthens differential privacy.

title: Privacy Amplification by Mixing and Diffusion Mechanisms

abstract: Deep Neural Network (DNN) is powerful but computationally expensive and memory intensive, thus impeding its practical usage on resource-constrained front-end devices. DNN pruning is an approach for deep model compression, which aims at eliminating some parameters with tolerable performance degradation. In this paper, we propose a novel momentum-SGD-based optimization method to reduce the network complexity by on-the-fly pruning. Concretely, given a global compression ratio, we categorize all the parameters into two parts at each training iteration which are updated using different rules. In this way, we gradually zero out the redundant parameters, as we update them using only the ordinary weight decay but no gradients derived from the objective function. As a departure from prior methods that require heavy human works to tune the layer-wise sparsity ratios, prune by solving complicated non-differentiable problems or finetune the model after pruning, our method is characterized by 1) global compression that automatically finds the appropriate per-layer sparsity ratios; 2) end-to-end training; 3) no need for a time-consuming re-training process after pruning; and 4) superior capability to find better winning tickets which have won the initialization lottery.

DNN pruning is an approach for deep model compression, which aims at eliminating some parameters with tolerable performance degradation. In this paper, we propose a novel momentum-SGD-based optimization method to reduce the network complexity by on-the-fly pruning. Concretely, given a global compression ratio, we categorize all the parameters into two parts at each training iteration which are updated using different rules. In this way, we gradually zero out the redundant parameters, as we update them using only the ordinary weight decay but no gradients derived from the objective function. This paper proposes a momentum-SGD-based method that performs pruning during training, using a compression target for the network as a whole.

At each training iteration, the method divides parameters into two groups and applies different update rules. Parameters treated as redundant receive ordinary weight decay without gradients from the task objective, gradually driving them toward zero. The global compression target allows the method to determine how sparsity is distributed across layers automatically.

The authors describe an end-to-end procedure that avoids manually tuning each layer's sparsity and does not require a separate, time-consuming retraining stage after pruning. They also report a stronger ability to find winning tickets: sparse subnetworks associated with favorable initialization. The contribution brings parameter removal into the optimization process itself, reducing the separate decisions and training stages needed for compression.
summary.tldr: A momentum-SGD pruning method meets a global compression target during training by applying weight decay alone to redundant parameters.

title: Global Sparse Momentum SGD for Pruning Very Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Semantic cues and statistical regularities in real-world environment layouts can improve efficiency for navigation in novel environments. This paper learns and leverages such semantic cues for navigating to objects of interest in novel environments, by simply watching YouTube videos. This is challenging because YouTube videos don't come with labels for actions or goals, and may not even showcase optimal behavior. Our method tackles these challenges through the use of Q-learning on pseudo-labeled transition quadruples (image, action, next image, reward). We show that such off-policy Q-learning from passive data is able to learn meaningful semantic cues for navigation. These cues, when used in a hierarchical navigation policy, lead to improved efficiency at the ObjectGoal task in visually realistic simulations. We observe a relative improvement of 15-83% over end-to-end RL, behavior cloning, and classical methods, while using minimal direct interaction.

Such videos present a difficult learning source because they lack action and goal labels, and the behavior they show may be suboptimal.

The method creates pseudo-labeled transitions containing an image, an action, a following image, and a reward. It then applies off-policy Q-learning to these transitions. The authors show that this passive data can provide meaningful semantic cues for navigation. summary.tldr: Q-learning from pseudo-labeled YouTube video transitions supplies semantic cues that improve simulated object navigation with minimal direct interaction.

title: Semantic Visual Navigation by Watching YouTube Videos

abstract: Generalized linear models are one of the most efficient paradigms for predicting the correlated stochastic activity of neuronal networks in response to external stimuli, with applications in many brain areas. However, when dealing with complex stimuli, the inferred coupling parameters often do not generalise across different stimulus statistics, leading to degraded performance and blowup instabilities. Here, we develop a two-step inference strategy that allows us to train robust generalised linear models of interacting neurons, by explicitly separating the effects of correlations in the stimulus from network interactions in each training step. Applying this approach to the responses of retinal ganglion cells to complex visual stimuli, we show that, compared to classical methods, the models trained in this way exhibit improved performance, are more stable, yield robust interaction networks, and generalise well across complex visual statistics. The method can be extended to deep convolutional neural networks, leading to models with high predictive accuracy for both the neuron firing rates and their correlations.

Generalized linear models can predict this activity, but fitting these influences together can produce interaction parameters that fail when stimulus statistics change. The abstract identifies degraded predictions and unstable activity as consequences of this problem.

The paper develops a two-step inference procedure that explicitly separates stimulus correlations from network interactions during training. This separation matters because an inferred connection should not simply absorb statistical patterns belonging to the input. The approach aims to make the learned interaction network more robust across different kinds of stimulation.

Applied to retinal ganglion cell responses to complex visual inputs, the procedure improves predictions and stability relative to classical methods, while yielding more robust interactions and generalizing across visual statistics. The authors also extend it to deep convolutional networks, reporting high predictive accuracy for both individual firing rates and correlations between neurons.
summary.tldr: Separating stimulus correlations from neural interactions during training improves the accuracy, stability, and transfer of models of neuronal activity.

title: A new inference approach for training shallow and deep generalized linear models of noisy interacting neurons

abstract: Normalizing flows are deep generative models that allow efficient likelihood calculation and sampling. The core requirement for this advantage is that they are constructed using functions that can be efficiently inverted and for which the determinant of the function's Jacobian can be efficiently computed. Researchers have introduced various such flow operations, but few of these allow rich interactions among variables without incurring significant computational costs. In this paper, we introduce Woodbury transformations, which achieve efficient invertibility via the Woodbury matrix identity and efficient determinant calculation via Sylvester's determinant identity. In contrast with other operations used in state-of-the-art normalizing flows, Woodbury transformations enable (1) high-dimensional interactions, (2) efficient sampling, and (3) efficient likelihood evaluation. Other similar operations, such as 1x1 convolutions, emerging convolutions, or periodic convolutions allow at most two of these three advantages. In our experiments on multiple image datasets, we find that Woodbury transformations allow learning of higher-likelihood models than other flow architectures while still enjoying their efficiency advantages.

Designing those transformations creates a tension: allowing many variables to interact can make inversion or determinant calculation expensive. This paper introduces Woodbury transformations to address that computational bottleneck.

The construction uses the Woodbury matrix identity for efficient inversion and Sylvester's determinant identity for efficient determinant calculation. The authors contrast this combination with operations such as 1×1, emerging, and periodic convolutions, which provide at most two of those three advantages.

The stated result concerns likelihood and computation in those evaluations. The broader contribution is a flow operation that makes richer interaction among variables computationally practical, expanding the kinds of transformations that can be used without giving up the core computational benefits of normalizing flows.
summary.tldr: Woodbury transformations give normalizing flows high-dimensional variable interactions alongside efficient sampling and likelihood evaluation.

title: Woodbury Transformations for Deep Generative Flows

abstract: One of the key reasons for the high sample complexity in reinforcement learning (RL) is the inability to transfer knowledge from one task to another. In standard multi-task RL settings, low-reward data collected while trying to solve one task provides little to no signal for solving that particular task and is hence effectively wasted. However, we argue that this data, which is uninformative for one task, is likely a rich source of information for other tasks. To leverage this insight and efficiently reuse data, we present Generalized Hindsight: an approximate inverse reinforcement learning technique for relabeling behaviors with the right tasks. Intuitively, given a behavior generated under one task, Generalized Hindsight returns a different task that the behavior is better suited for. Then, the behavior is relabeled with this new task before being used by an off-policy RL optimizer. Compared to standard relabeling techniques, Generalized Hindsight provides a substantially more efficient re-use of samples, which we empirically demonstrate on a suite of multi-task navigation and manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: An agent’s attempt at one task may earn little reward yet contain useful experience for another. In standard multi-task reinforcement learning, that experience can provide little learning signal when interpreted only through the original task. This paper proposes recovering more of its value by reconsidering which task a recorded behavior is suited to.

Generalized Hindsight uses approximate inverse reinforcement learning to make that reassignment. Given behavior collected while pursuing one task, it identifies another task for which that behavior is better suited. The recorded behavior is then relabeled with the new task and passed to an off-policy reinforcement-learning optimizer. The central change is therefore how existing experience is interpreted and reused across tasks.

The authors compare this approach with standard relabeling techniques on a suite of navigation and manipulation tasks. They report substantially more efficient sample reuse in those experiments. The findings support treating low-reward experience as potentially useful evidence for other objectives, with task selection providing a mechanism for turning that potential into a stronger training signal.
summary.tldr: Generalized Hindsight relabels recorded behaviors with better-suited tasks to improve sample reuse in multi-task reinforcement learning.

title: Generalized Hindsight for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider a matrix completion problem that exploits social or item similarity graphs as side information. We develop a universal, parameter-free, and computationally efficient algorithm that starts with hierarchical graph clustering and then iteratively refines estimates both on graph clustering and matrix ratings. Under a hierarchical stochastic block model that well respects practically-relevant social graphs and a low-rank rating matrix model (to be detailed), we demonstrate that our algorithm achieves the information-theoretic limit on the number of observed matrix entries (i.e., optimal sample complexity) that is derived by maximum likelihood estimation together with a lower-bound impossibility result. One consequence of this result is that exploiting the hierarchical structure of social graphs yields a substantial gain in sample complexity relative to the one that simply identifies different groups without resorting to the relational structure across them. We conduct extensive experiments both on synthetic and real-world datasets to corroborate our theoretical results as well as to demonstrate significant performance improvements over other matrix completion algorithms that leverage graph side information.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries using the entries already observed. This paper supplements those observations with graphs describing social relationships or item similarity. Its central idea is to exploit a graph's hierarchy, including relationships between groups, rather than using only a flat division into separate communities.

The authors propose a parameter-free, computationally efficient algorithm that begins with hierarchical graph clustering. It then repeatedly improves both the graph clustering and the estimated matrix ratings. This alternating refinement allows the two sources of information to support one another as the estimates develop.

Under a hierarchical stochastic block model for the graph and a specified low-rank rating model, the algorithm reaches the information-theoretic limit on the required number of observed entries. The authors establish that limit through maximum-likelihood analysis and an impossibility lower bound. Their result shows that using relationships across groups can substantially reduce sample requirements compared with identifying groups alone. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support the theory and report significant gains over other graph-assisted matrix completion methods.
summary.tldr: An iterative matrix-completion algorithm exploits hierarchical graph relationships to achieve optimal sample complexity under the paper's graph and rating models.

title: Matrix Completion with Hierarchical Graph Side Information

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have been attracting increasing popularity due to their simplicity and effectiveness in a variety of fields. However, a large number of labeled data is generally required to train these networks, which could be very expensive to obtain in some domains. In this paper, we study active learning for GNNs, i.e., how to efficiently label the nodes on a graph to reduce the annotation cost of training GNNs. We formulate the problem as a sequential decision process on graphs and train a GNN-based policy network with reinforcement learning to learn the optimal query strategy. By jointly training on several source graphs with full labels, we learn a transferable active learning policy which can directly generalize to unlabeled target graphs. Experimental results on multiple datasets from different domains prove the effectiveness of the learned policy in promoting active learning performance in both settings of transferring between graphs in the same domain and across different domains.

paragraphs: Training graph neural networks can require many labeled nodes, and obtaining those labels can be expensive. Active learning addresses this cost by choosing which nodes to label. This paper studies how to learn that selection strategy so it can be reused on new graphs rather than devised separately for each graph.

The authors formulate node selection as a sequence of decisions on a graph. A graph neural network serves as the policy, and reinforcement learning trains it to choose label queries. Training jointly on several fully labeled source graphs provides experience from which the policy can learn a transferable query strategy.

The learned policy is then applied directly to unlabeled target graphs. Experiments across multiple datasets show improvements in active learning both when transferring within a domain and when transferring across domains. The result supports transferring knowledge about which labels to request, alongside the usual goal of transferring predictive representations. Full labels on the source graphs are part of the training setup; the intended savings concern annotation choices on the target graphs.
summary.tldr: A graph-based reinforcement learning policy learns node-label query strategies on source graphs and transfers them to unlabeled target graphs.

title: Graph Policy Network for Transferable Active Learning on Graphs

abstract: We prove dimension free representation results for neural networks with D ReLU layers under square loss for a class of functions G_D defined in the paper. These results capture the precise benefits of depth in the following sense: 1. The rates for representing the class of functions G_D via D ReLU layers is sharp up to constants, as shown by matching lower bounds. 2.G_D is a proper subset of G_{D+1} and as D grows the class of functions G_D grow to contain less smooth functions. 3. If D^{\prime} < D, then the approximation rate achieved by depth D^{\prime} networks is strictly worse than that achieved by depth D networks for the class G_D. This constitutes a fine-grained characterization of the representation power of feedforward networks of arbitrary depth D and number of neurons N, in contrast to existing representation results which either require D growing quickly with N or assume that the function being represented is highly smooth. In the latter case similar rates can be obtained with a single nonlinear layer. Our results confirm the prevailing hypothesis that deeper networks are better at representing less smooth functions, and indeed, the main technical novelty is to fully exploit the fact that deep networks can produce highly oscillatory functions with few activation functions.

It develops dimension-free representation results under squared loss for a depth-indexed family of function classes, G_D. The analysis tracks both depth and neuron count, making the benefits of additional layers explicit.

Each class G_D is strictly contained in the next class, and increasing depth brings less smooth functions into the family. Moreover, using fewer than D layers gives a strictly worse approximation rate on G_D.

The technical insight is to exploit deep networks' ability to produce highly oscillatory functions using few activation functions. This supports the hypothesis that depth helps represent less smooth functions, with a graded result across depths rather than a single shallow-versus-deep comparison. The guarantees concern the function classes defined in the paper and their squared-loss approximation rates, providing a precise account of representational benefits within that setting.
summary.tldr: Sharp approximation bounds show how additional ReLU layers improve representation of increasingly less smooth function classes.

title: Sharp Representation Theorems for ReLU Networks with Precise Dependence on Depth

abstract: Classical learning theory suggests that the optimal generalization performance of a machine learning model should occur at an intermediate model complexity, with simpler models exhibiting high bias and more complex models exhibiting high variance of the predictive function. However, such a simple trade-off does not adequately describe deep learning models that simultaneously attain low bias and variance in the heavily overparameterized regime. A primary obstacle in explaining this behavior is that deep learning algorithms typically involve multiple sources of randomness whose individual contributions are not visible in the total variance. To enable fine-grained analysis, we describe an interpretable, symmetric decomposition of the variance into terms associated with the randomness from sampling, initialization, and the labels. Moreover, we compute the high-dimensional asymptotic behavior of this decomposition for random feature kernel regression, and analyze the strikingly rich phenomenology that arises. We find that the bias decreases monotonically with the network width, but the variance terms exhibit non-monotonic behavior and can diverge at the interpolation boundary, even in the absence of label noise. The divergence is caused by the interaction between sampling and initialization and can therefore be eliminated by marginalizing over samples (i.e. bagging) or over the initial parameters (i.e. ensemble learning).

paragraphs: A simple bias-variance story suggests that increasing model complexity eventually harms generalization by increasing variance. Heavily overparameterized models can instead have both low bias and low variance. This paper argues that understanding such behavior requires separating the different sources of randomness hidden inside total prediction variance.

The authors introduce a symmetric, interpretable decomposition involving randomness from data sampling, initialization, and labels. They calculate its high-dimensional asymptotic behavior for random feature kernel regression. In that analysis, bias decreases monotonically as network width increases, while variance components behave non-monotonically and can diverge at the interpolation boundary, where fitting the training data becomes possible.

Crucially, that divergence can occur without label noise. The analysis attributes it to an interaction between sampling and initialization, identifying a mechanism that a single total-variance number obscures. Marginalizing over samples through bagging or over initial parameters through ensemble learning can eliminate this divergence in the analyzed setting. The result explains why averaging over a particular source of randomness can address a specific source of instability.
summary.tldr: A detailed variance decomposition traces interpolation instability in random feature regression to interactions between data sampling and initialization.

title: Understanding Double Descent Requires A Fine-Grained Bias-Variance Decomposition

abstract: We introduce JAX MD, a software package for performing differentiable physics simulations with a focus on molecular dynamics. JAX MD includes a number of statistical physics simulation environments as well as interaction potentials and neural networks that can be integrated into these environments without writing any additional code. Since the simulations themselves are differentiable functions, entire trajectories can be differentiated to perform meta-optimization. These features are built on primitive operations, such as spatial partitioning, that allow simulations to scale to hundreds-of-thousands of particles on a single GPU. These primitives are flexible enough that they can be used to scale up workloads outside of molecular dynamics. We present several examples that highlight the features of JAX MD including: integration of graph neural networks into traditional simulations, meta-optimization through minimization of particle packings, and a multi-agent flocking simulation. JAX MD is available at www.github.com/google/jax-md.

This lets users compute derivatives through an entire simulated trajectory and use them for meta-optimization, connecting the behavior produced by a simulation to an optimization process.

The contribution is a reusable framework that brings differentiability, simulation components, and scaling operations together.
summary.tldr: JAX MD combines scalable physics simulation with differentiable trajectories and integrated neural components to support simulation-based meta-optimization.

title: JAX MD: A Framework for Differentiable Physics

abstract: Pruning neural network parameters is often viewed as a means to compress models, but pruning has also been motivated by the desire to prevent overfitting. This motivation is particularly relevant given the perhaps surprising observation that a wide variety of pruning approaches increase test accuracy despite sometimes massive reductions in parameter counts. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyze the behavior of pruning over the course of training, finding that pruning's benefit to generalization increases with pruning's instability (defined as the drop in test accuracy immediately following pruning). We demonstrate that this "generalization-stability tradeoff'' is present across a wide variety of pruning settings and propose a mechanism for its cause: pruning regularizes similarly to noise injection. Supporting this, we find less pruning stability leads to more model flatness and the benefits of pruning do not depend on permanent parameter removal. These results explain the compatibility of pruning-based generalization improvements and the high generalization recently observed in overparameterized networks.

paragraphs: Pruning removes neural network parameters, but it can also improve test accuracy despite greatly reducing model size. This paper investigates that improvement by studying pruning during training. It defines pruning instability as the immediate drop in test accuracy caused by a pruning step, separating that short-term disruption from later generalization benefits.

Across a wide variety of pruning settings, the authors find that greater instability accompanies larger improvements in generalization. They propose that pruning acts similarly to noise injection, regularizing the training process through the disturbance it creates. Supporting evidence includes an association between lower pruning stability and flatter models, along with benefits that do not require permanent parameter removal.

The findings provide an explanation for why pruning can improve generalization even though highly overparameterized networks can also generalize well. On the proposed account, the training disturbance matters alongside any reduction in model size. This is an empirically supported mechanism across the studied settings, rather than a claim that every larger accuracy drop will necessarily produce a better final model.
summary.tldr: Across studied settings, more disruptive pruning brings larger generalization gains, supporting a noise-like regularization explanation.

title: The Generalization-Stability Tradeoff In Neural Network Pruning

abstract: Although recent advances in voice conversion have shown significant improvement, there still remains a gap between the converted voice and target voice. A key factor that maintains this gap is the insufficient decomposition of content and voice style from the source speech. This insufficiency leads to the converted speech containing source speech style or losing source speech content. In this paper, we present VoiceMixer which can effectively decompose and transfer voice style through a novel information bottleneck and adversarial feedback. With self-supervised representation learning, the proposed information bottleneck can decompose the content and style with only a small loss of content information. Also, for adversarial feedback of each information, the discriminator is decomposed into content and style discriminator with self-supervision, which enable our model to achieve better generalization to the voice style of the converted speech. The experimental results show the superiority of our model in disentanglement and transfer performance, and improve audio quality by preserving content information.

Also, for adversarial feedback of each information, the discriminator is decomposed into content and style discriminator with self-supervision, which enable our model to achieve better generalization to the voice style of the converted speech. paragraphs: Voice conversion aims to transfer voice style while retaining the content of the source speech. When content and style are not sufficiently separated, converted speech can retain the original style or lose content. VoiceMixer addresses this entanglement through an information bottleneck and adversarial feedback designed to distinguish the two kinds of information.

The bottleneck uses self-supervised representation learning to separate content from style with only a small loss of content information. For adversarial feedback, the approach separates the discriminator into content and style discriminators, also using self-supervision. This provides distinct feedback for the two components and supports better generalization of the converted voice style.

The reported experiments show stronger disentanglement and transfer performance, along with improved audio quality through preservation of content information. The findings connect the quality of voice conversion to how effectively the representation separates what is said from voice style. The method’s stated benefit includes preserving content with a small loss, rather than claiming that the separation removes all information loss.
summary.tldr: VoiceMixer separates speech content and voice style using a self-supervised bottleneck and distinct adversarial feedback, improving transfer and audio quality.

title: VoiceMixer: Adversarial Voice Style Mixup

abstract: Despite tremendous success in many application scenarios, the training and inference costs of using deep learning are also rapidly increasing over time. The lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) emerges as a promising framework to leverage a special sparse subnetwork (i.e., $\textit{winning ticket}$) instead of a full model for both training and inference, that can lower both costs without sacrificing the performance. The main resource bottleneck of LTH is however the extraordinary cost to find the sparse mask of the winning ticket. That makes the found winning ticket become a valuable asset to the owners, highlighting the necessity of protecting its copyright. Our setting adds a new dimension to the recently soaring interest in protecting against the intellectual property (IP) infringement of deep models and verifying their ownerships, since they take owners' massive/unique resources to develop or train. While existing methods explored encrypted weights or predictions, we investigate a unique way to leverage sparse topological information to perform $\textit{lottery verification}$, by developing several graph-based signatures that can be embedded as credentials. By further combining trigger set-based methods, our proposal can work in both white-box and black-box verification scenarios. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of lottery verification in diverse models (ResNet-20, ResNet-18, ResNet-50) on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Specifically, our verification is shown to be robust to removal attacks such as model fine-tuning and pruning, as well as several ambiguity attacks. Our codes are available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/NO-stealing-LTH.

These findings support sparse topology as a useful place to encode ownership evidence, with the demonstrated robustness tied to the models and attacks evaluated.
summary.tldr: Graph-based signatures embedded in winning-ticket topology enable ownership verification and withstand several tested removal and ambiguity attacks.

title: You are caught stealing my winning lottery ticket! Making a lottery ticket claim its ownership

abstract: We consider the problem of offline reinforcement learning (RL) --- a well-motivated setting of RL that aims at policy optimization using only historical data. Despite its wide applicability, theoretical understandings of offline RL, such as its optimal sample complexity, remain largely open even in basic settings such as \emph{tabular} Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). In this paper, we propose \emph{Off-Policy Double Variance Reduction} (OPDVR), a new variance reduction-based algorithm for offline RL. Our main result shows that OPDVR provably identifies an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with $\widetilde{O}(H^2/d_m\epsilon^2)$ episodes of offline data in the finite-horizon \emph{stationary transition} setting, where $H$ is the horizon length and $d_m$ is the minimal marginal state-action distribution induced by the behavior policy. This improves over the best-known upper bound by a factor of $H$. Moreover, we establish an information-theoretic lower bound of $\Omega(H^2/d_m\epsilon^2)$ which certifies that OPDVR is optimal up to logarithmic factors. Lastly, we show that OPDVR also achieves rate-optimal sample complexity under alternative settings such as the finite-horizon MDPs with non-stationary transitions and the infinite horizon MDPs with discounted rewards.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning seeks a good policy using historical data alone. A central theoretical question is how much recorded experience is sufficient, even when states and actions have a tabular representation. This paper introduces Off-Policy Double Variance Reduction, or OPDVR, and analyzes its sample requirements across several Markov decision process settings.

For a finite horizon with stationary transitions, OPDVR identifies a policy within epsilon of optimal using approximately H squared divided by d_m times epsilon squared episodes, ignoring logarithmic factors. Here H is the horizon and d_m measures the smallest marginal state-action probability under the behavior policy. The guarantee therefore explicitly depends on how well that policy covers state-action pairs.

The upper bound improves the previously best-known result by a factor of H. The authors also prove an information-theoretic lower bound with the same main dependence, establishing optimality up to logarithmic factors in this setting. They further report rate-optimal sample complexity for finite-horizon problems with non-stationary transitions and infinite-horizon problems with discounted rewards. The contribution is a variance-reduction algorithm accompanied by matching efficiency guarantees.
summary.tldr: OPDVR achieves near-optimal offline reinforcement learning sample complexity through double variance reduction, with matching lower bounds in the stationary finite-horizon setting.

title: Near-Optimal Offline Reinforcement Learning via Double Variance Reduction

abstract: In reinforcement learning, experience replay stores past samples for further reuse. Prioritized sampling is a promising technique to better utilize these samples. Previous criteria of prioritization include TD error, recentness and corrective feedback, which are mostly heuristically designed. In this work, we start from the regret minimization objective, and obtain an optimal prioritization strategy for Bellman update that can directly maximize the return of the policy. The theory suggests that data with higher hindsight TD error, better on-policiness and more accurate Q value should be assigned with higher weights during sampling. Thus most previous criteria only consider this strategy partially. We not only provide theoretical justifications for previous criteria, but also propose two new methods to compute the prioritization weight, namely ReMERN and ReMERT. ReMERN learns an error network, while ReMERT exploits the temporal ordering of states. Both methods outperform previous prioritized sampling algorithms in challenging RL benchmarks, including MuJoCo, Atari and Meta-World.

paragraphs: Experience replay lets a reinforcement learning agent reuse past interactions. Choosing which stored experiences to revisit can strongly affect learning. Earlier prioritization rules commonly emphasize prediction errors, recent experiences, or corrective feedback. This paper derives a prioritization strategy from a regret-minimization objective rather than starting with an isolated sampling heuristic.

The derived strategy identifies priorities for Bellman updates aimed directly at maximizing policy return. Its theory favors experiences with larger hindsight temporal-difference errors, closer alignment with the current policy, and more accurate Q-values. These factors explain why existing prioritization criteria can be useful while also showing that each captures only part of the proposed strategy.

The authors introduce two ways to compute prioritization weights. ReMERN learns an additional error network, while ReMERT uses the temporal ordering of states. Both outperform previous prioritized-sampling algorithms on the reported MuJoCo, Atari, and Meta-World benchmarks. The work connects a theoretical sampling objective with two concrete methods for making stored experiences more useful.
summary.tldr: A regret-based analysis motivates two replay-prioritization methods that outperform earlier sampling approaches on the reported reinforcement learning benchmarks.

title: Regret Minimization Experience Replay in Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Verification is a serious bottleneck in the industrial hardware design cycle, routinely requiring person-years of effort. Practical verification relies on a "best effort" process that simulates the design on test inputs. This suggests a new research question: Can this simulation data be exploited to learn a continuous representation of a hardware design that allows us to predict its functionality? As a first approach to this new problem, we introduce Design2Vec, a deep architecture that learns semantic abstractions of hardware designs. The key idea is to work at a higher level of abstraction than the gate or the bit level, namely the Register Transfer Level (RTL), which is somewhat analogous to software source code, and can be represented by a graph that incorporates control and data flow. This allows us to learn representations of RTL syntax and semantics using a graph neural network. We apply these representations to several tasks within verification, including predicting what cover points of the design will be exercised by a test, and generating new tests that will exercise desired cover points. We evaluate Design2Vec on three real-world hardware designs, including an industrial chip used in commercial data centers. Our results demonstrate that Design2Vec dramatically outperforms baseline approaches that do not incorporate the RTL semantics, scales to industrial designs, and can generate tests that exercise design points that are currently hard to cover with manually written tests by design verification experts.

Design2Vec asks whether those simulations can help train a representation that predicts how a design behaves. The aim is to make existing verification data useful for choosing and generating tests, including tests that exercise difficult-to-reach parts of a design.

It substantially outperforms baselines that omit RTL semantics and scales to industrial designs. It also generates tests that exercise points experts have difficulty covering manually. The findings show the practical value of incorporating design behavior into learned verification representations.
summary.tldr: Design2Vec learns hardware representations from RTL graphs and simulation data to predict test coverage and generate tests for difficult coverage points.

title: Learning Semantic Representations to Verify Hardware Designs

abstract: We propose and analyze a stochastic Newton algorithm for homogeneous distributed stochastic convex optimization, where each machine can calculate stochastic gradients of the same population objective, as well as stochastic Hessian-vector products (products of an independent unbiased estimator of the Hessian of the population objective with arbitrary vectors), with many such stochastic computations performed between rounds of communication. We show that our method can reduce the number, and frequency, of required communication rounds, compared to existing methods without hurting performance, by proving convergence guarantees for quasi-self-concordant objectives (e.g., logistic regression), alongside empirical evidence.

We show that our method can reduce the number, and frequency, of required communication rounds, compared to existing methods without hurting performance, by proving convergence guarantees for quasi-self-concordant objectives (e.g., logistic regression), alongside empirical evidence.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization divides learning work across machines, but those machines still need to exchange information. This paper studies how to reduce that communication while solving a shared convex optimization problem. Its setting is homogeneous: every machine can estimate gradients of the same population objective, so the analysis concerns workers pursuing a common underlying target.

The proposed stochastic Newton algorithm also uses information about curvature through stochastic Hessian-vector products. These products apply an independent, unbiased estimate of the objective's Hessian to a chosen vector. They give the algorithm access to second-order information alongside ordinary gradient estimates. Each machine can perform many such stochastic computations between communication rounds, allowing more local computation to support less frequent coordination.

The authors prove convergence guarantees for quasi-self-concordant objectives, a class that includes logistic regression, and provide empirical evidence. Within this setting, their method can reduce both the number and frequency of communication rounds without sacrificing performance relative to existing methods. The contribution connects access to stochastic curvature information with a concrete reduction in distributed communication requirements.
summary.tldr: A stochastic Newton method uses local gradient and curvature computations to reduce communication in homogeneous distributed convex optimization.

title: A Stochastic Newton Algorithm for Distributed Convex Optimization

abstract: Masked Image Modeling (MIM) has recently been established as a potent pre-training paradigm. A pretext task is constructed by masking patches in an input image, and this masked content is then predicted by a neural network using visible patches as sole input. This pre-training leads to state-of-the-art performance when finetuned for high-level semantic tasks, e.g. image classification and object detection. In this paper we instead seek to learn representations that transfer well to a wide variety of 3D vision and lower-level geometric downstream tasks, such as depth prediction or optical flow estimation. Inspired by MIM, we propose an unsupervised representation learning task trained from pairs of images showing the same scene from different viewpoints. More precisely, we propose the pretext task of cross-view completion where the first input image is partially masked, and this masked content has to be reconstructed from the visible content and the second image. In single-view MIM, the masked content often cannot be inferred precisely from the visible portion only, so the model learns to act as a prior influenced by high-level semantics. In contrast, this ambiguity can be resolved with cross-view completion from the second unmasked image, on the condition that the model is able to understand the spatial relationship between the two images. Our experiments show that our pretext task leads to significantly improved performance for monocular 3D vision downstream tasks such as depth estimation. In addition, our model can be directly applied to binocular downstream tasks like optical flow or relative camera pose estimation, for which we obtain competitive results without bells and whistles, i.e., using a generic architecture without any task-specific design.

paragraphs: CroCo adapts masked image reconstruction to teach representations useful for geometry and 3D vision. Reconstructing missing patches from a single image can leave substantial ambiguity, encouraging a model to rely on semantic expectations. The paper instead supplies a second image of the same scene from another viewpoint as additional evidence for filling the gaps.

During pretraining, one image is partially masked and the model reconstructs its missing content using both the remaining visible patches and the second, unmasked image. The second view can resolve uncertainty if the model understands the spatial relationship between the views. The reconstruction task therefore creates an incentive to learn geometric relationships without requiring supervised labels for that pretext task.

Experiments show significantly improved performance after transfer to monocular 3D tasks such as depth estimation. The model can also be applied directly to binocular tasks, including optical flow and relative camera pose estimation, with competitive results using a generic architecture. These findings indicate that cross-view completion can support both representations for single-image geometry and processing that relates two views.
summary.tldr: CroCo learns transferable geometric representations by reconstructing masked image regions with help from another view of the same scene.

title: CroCo: Self-Supervised Pre-training for 3D Vision Tasks by Cross-View Completion

abstract: In the infinite-armed bandit problem, each arm's average reward is sampled from an unknown distribution, and each arm can be sampled further to obtain noisy estimates of the average reward of that arm. Prior work focuses on the best arm, i.e. estimating the maximum of the average reward distribution. We consider a general class of distribution functionals beyond the maximum and obtain optimal sample complexities in both offline and online settings. We show that online estimation, where the learner can sequentially choose whether to sample a new or existing arm, offers no advantage over the offline setting for estimating the mean functional, but significantly reduces the sample complexity for other functionals such as the median, maximum, and trimmed mean. We propose unified meta algorithms for the online and offline settings and derive matching lower bounds using different Wasserstein distances. For the special case of median estimation, we identify a curious thresholding phenomenon on the indistinguishability between Gaussian convolutions with respect to the noise level, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: In this bandit setting, each available arm has an average reward drawn from an unknown distribution. Sampling an arm produces noisy evidence about its average. Instead of concentrating only on the best arm, the paper asks how many observations are needed to estimate broader properties of that distribution, including its mean, median, maximum, and trimmed mean.

The authors compare offline estimation with an online setting where the learner can repeatedly decide whether to investigate a new arm or sample an existing one again. This flexibility does not improve the sample complexity of estimating the mean. It does significantly reduce the observations needed for several other properties, showing that the value of adaptive sampling depends on the quantity being estimated.

The paper supplies general algorithmic frameworks for both settings and matching lower bounds based on Wasserstein distances, establishing optimal sample complexities. For median estimation, it also identifies a noise-dependent threshold phenomenon concerning when Gaussian-smoothed distributions become indistinguishable. This connects a particular estimation challenge to the broader question of how noise hides differences between distributions.
summary.tldr: Adaptive sampling improves optimal estimation costs for several reward-distribution properties, but offers no advantage for estimating the mean.

title: Beyond the Best: Distribution Functional Estimation in Infinite-Armed Bandits

abstract: We derive information theoretic generalization bounds for supervised learning algorithms based on a new measure of leave-one-out conditional mutual information (loo-CMI). In contrast to other CMI bounds, which may be hard to evaluate in practice, our loo-CMI bounds are easier to compute and can be interpreted in connection to other notions such as classical leave-one-out cross-validation, stability of the optimization algorithm, and the geometry of the loss-landscape. It applies both to the output of training algorithms as well as their predictions. We empirically validate the quality of the bound by evaluating its predicted generalization gap in scenarios for deep learning. In particular, our bounds are non-vacuous on image-classification tasks.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds seek to control the difference between a learning algorithm's training performance and its performance beyond the training data. This paper derives information-theoretic bounds using a new quantity called leave-one-out conditional mutual information, or loo-CMI. The motivation is practical as well as theoretical: other CMI-based bounds can be difficult to evaluate.

The proposed bounds are easier to compute and admit connections to several familiar ways of understanding learning. These include leave-one-out cross-validation, optimization stability, and the geometry of the loss landscape. The framework applies both to the output of a training algorithm and to its predictions, providing two places at which the information-based analysis can be used.

The authors evaluate the predicted generalization gap in deep-learning settings and obtain non-vacuous bounds on image-classification tasks. Non-vacuous means the guarantee provides meaningful information rather than an uninformative allowance for error. The findings support loo-CMI as a usable approach to generalization analysis, combining interpretable connections with empirical evidence that the bounds can be informative.
summary.tldr: Leave-one-out conditional mutual information yields easier-to-compute generalization bounds that are non-vacuous on evaluated image-classification tasks.

title: On Leave-One-Out Conditional Mutual Information For Generalization

abstract: Setting up a well-designed reward function has been challenging for many reinforcement learning applications. Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) provides a new framework that avoids reward engineering by leveraging human preferences (i.e., preferring apples over oranges) as the reward signal. Therefore, improving the efficacy of data usage for preference data becomes critical. In this work, we propose Meta-Reward-Net (MRN), a data-efficient PbRL framework that incorporates bi-level optimization for both reward and policy learning. The key idea of MRN is to adopt the performance of the Q-function as the learning target. Based on this, MRN learns the Q-function and the policy in the inner level while updating the reward function adaptively according to the performance of the Q-function on the preference data in the outer level. Our experiments on robotic simulated manipulation tasks and locomotion tasks demonstrate that MRN outperforms prior methods in the case of few preference labels and significantly improves data efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art in preference-based RL. Ablation studies further demonstrate that MRN learns a more accurate Q-function compared to prior work and shows obvious advantages when only a small amount of human feedback is available. The source code and videos of this project are released at https://sites.google.com/view/meta-reward-net.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning uses human comparisons to guide behavior, reducing the need to hand-design a reward function. Because human feedback can be scarce, learning effectively from a small number of preferences is central to this approach. Meta-Reward-Net focuses on improving how those preferences shape reward and policy learning.

The method uses a two-level optimization process. At the inner level, it learns the policy and the Q-function, which evaluates actions. At the outer level, it adjusts the reward function according to how well the Q-function performs on the preference data. This makes the quality of the learned action evaluation a target for reward learning.

Experiments on simulated robotic manipulation and locomotion tasks report stronger performance than prior methods when preference labels are few, along with improved data efficiency. Ablation studies also find a more accurate Q-function and particular advantages when little human feedback is available. These findings support coordinating reward learning with downstream learning performance as a way to make scarce preferences more useful.
summary.tldr: Meta-Reward-Net uses two-level optimization to learn rewards through Q-function performance, improving reinforcement learning with limited preference feedback.

title: Meta-Reward-Net: Implicitly Differentiable Reward Learning for Preference-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Most of the existing algorithms for zero-shot classification problems typically rely on the attribute-based semantic relations among categories to realize the classification of novel categories without observing any of their instances. However, training the zero-shot classification models still requires attribute labeling for each class (or even instance) in the training dataset, which is also expensive. To this end, in this paper, we bring up a new problem scenario: ''Can we derive zero-shot learning for novel attribute detectors/classifiers and use them to automatically annotate the dataset for labeling efficiency?'' Basically, given only a small set of detectors that are learned to recognize some manually annotated attributes (i.e., the seen attributes), we aim to synthesize the detectors of novel attributes in a zero-shot learning manner. Our proposed method, Zero-Shot Learning for Attributes (ZSLA), which is the first of its kind to the best of our knowledge, tackles this new research problem by applying the set operations to first decompose the seen attributes into their basic attributes and then recombine these basic attributes into the novel ones. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify the capacity of our synthesized detectors for accurately capturing the semantics of the novel attributes and show their superior performance in terms of detection and localization compared to other baseline approaches. Moreover, we demonstrate the application of automatic annotation using our synthesized detectors on Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 dataset. Various generalized zero-shot classification algorithms trained upon the dataset re-annotated by ZSLA shows comparable performance with those trained with the manual ground-truth annotations.

Moreover, we demonstrate the application of automatic annotation using our synthesized detectors on Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 dataset. Various generalized zero-shot classification algorithms trained upon the dataset re-annotated by ZSLA shows comparable performance with those trained with the manual ground-truth annotations.

paragraphs: Zero-shot classification often recognizes unseen categories through attributes that connect them to known categories. However, obtaining the attribute annotations used during training can itself be expensive. This paper asks whether zero-shot learning can instead produce detectors for unseen attributes, allowing those detectors to help annotate data automatically.

Zero-Shot Learning for Attributes starts with a small set of detectors trained on manually labeled attributes. It applies set operations to decompose those seen attributes into basic components, then recombines the components to synthesize detectors for novel attributes. The approach uses structure within known attributes to build new detection capabilities.

Experiments show that the synthesized detectors capture novel attribute semantics and outperform the compared baselines in detection and localization. The authors also use them to re-annotate the Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 dataset. Several generalized zero-shot classification algorithms trained with these automatic annotations achieve performance comparable to training with manual ground-truth annotations. This supports the proposed detectors as a way to reduce annotation effort in the demonstrated application.
summary.tldr: ZSLA synthesizes unseen attribute detectors by decomposing and recombining known attributes, supporting automatic dataset annotation.

title: Make an Omelette with Breaking Eggs: Zero-Shot Learning for Novel Attribute Synthesis

abstract: In this paper, we present a capacity-aware neuron steganography scheme (i.e., Cans) to covertly transmit multiple private machine learning (ML) datasets via a scheduled-to-publish deep neural network (DNN) as the carrier model. Unlike existing steganography schemes which treat the DNN parameters as bit strings, \textit{Cans} for the first time exploits the learning capacity of the carrier model via a novel parameter sharing mechanism. Extensive evaluation shows, Cans is the first working scheme which can covertly transmit over $10000$ real-world data samples within a carrier model which has $220\times$ less parameters than the total size of the stolen data, and simultaneously transmit multiple heterogeneous datasets within a single carrier model, under a trivial distortion rate ($<10^{-5}$) and with almost no utility loss on the carrier model ($<1\%$). Besides, Cans implements by-design redundancy to be resilient against common post-processing techniques on the carrier model before the publishing.

The proposed scheme, Cans, uses the network as a carrier while preserving nearly all of its ordinary task utility. The research demonstrates how a published model can carry information beyond its intended predictive function.

Cans makes use of the carrier's learning capacity through a parameter-sharing mechanism. Existing schemes described in the abstract instead treat model parameters as strings of bits. The proposed approach can place multiple heterogeneous datasets within one carrier model. It also includes redundancy designed to preserve the hidden information through common model post-processing performed before publication.

In the reported evaluations, Cans transmits more than 10,000 real-world samples using a carrier with 220 times fewer parameters than the total size of the transmitted data. The authors report distortion below 10^-5 and carrier utility loss below 1%. These findings demonstrate substantial covert data capacity in the evaluated models, together with resilience to the common post-processing techniques considered in the work.
summary.tldr: Cans exploits a neural network's learning capacity to covertly carry multiple private datasets with little reported loss of model utility.

title: House of Cans: Covert Transmission of Internal Datasets via Capacity-Aware Neuron Steganography

abstract: Despite extensive theoretical work on biologically plausible learning rules, clear evidence about whether and how such rules are implemented in the brain has been difficult to obtain. We consider biologically plausible supervised- and reinforcement-learning rules and ask whether changes in network activity during learning can be used to determine which learning rule is being used. Supervised learning requires a credit-assignment model estimating the mapping from neural activity to behavior, and, in a biological organism, this model will inevitably be an imperfect approximation of the ideal mapping, leading to a bias in the direction of the weight updates relative to the true gradient. Reinforcement learning, on the other hand, requires no credit-assignment model and tends to make weight updates following the true gradient direction. We derive a metric to distinguish between learning rules by observing changes in the network activity during learning, given that the mapping from brain to behavior is known by the experimenter. Because brain-machine interface (BMI) experiments allow for precise knowledge of this mapping, we model a cursor-control BMI task using recurrent neural networks, showing that learning rules can be distinguished in simulated experiments using only observations that a neuroscience experimenter would plausibly have access to.

paragraphs: Many biologically plausible learning rules have been proposed, but identifying which rules operate in the brain remains difficult. This paper asks whether changes in neural activity during learning can distinguish supervised learning from reinforcement learning. Its approach depends on the experimenter knowing how neural activity is mapped to behavior.

The distinction comes from credit assignment. In the supervised rules considered, learning uses an internal estimate of how activity affects behavior. An imperfect estimate biases weight updates away from the true gradient direction. The reinforcement-learning rules require no such credit-assignment model and tend to update along the true gradient. The authors derive a metric that uses this difference to distinguish rules through observed activity changes.

This establishes a discrimination method in simulation under the known-mapping condition.
summary.tldr: A metric distinguishes supervised and reinforcement learning rules in simulated brain-machine interfaces using observed neural activity changes.

title: Distinguishing Learning Rules with Brain Machine Interfaces

abstract: Deep networks on 3D point clouds have achieved remarkable success in 3D classification, while they are vulnerable to geometry variations caused by inconsistent data acquisition procedures. This results in a challenging 3D domain generalization (3DDG) problem, that is to generalize a model trained on source domain to an unseen target domain. Based on the observation that local geometric structures are more generalizable than the whole shape, we propose to reduce the geometry shift by a generalizable part-based feature representation and design a novel part-based domain generalization network (PDG) for 3D point cloud classification. Specifically, we build a part-template feature space shared by source and target domains. Shapes from distinct domains are first organized to part-level features and then represented by part-template features. The transformed part-level features, dubbed aligned part-based representations, are then aggregated by a part-based feature aggregation module. To improve the robustness of the part-based representations, we further propose a contrastive learning framework upon part-based shape representation. Experiments and ablation studies on 3DDA and 3DDG benchmarks justify the efficacy of the proposed approach for domain generalization, compared with the previous state-of-the-art methods. Our code will be available on http://github.com/weixmath/PDG.

paragraphs: A point-cloud classifier can perform well on familiar data yet struggle when different acquisition procedures change the geometry it sees. This paper studies generalization from a source domain to an unseen target domain. Its starting observation is that local geometric structures transfer more readily than representations of an entire shape.

The proposed part-based domain generalization network, PDG, builds a common part-template feature space for source and target domains. It first organizes shapes into part-level features, then expresses those features through the shared templates. A dedicated aggregation module combines these aligned part representations into a shape representation. This gives differently acquired shapes a shared way to describe their constituent geometry.

The authors further apply contrastive learning to the part-based shape representations to improve robustness. Experiments and ablations on 3DDA and 3DDG benchmarks support the approach relative to previous leading methods. The findings suggest that aligning local parts can reduce the impact of geometry differences and improve classification when a model encounters an unfamiliar domain.
summary.tldr: PDG aligns point-cloud parts through shared templates to improve classification generalization across changes in data acquisition.

title: Learning Generalizable Part-based Feature Representation for 3D Point Clouds

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViT) become widely-adopted architectures for various vision tasks. Masked auto-encoding for feature pretraining and multi-scale hybrid convolution-transformer architectures can further unleash the potentials of ViT, leading to state-of-the-art performances on image classification, detection and semantic segmentation. In this paper, our MCMAE framework demonstrates that multi-scale hybrid convolution-transformer can learn more discriminative representations via the mask auto-encoding scheme. However, directly using the original masking strategy leads to the heavy computational cost and pretraining-finetuning discrepancy. To tackle the issue, we adopt the masked convolution to prevent information leakage in the convolution blocks. A simple block-wise masking strategy is proposed to ensure computational efficiency. We also propose to more directly supervise the multi-scale features of the encoder to boost multi-scale features. Based on our pretrained MCMAE models, MCMAE-Base improves ImageNet-1K finetuning accuracy by 1.4% compared with MAE-Base. On object detection, MCMAE-Base finetuned for only 25 epochs surpasses MAE-Base fined-tuned for 100 epochs by 2.9% box AP and 2.2% mask AP respectively. Code and pretrained models are available at \url{https://github.com/Alpha-VL/ConvMAE}.

paragraphs: Masked autoencoding provides a way to pretrain visual representations, while hybrid convolution-transformer networks capture information at multiple scales. MCMAE brings these ideas together. The paper shows that such hybrid architectures can learn more discriminative features through masked autoencoding, but also identifies problems with directly applying the original masking strategy.

Those problems include heavy computation and a mismatch between pretraining and fine-tuning. MCMAE uses masked convolutions to prevent information leakage within convolution blocks and a block-wise masking strategy to improve efficiency. It also supervises the encoder’s multiscale features more directly, strengthening the representations available at different resolutions.

The reported comparisons show benefits in classification and object detection. MCMAE-Base improves ImageNet-1K fine-tuning accuracy by 1.4% over MAE-Base. For object detection, MCMAE-Base fine-tuned for 25 epochs exceeds MAE-Base fine-tuned for 100 epochs by the reported 2.9% box AP and 2.2% mask AP. These results support adapting the masking and supervision scheme to the hybrid architecture, rather than simply applying an existing pretraining recipe unchanged.
summary.tldr: MCMAE adapts masked autoencoding to multiscale convolution-transformer networks and improves reported classification and detection results.

title: MCMAE: Masked Convolution Meets Masked Autoencoders

abstract: Keyphrases are an important tool for efficiently dealing with the ever-increasing amount of information present on the internet. While there are many recent papers on English keyphrase generation, keyphrase generation for other languages remains vastly understudied, mostly due to the absence of datasets. To address this, we present a novel dataset called Papyrus, composed of 16427 pairs of abstracts and keyphrases. We release four versions of this dataset, corresponding to different subtasks. Papyrus-e considers only English keyphrases, Papyrus-f considers French keyphrases, Papyrus-m considers keyphrase generation in any language (mostly French and English), and Papyrus-a considers keyphrase generation in several languages. We train a state-of-the-art model on all four tasks and show that they lead to better results for non-English languages, with an average improvement of 14.2\% on keyphrase extraction and 2.0\% on generation. We also show an improvement of 0.4\% on extraction and 0.7\% on generation over English state-of-the-art results by concatenating Papyrus-e with the Kp20K training set.
