They find that existing benchmarks favor simpler layouts with low scores. OverLayBench addresses that imbalance with high-quality annotations and a balanced distribution of OverLayScore values, making demanding overlap cases a more deliberate part of evaluation.

The paper also proposes CreatiLayout-AM, trained on a curated amodal mask dataset, as an initial approach to improving generation under complex overlaps. Its contributions connect a diagnosed failure mode with a metric, a benchmark, and a model direction. This gives researchers a more focused basis for assessing progress on crowded layouts where conventional evaluations provide limited coverage.
summary.tldr: OverLayBench and OverLayScore make dense object overlap a systematic test of layout-to-image generation.

title: OverLayBench: A Benchmark for Layout-to-Image Generation with Dense Overlaps

abstract: The global rise in wildfire frequency and intensity over the past decade underscores the need for improved fire monitoring techniques. To advance deep learning research on wildfire detection and its associated human health impacts, we introduce **SmokeViz**, a large-scale machine learning dataset of smoke plumes in satellite imagery. The dataset is derived from expert annotations created by smoke analysts at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which provide coarse temporal and spatial approximations of smoke presence. To enhance annotation precision, we propose **pseudo-label dimension reduction (PLDR)**, a generalizable method that applies pseudo-labeling to refine datasets with mismatching temporal and/or spatial resolutions. Unlike typical pseudo-labeling applications that aim to increase the number of labeled samples, PLDR maintains the original labels but increases the dataset quality by solving for intermediary pseudo-labels (IPLs) that align each annotation to the most representative input data. For SmokeViz, a parent model produces IPLs to identify the single satellite image within each annotations time window that best corresponds with the smoke plume. This refinement process produces a succinct and relevant deep learning dataset consisting of over 160,000 manual annotations. The SmokeViz dataset is expected to be a valuable resource to develop further wildfire-related machine learning models and is publicly available at \url{https://noaa-gsl-experimental-pds.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html#SmokeViz/}.

title: SmokeViz: A Large-Scale Satellite Dataset for Wildfire Smoke Detection and Segmentation

abstract: Dynamic pricing algorithms typically assume continuous price variables, which may not reflect real-world scenarios where prices are often discrete. This paper demonstrates that leveraging discrete price information within a semi-parametric model can substantially improve performance, depending on the size of the support set of the price variable relative to the time horizon. Specifically, we propose a novel semi-parametric contextual dynamic pricing algorithm, namely BayesCoxCP, based on a Bayesian approach to the Cox proportional hazards model. Our theoretical analysis establishes high-probability regret bounds that adapt to the sparsity level $\gamma$, proving that our algorithm achieves a regret upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(T^{(1+\gamma)/2}+\sqrt{dT})$ for $\gamma < 1/3$ and $\widetilde{O}(T^{2/3}+\sqrt{dT})$ for $\gamma \geq 1/3$, where $\gamma$ represents the sparsity of the price grid relative to the time horizon $T$. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed algorithm significantly outperforms an existing method, particularly in scenarios with sparse discrete price points.

paragraphs: Dynamic pricing methods often treat prices as continuously adjustable, although actual sellers may choose from a discrete menu. This paper studies how explicitly using that menu can improve contextual pricing. Its central point is conditional: the benefit depends on how many available price points there are relative to the number of pricing decisions.

The proposed algorithm, BayesCoxCP, combines Bayesian learning with a semiparametric Cox proportional hazards model. Its theoretical analysis bounds regret, the accumulated cost of decisions relative to an optimal reference. The bounds adapt to a parameter gamma describing price-grid sparsity relative to the time horizon T, alongside a term involving the contextual dimension d.

For gamma below one third, the reported high-probability upper bound scales as T raised to (1 + gamma)/2 plus the square root of dT, with logarithmic factors suppressed. At or above that threshold, the first term becomes T raised to two thirds. Numerical experiments also show substantial improvements over an existing method, particularly for sparse price menus. Together, these findings identify when discrete pricing structure can provide a useful learning advantage.
summary.tldr: BayesCoxCP uses discrete price information in Bayesian contextual pricing, with regret guarantees and empirical gains that are especially favorable for sparse price grids.

title: A Bayesian Approach to Contextual Dynamic Pricing using the Proportional Hazards Model with Discrete Price Data

abstract: With the rapid advancement of generative models, general-purpose generation has gained increasing attention as a promising approach to unify diverse tasks across modalities within a single system. Despite this progress, existing open-source frameworks often remain fragile and struggle to support complex real-world applications due to the lack of structured workflow planning and execution-level feedback. To address these limitations, we present ComfyMind, a collaborative AI system designed to enable robust and scalable general-purpose generation, built on the ComfyUI platform. ComfyMind introduces two core innovations: Semantic Workflow Interface (SWI) that abstracts low-level node graphs into callable functional modules described in natural language, enabling high-level composition and reducing structural errors; Search Tree Planning mechanism with localized feedback execution, which models generation as a hierarchical decision process and allows adaptive correction at each stage. Together, these components improve the stability and flexibility of complex generative workflows. We evaluate ComfyMind on three public benchmarks: ComfyBench, GenEval, and Reason-Edit, which span generation, editing, and reasoning tasks. Results show that ComfyMind consistently outperforms existing open-source baselines and achieves performance comparable to GPT-Image-1. ComfyMind paves a promising path for the development of open-source general-purpose generative AI systems.

paragraphs: ComfyMind addresses the difficulty of assembling reliable workflows for varied generative tasks. The results suggest that organizing and revising the workflow itself can improve a generative system's stability and flexibility, alongside the capabilities of the models it uses.
summary.tldr: ComfyMind combines natural-language workflow modules, tree-based planning, and execution feedback to improve complex generative workflows.

title: ComfyMind: Toward General-Purpose Generation via Tree-Based Planning and Reactive Feedback

abstract: Training Long-Context Large Language Models (LLMs) is challenging, as hybrid training with long-context and short-context data often leads to workload imbalances. Existing works mainly use data packing to alleviate this issue, but fail to consider imbalanced attention computation and wasted communication overhead. This paper proposes Hierarchical Balance Packing (HBP), which designs a novel batch-construction method and training recipe to address those inefficiencies. In particular, the HBP constructs multi-level data packing groups, each optimized with a distinct packing length. It assigns training samples to their optimal groups and configures each group with the most effective settings, including sequential parallelism degree and gradient checkpointing configuration. To effectively utilize multi-level groups of data, we design a dynamic training pipeline specifically tailored to HBP, including curriculum learning, adaptive sequential parallelism, and stable loss. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly reduces training time over multiple datasets and open-source models while maintaining strong performance. For the largest DeepSeek-V2 (236B) MoE model, our method speeds up the training by 2.4$\times$ with competitive performance. Codes will be released at https://github.com/ModelTC/HBP.

paragraphs: Training a language model on both long and short examples can distribute work unevenly. Simply packing examples together does not fully account for differences in attention computation or unnecessary communication. Hierarchical Balance Packing addresses these inefficiencies by coordinating how batches are formed with how each batch is processed.

The method creates several packing groups with different target lengths and assigns examples to their appropriate groups. Each group receives its own settings for sequence parallelism and gradient checkpointing. A dynamic training pipeline combines curriculum learning, adaptive sequence parallelism, and a stable-loss component so that training can make effective use of these differently configured groups.

The authors report reduced training time across multiple datasets and open-source models while maintaining strong performance. For the 236-billion-parameter DeepSeek-V2 mixture-of-experts model, they report a 2.4-fold training speedup with competitive performance. The approach matters because it treats data organization and execution settings as a joint efficiency problem, allowing mixed-length training to use computing resources more effectively than packing alone.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Balance Packing coordinates mixed-length batches and training settings, reporting a 2.4-fold speedup for DeepSeek-V2 with competitive performance.

title: Hierachical Balance Packing: Towards Efficient Supervised Fine-tuning for Long-Context LLM

abstract: Long video understanding is inherently challenging for vision-language models (VLMs) because of the extensive number of frames. With each video frame typically expanding into tens or hundreds of tokens, the limited context length of large language models (LLMs) forces the VLMs to perceive the frames sparsely and lose temporal information. To address this, we explore extreme video token compression towards *one token per frame* at the final LLM layer. Our key insight is that heuristic-based compression, widely adopted by previous methods, is prone to information loss, and this necessitates supervising LLM layers into *learnable* and *progressive* modules for *token-level compression* (LP-Comp). Such compression enables our VLM to digest 2x-4x more frames with improved performance. To further increase the token efficiency, we investigate \emph{frame-level compression}, which selects the frames most relevant to the queries via the internal attention scores of the LLM layers, named *question-conditioned compression* (QC-Comp). As a notable distinction from previous studies, we mitigate the position bias of LLM attention in long contexts, *i.e.*, the over-concentration on the beginning and end of a sequence, by splitting long videos into short segments and employing local attention. Collectively, our combined *token-level* and *frame-level* leads to an e**x**treme compression model for long video understanding, named **XComp**, achieving a significantly larger compression ratio and enabling denser frame sampling. Our XComp is finetuned from VideoChat-Flash with a data-efficient *supervised compression tuning* stage that only requires 2.5\% of the supervised fine-tuning data, yet boosts the accuracy from 42.9\% to 46.2\% on LVBench and enhances multiple other long video benchmarks.

Collectively, our combined *token-level* and *frame-level* leads to an e**x**treme compression model for long video understanding, named **XComp**, achieving a significantly larger compression ratio and enabling denser frame sampling. Our XComp is finetuned from VideoChat-Flash with a data-efficient *supervised compression tuning* stage that only requires 2.5\% of the supervised fine-tuning data, yet boosts the accuracy from 42.9\% to 46.2\% on LVBench and enhances multiple other long video benchmarks.

paragraphs: Long videos overwhelm vision-language models when each frame requires many tokens. Limited context then forces sparse frame sampling, losing temporal information. XComp addresses this by compressing both the representation of individual frames and the set of frames retained for a particular question.

Its token-level component, LP-Comp, trains progressive compression modules within language-model layers, targeting one token per frame at the final layer. This enables processing two to four times as many frames with improved performance. Its frame-level component, QC-Comp, uses internal attention scores to select question-relevant frames. To reduce attention's bias toward the beginning and end of long sequences, it splits videos into short segments and applies local attention.

XComp combines these mechanisms to support denser sampling with a larger compression ratio. Fine-tuning VideoChat-Flash with supervised compression tuning uses only 2.5% of the supervised fine-tuning data and raises LVBench accuracy from 42.9% to 46.2%, alongside gains on other long-video benchmarks. The results support learning compression jointly with question-sensitive frame selection as a way to retain useful information under context constraints.
summary.tldr: XComp combines learned token compression and question-guided frame selection to fit more video information into limited context.

title: One Token per Highly Selective Frame: Towards Extreme Compression for Long Video Understanding

abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) is widely prevalent in scenarios such as financial fraud detection, anti-money laundering, and social bot detection. However, structural distribution shifts are commonly observed in real-world GAD data due to selection bias, resulting in reduced homophily. Existing GAD methods tend to rely on homophilic shortcuts when trained on high-homophily structures, limiting their ability to generalize well to data with low homophily under structural distribution shifts. In this study, we propose to handle structural distribution shifts by generating novel environments characterized by diverse homophilic structures and utilizing invariant patterns, i.e., features and structures with the capability of stable prediction across structural distribution shifts, which face two challenges: (1) How to discover invariant patterns from entangled features and structures, as structures are sensitive to varying homophilic distributions. (2) How to systematically construct new environments with diverse homophilic structures. To address these challenges, we propose the Ego-Neighborhood Disentangled Encoder with Homophily-aware Environment Mixup (HEM), which effectively handles structural distribution shifts in GAD by discovering invariant patterns. Specifically, we first propose an ego-neighborhood disentangled encoder to decouple the learning of feature embeddings and structural embeddings, which facilitates subsequent improvements in the invariance of structural embeddings for prediction. Next, we introduce a homophily-aware environment mixup that dynamically adjusts edge weights through adversarial learning, effectively generating environments with diverse structural distributions. Finally, we iteratively train the classifier and environment mixup via adversarial training, simultaneously improving the diversity of constructed environments and discovering invariant patterns under structural distribution shifts. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance under structural distribution shift conditions.

paragraphs: Graph anomaly detectors can learn to rely on homophily, the tendency for connected examples to resemble one another. That reliance becomes fragile when a new graph has less homophily than the training graph. The paper addresses structural distribution shifts of this kind, aiming to find predictive patterns that remain useful as connection patterns change.

HEM first separates the learning of an example's own features from the learning of its neighborhood structure. This disentangling supports efforts to make structural representations more stable. A homophily-aware environment mixup then changes edge weights through adversarial learning, generating environments with different structural distributions. The classifier and environment generator train iteratively, combining more diverse training structures with a search for invariant predictive information.

Experiments on real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance under structural distribution shifts. The central idea is to challenge the detector with changing graph relationships during training, reducing its reliance on structural regularities that may disappear later. Separating feature and neighborhood representations gives the method a way to address the unstable structural component while learning from both sources of information.
summary.tldr: HEM separates feature and neighborhood learning and generates varied graph environments to improve anomaly detection under structural shifts.

title: Out-of-Distribution Generalized Graph Anomaly Detection with Homophily-aware Environment Mixup

abstract: In the molecular domain, numerous studies have explored the use of multimodal large language models (LLMs) to construct a general-purpose, multi-task molecular model. However, these efforts are still far from achieving a truly universal molecular model. We identify three key challenges in this endeavor: (1) Existing molecular task datasets are typically small in scale and lack comprehensive domain coverage. (2) Tasks from different molecular subfields are difficult to effectively learn jointly through LLMs due to significant distributional shifts and competition among tasks, which introduces instability in the learning process. (3) Both inter-task and intra-task molecular representations demand different intrinsic dimensions in the language space, making it challenging to balance between redundancy and insufficiency in language model representations. To address these challenges, we innovatively categorize existing small-molecule tasks into four types: Mol2Mol, Mol2Text, Mol2Num, and Text2Mol. We then collect a dataset encompassing over 16 tasks with more than 1.4 million samples, making it the largest molecular instruction-tuning dataset to date. Leveraging the extensive pretraining of LLMs on existing chemical literature, we propose a novel multimodal LLM framework, named **Omni-Mol**, which unifies all small-molecule tasks and supports both molecular generation and understanding. The core of Omni-Mol is our proposed MoGE, which dynamically adapts to the intrinsic rank of different tasks. This mixture-of-experts architecture enhances the model's ability to handle diverse tasks and modalities effectively. Our model achieves unified instruction tuning across 16 tasks and attains state-of-the-art performance on 13 of them. Extensive experiments further demonstrate the scalability and versatility of Omni-Mol.

A shared model must accommodate these differences while learning useful common structure.

The model builds on chemical knowledge available through language-model pretraining and introduces MoGE, a mixture-of-experts architecture that dynamically adjusts to the intrinsic rank required by different tasks.

Unified instruction tuning covers 16 tasks, with state-of-the-art performance reported on 13. Additional experiments support the model's scalability and versatility. summary.tldr: Omni-Mol combines a large molecular instruction dataset with task-adaptive experts, achieving state-of-the-art results on 13 of 16 jointly tuned tasks.

title: Omni-Mol: Multitask Molecular Model for Any-to-any Modalities

abstract: 3D visual illusion is a perceptual phenomenon where a two-dimensional plane is manipulated to simulate three-dimensional spatial relationships, making a flat artwork or object look three-dimensional in the human visual system. In this paper, we reveal that the machine visual system is also seriously fooled by 3D visual illusions, including monocular and binocular depth estimation. In order to explore and analyze the impact of 3D visual illusion on depth estimation, we collect a large dataset containing almost 3k scenes and 200k images to train and evaluate SOTA monocular and binocular depth estimation methods. We also propose a 3D visual illusion depth estimation framework that uses common sense from the vision language model to adaptively fuse depth from binocular disparity and monocular depth. Experiments show that SOTA monocular, binocular, and multi-view depth estimation approaches are all fooled by various 3D visual illusions, while our method achieves SOTA performance.

paragraphs: A flat picture can appear to contain three-dimensional objects or spaces. This paper investigates whether depth-estimation systems make a similar mistake: interpreting depicted depth as actual physical depth. The authors find that these illusions can seriously mislead systems using a single image, stereo image pairs, or multiple views.

To study the problem systematically, they collect a dataset with almost 3,000 scenes and 200,000 images for training and evaluating depth-estimation methods. They also introduce a framework that combines depth inferred from a single image with depth derived from binocular disparity. A vision-language model supplies common-sense information to guide how the two estimates are combined adaptively.

The experiments show that leading methods across all three input settings are vulnerable to various visual illusions, while the proposed framework achieves the strongest reported performance. The contribution is both an evaluation resource and a method for handling conflicting depth cues. The findings show that access to additional views does not, by itself, prevent the tested systems from being fooled by apparent three-dimensional structure.
summary.tldr: A new dataset reveals visual-illusion failures in depth estimation, and a vision-language-guided fusion method improves performance.

title: 3D Visual Illusion Depth Estimation

abstract: Agile Earth Observation Satellites (AEOSs) constellations offer unprecedented flexibility for monitoring the Earth’s surface, but their scheduling remains challenging under large-scale scenarios, dynamic environments, and stringent constraints. Existing methods often simplify these complexities, limiting their real-world performance. We address this gap with a unified framework integrating a standardized benchmark suite and a novel scheduling model. Our benchmark suite, AEOS-Bench, contains $3,907$ finely tuned satellite assets and $16,410$ scenarios. Each scenario features $1$ to $50$ satellites and $50$ to $300$ imaging tasks. These scenarios are generated via a high-fidelity simulation platform, ensuring realistic satellite behavior such as orbital dynamics and resource constraints. Ground truth scheduling annotations are provided for each scenario. To our knowledge, AEOS-Bench is the first large-scale benchmark suite tailored for realistic constellation scheduling. Building upon this benchmark, we introduce AEOS-Former, a Transformer-based scheduling model that incorporates a constraint-aware attention mechanism. A dedicated internal constraint module explicitly models the physical and operational limits of each satellite. Through simulation-based iterative learning, AEOS-Former adapts to diverse scenarios, offering a robust solution for AEOS constellation scheduling. Experimental results demonstrate that AEOS-Former outperforms baseline models in task completion and energy efficiency, with ablation studies highlighting the contribution of each component. Code and data are provided in https://github.com/buaa-colalab/AEOSBench.

paragraphs: Scheduling an Earth-observation constellation requires assigning imaging work while respecting satellite motion, available resources, and operational restrictions. Simplified scheduling settings can miss these interacting constraints. This paper supplies both a benchmark intended to capture realistic behavior and a scheduling model designed to account for the resulting limits.

AEOS-Bench contains 3,907 configured satellite assets and 16,410 scenarios. Each scenario includes between one and 50 satellites and between 50 and 300 imaging tasks. A high-fidelity simulator generates orbital dynamics and resource constraints, and each scenario includes ground-truth scheduling annotations. The benchmark provides a common evaluation setting for schedules involving different constellation sizes and workloads.

It learns iteratively through simulation to adapt across scenarios. Experiments report better task completion and energy efficiency than baseline models, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components. The results support the proposed combination of realistic simulated evaluation and explicit constraint modeling for constellation scheduling.
summary.tldr: AEOS-Bench and AEOS-Former pair realistic satellite scheduling scenarios with a constraint-aware model that improves task completion and energy efficiency.

title: Towards Realistic Earth-Observation Constellation Scheduling: Benchmark and Methodology

abstract: Generative models have recently gained attention in recommendation systems by directly predicting item identifiers from user interaction sequences. However, existing methods suffer from significant information loss due to the separation of stages such as quantization and sequence modeling, hindering their ability to achieve the modeling precision and accuracy of sequential dense retrieval techniques. Integrating generative and dense retrieval methods remains a critical challenge. To address this, we introduce the Cascaded Organized Bi-Represented generAtive retrieval (COBRA) framework, which innovatively integrates sparse semantic IDs and dense vectors through a cascading process. Our method alternates between generating these representations by first generating sparse IDs, which serve as conditions to aid in the generation of dense vectors. End-to-end training enables dynamic refinement of dense representations, capturing both semantic insights and collaborative signals from user-item interactions. During inference, COBRA employs a coarse-to-fine strategy, starting with sparse ID generation and refining them into dense vectors via the generative model. We further propose BeamFusion, an innovative approach combining beam search with nearest neighbor scores to enhance inference flexibility and recommendation diversity. Extensive experiments on public datasets and offline tests validate our method's robustness. Online A/B tests on a real-world advertising platform with over 200 million daily users demonstrate substantial improvements in key metrics, highlighting COBRA's practical advantages.

paragraphs: Generative recommenders predict item identifiers from a user’s interaction history, but separating identifier construction from sequence modeling can lose useful information. Dense retrieval represents items with richer vectors and can offer finer distinctions. COBRA combines these representations in one generative framework to connect broad semantic organization with more detailed recommendation signals.

The model first generates sparse semantic identifiers, then uses them to condition the generation of dense vectors. End-to-end training allows the dense representations to change as the recommendation task is learned, incorporating semantic information and patterns in user-item interactions. Inference follows the same coarse-to-fine progression. BeamFusion further combines beam-search scores with nearest-neighbor scores to support flexible inference and recommendation diversity.

The authors evaluate the framework on public datasets, through offline tests, and in online A/B tests on an advertising platform serving more than 200 million daily users. They report robustness and substantial improvements in key online metrics. These findings support the practical value of training sparse and dense recommendation representations together and combining their strengths during retrieval.
summary.tldr: COBRA generates sparse item identifiers and conditioned dense vectors together, improving recommendation quality in offline and large-scale online evaluations.

title: Sparse Meets Dense: Unified Generative Recommendations with Cascaded Sparse-Dense Representations

abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) excel at complex reasoning tasks but typically generate lengthy sequential chains-of-thought, resulting in long inference times before arriving at the final answer. To address this challenge, we introduce SPRINT, a novel post-training and inference-time framework designed to enable LRMs to dynamically identify and exploit opportunities for parallelization during their reasoning process. SPRINT incorporates an innovative data curation pipeline that reorganizes natural language reasoning trajectories into structured rounds of long-horizon planning and parallel execution. By fine-tuning LRMs on a small amount of such curated data, the models learn to dynamically identify independent subtasks within extended reasoning processes and effectively execute them in parallel. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that models fine-tuned with the SPRINT framework match the performance of reasoning models on complex domains such as mathematics while generating up to 39% fewer sequential tokens on problems requiring more than 8,000 output tokens. Finally, we observe consistent results transferred to two out-of-distribution tasks, namely GPQA and Countdown, with up to 45% and 65% reduction in average sequential tokens respectively for longer reasoning trajectories, while matching the performance of the fine-tuned reasoning model.

paragraphs: Large reasoning models often produce long sequential reasoning traces, delaying the final answer. SPRINT aims to shorten the sequential portion by teaching models to identify independent subtasks that can run in parallel. Its framework covers both post-training and execution at inference time.

A data-curation pipeline reorganizes natural-language reasoning into rounds of longer-horizon planning and parallel execution. Fine-tuning on a small amount of this material teaches models to find parallelization opportunities as reasoning unfolds. Interleaving planning with execution allows the model to make those decisions dynamically throughout an extended solution.

In evaluations including mathematics, SPRINT-trained models match reasoning-model performance while generating up to 39% fewer sequential tokens on problems requiring more than 8,000 output tokens. On the out-of-distribution tasks GPQA and Countdown, longer trajectories show reductions of up to 45% and 65% in average sequential tokens while matching the fine-tuned reasoning model's performance. These measurements concern sequential tokens, showing reduced serial reasoning work in the reported settings.
summary.tldr: SPRINT teaches reasoning models to interleave planning with parallel subtask execution, reducing sequential tokens while preserving reported task performance.

title: SPRINT: Enabling Interleaved Planning and Parallelized Execution in Reasoning Models

abstract: We introduce IndEgo, a multimodal egocentric and exocentric dataset addressing common industrial tasks, including assembly/disassembly, logistics and organisation, inspection and repair, woodworking, and others. The dataset contains 3,460 egocentric recordings (approximately 197 hours), along with 1,092 exocentric recordings (approximately 97 hours). A key focus of the dataset is collaborative work, where two workers jointly perform cognitively and physically intensive tasks. The egocentric recordings include rich multimodal data and added context via eye gaze, narration, sound, motion, and others. We provide detailed annotations (actions, summaries, mistake annotations, narrations), metadata, processed outputs (eye gaze, hand pose, semi-dense point cloud), and benchmarks on procedural and non-procedural task understanding, Mistake Detection, and reasoning-based Question Answering. Baseline evaluations for Mistake Detection, Question Answering and collaborative task understanding show that the dataset presents a challenge for the state-of-the-art multimodal models. Our dataset is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/FraunhoferIPK/IndEgo

paragraphs: IndEgo is a dataset for studying assistants that understand industrial work from a worker's viewpoint and from external cameras. It covers activities such as assembly, disassembly, logistics, inspection, repair, and woodworking. A central emphasis is collaboration: two workers jointly carry out tasks that demand both physical effort and reasoning.

The collection includes 3,460 first-person recordings totaling approximately 197 hours, plus 1,092 external-view recordings totaling about 97 hours. First-person recordings combine contextual signals such as gaze, narration, audio, and motion. Annotations describe actions, summaries, mistakes, and narrations, while processed outputs include hand poses, gaze information, and semi-dense three-dimensional point clouds.

The authors also provide benchmarks for procedural and non-procedural task understanding, mistake detection, and reasoning-based question answering. Baseline evaluations show that mistake detection, question answering, and collaborative task understanding remain challenging for leading multimodal models. The dataset therefore supplies both varied observations of industrial work and structured ways to measure whether models understand the activities and interactions they observe.
summary.tldr: IndEgo combines first-person and external recordings of industrial collaboration with rich annotations and challenging multimodal understanding benchmarks.

title: IndEgo: A Dataset of Industrial Scenarios and Collaborative Work for Egocentric Assistants

abstract: Characterizing a large language model's (LLM's) knowledge of a given question is challenging. As a result, prior work has primarily examined LLM behavior under knowledge conflicts, where the model's internal parametric memory contradicts information in the external context. However, this does not fully reflect how well the model knows the answer to the question. In this paper, we first introduce a taxonomy of five knowledge statuses based on the consistency and correctness of LLM knowledge modes. We then propose KScope, a hierarchical framework of statistical tests that progressively refines hypotheses about knowledge modes and characterizes LLM knowledge into one of these five statuses. We apply KScope to nine LLMs across four datasets and systematically establish: (1) Supporting context narrows knowledge gaps across models. (2) Context features related to difficulty, relevance, and familiarity drive successful knowledge updates. (3) LLMs exhibit similar feature preferences when partially correct or conflicted, but diverge sharply when consistently wrong. (4) Context summarization constrained by our feature analysis, together with enhanced credibility, further improves update effectiveness and generalizes across LLMs.

paragraphs: A model's response to conflicting information reveals only part of what it knows. KScope instead characterizes knowledge using both correctness and consistency, distinguishing five possible statuses. This provides a richer description of a model's relationship to a question than simply checking whether its stored knowledge disagrees with supplied context.

The framework uses a hierarchy of statistical tests to refine hypotheses about the model's knowledge modes and assign a status. Applied to nine language models across four datasets, it shows that supporting context narrows knowledge gaps. Context difficulty, relevance, and familiarity are associated with successful updates, making the properties of the supplied information central to understanding when it helps.

The study also finds that models have similar preferences for context features when partially correct or conflicted, but differ sharply when consistently wrong. Guided by this feature analysis, context summarization combined with increased credibility improves update effectiveness and generalizes across models. KScope therefore connects measurement of existing knowledge with evidence about how to present useful new information.
summary.tldr: KScope statistically classifies five language-model knowledge statuses and identifies context properties that improve knowledge updates across evaluated models.

title: KScope: A Framework for Characterizing the Knowledge Status of Language Models

abstract: Joint Alignment (JA) of images aims to align a collection of images into a unified coordinate frame, such that semantically-similar features appear at corresponding spatial locations. Most existing approaches often require long training times, large-capacity models, and extensive hyperparameter tuning. We introduce FastJAM, a rapid, graph-based method that drastically reduces the computational complexity of joint alignment tasks. FastJAM leverages pairwise matches computed by an off-the-shelf image matcher, together with a rapid nonparametric clustering, to construct a graph representing intra- and inter-image keypoint relations. A graph neural network propagates and aggregates these correspondences, efficiently predicting per-image homography parameters via image-level pooling. Utilizing an inverse-compositional loss, that eliminates the need for a regularization term over the predicted transformations (and thus also obviates the hyperparameter tuning associated with such terms), FastJAM performs image JA quickly and effectively. Experimental results on several benchmarks demonstrate that FastJAM achieves results better than existing modern JA methods in terms of alignment quality, while reducing computation time from hours or minutes to mere seconds. Our code is available at our project webpage, https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/FastJAM/.

paragraphs: Joint image alignment places a collection of images into a shared coordinate system so corresponding semantic features occupy matching locations. Existing approaches can require lengthy training, large models, and extensive parameter tuning. FastJAM addresses these costs by organizing image correspondences into a graph and using that graph to predict the transformations needed for alignment.

The pipeline starts with pairwise matches from an existing image matcher. Rapid nonparametric clustering helps build a graph containing keypoint relationships within and across images. A graph neural network passes and combines correspondence information, then pools it at the image level to predict each image’s homography parameters. These parameters specify the transformations used to align the collection.

FastJAM also uses an inverse-compositional loss that removes the need for a regularization term on predicted transformations, along with the tuning associated with that term. Across several benchmarks, the authors report better alignment quality than modern comparison methods and computation reduced from minutes or hours to seconds. The results support a graph-based route to faster joint alignment.
summary.tldr: FastJAM uses a graph of image correspondences to improve joint alignment quality while reducing reported computation to seconds.

title: FastJAM: a Fast Joint Alignment Model for Images

abstract: Instruction tuning is essential for Large Language Models (LLMs) to effectively follow user instructions. To improve training efficiency and reduce data redundancy, recent works use LLM-based scoring functions, e.g., Instruction-Following Difficulty (IFD), to select high–quality instruction-tuning data with scores above a threshold. While these data selection methods often lead to models that can match or even exceed the performance of models trained on the full datasets, we identify two key limitations: (i) they assess quality at the sample level, ignoring token-level informativeness; and (ii) they overlook the robustness of the scoring method, often selecting a sample due to superficial lexical features instead of its true quality. In this work, we propose Token-Selective HIeRarchical Data Selection for Instruction Tuning (T-SHIRT), a novel data selection framework that introduces a new scoring method to include only informative tokens in quality evaluation and also promote robust and reliable samples whose neighbors also show high quality with less local inconsistencies. We demonstrate that models instruction-tuned on a curated dataset (only 5% of the original size) using T-SHIRT can outperform those trained on the entire large-scale dataset by up to 5.48 points on average across eight benchmarks. Across various LLMs and training set scales, our method consistently surpasses existing state-of-the-art data selection techniques, while also remaining both cost-effective and highly efficient. For instance, by using GPT-2 for score computation, we are able to process a dataset of 52k samples in 40 minutes on a single GPU. Our code is available at https://github.com/Dynamite321/T-SHIRT.

paragraphs: Selecting instruction-tuning examples can reduce redundant training data, but a high score for an entire example can hide two problems. Some tokens contribute little useful information, and superficial wording can distort the score. T-SHIRT addresses both the informativeness of individual tokens and the reliability of sample-level quality judgments.

Its scoring method considers only informative tokens when evaluating quality. It also favors examples whose neighboring samples receive consistently high scores, reducing reliance on isolated high scores with local inconsistencies. This hierarchical selection process combines evidence within an example with evidence about the stability of its quality assessment.

Models trained on T-SHIRT selections containing only 5% of the original data outperform full-dataset training by up to 5.48 points on average across eight benchmarks. The authors also report consistent advantages over existing selection methods across models and training scales. For scoring efficiency, a GPT-2-based setup processes 52,000 examples in 40 minutes on one GPU. Together, these results support selective curation as a means to improve both training efficiency and evaluated performance.
summary.tldr: T-SHIRT selects instruction data using informative tokens and locally consistent quality scores, achieving strong results with only 5% of the data.

title: T-SHIRT: Token-Selective Hierarchical Data Selection for Instruction Tuning

abstract: Recent advances in large reasoning models (LRMs) demonstrate that sophisticated behaviors such as multi-step reasoning and self-reflection can emerge via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards~(RLVR). However, existing RLVR approaches are inherently ``on-policy'', limiting learning to a model's own outputs and failing to acquire reasoning abilities beyond its initial capabilities. To address this issue, we introduce LUFFY (Learning to reason Under oFF-policY guidance), a framework that augments RLVR with off-policy reasoning traces. LUFFY dynamically balances imitation and exploration by combining off-policy demonstrations with on-policy rollouts during training. Specifically, LUFFY combines the Mixed-Policy GRPO framework, which has a theoretically guaranteed convergence rate, alongside policy shaping via regularized importance sampling to avoid superficial and rigid imitation during mixed-policy training. Compared with previous RLVR methods, LUFFY achieves an over +6.4 average gain across six math benchmarks and an advantage of over +6.2 points in out-of-distribution tasks. Most significantly, we show that LUFFY successfully trains weak models in scenarios where on-policy RLVR completely fails. These results provide compelling evidence that LUFFY transcends the fundamental limitations of on-policy RLVR and demonstrates the great potential of utilizing off-policy guidance in RLVR.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can develop multistep reasoning, but learning only from a model's own outputs restricts the reasoning examples it encounters. LUFFY introduces externally supplied reasoning traces into this process. Its aim is to let a model learn from demonstrations beyond its current behavior while continuing to explore through its own generated solutions.

The framework combines off-policy demonstrations with on-policy rollouts and dynamically balances imitation and exploration. Its Mixed-Policy GRPO component has a theoretically guaranteed convergence rate. A second component shapes the policy through regularized importance sampling, addressing the risk that mixed-policy learning becomes superficial or overly rigid imitation of the supplied traces.

Compared with previous methods, the authors report an average gain exceeding 6.4 points across six mathematics benchmarks and an advantage exceeding 6.2 points on out-of-distribution tasks. They also demonstrate successful training of weak models in scenarios where on-policy training fails completely. These results provide evidence that external reasoning guidance can overcome capability barriers encountered by learning solely from self-generated outputs in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: LUFFY mixes external reasoning demonstrations with a model's own rollouts, improving reasoning and enabling training where on-policy methods fail.

title: Learning to Reason under Off-Policy Guidance

abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong performance in general-purpose visual understanding and reasoning, but their ability to comprehend the visual grammar of movie shots remains underexplored and insufficiently evaluated. To bridge this gap, we present \textbf{ShotBench}, a dedicated benchmark for assessing VLMs’ understanding of cinematic language. ShotBench includes 3,049 still images and 500 video clips drawn from more than 200 films, with each sample annotated by trained annotators or curated from professional cinematography resources, resulting in 3,608 high-quality question-answer pairs. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of over 20 state-of-the-art VLMs across eight core cinematography dimensions. Our analysis reveals clear limitations in fine-grained perception and cinematic reasoning of current VLMs. To improve VLMs capability in cinematography understanding, we construct a large-scale multimodal dataset, named ShotQA, which contains about 70k Question-Answer pairs derived from movie shots. Besides, we propose ShotVL and train this VLM model with a two-stage training strategy, integrating both supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves substantial improvements, surpassing all existing strongest open-source and proprietary models evaluated on ShotBench, establishing a new state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: ShotBench evaluates whether vision-language models understand the visual language of filmmaking. Strong general visual reasoning does not by itself establish this specialized ability. It contains 3,049 still images and 500 clips from more than 200 films, with 3,608 question–answer pairs spanning eight cinematography dimensions. Evaluation of more than 20 leading models reveals limitations in fine-grained perception and cinematic reasoning. These results make the benchmark useful for distinguishing broad visual competence from the more specific understanding required to interpret movie shots.

The authors also create ShotQA, a training dataset of approximately 70,000 question–answer pairs, and train ShotVL through supervised fine-tuning followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization. ShotVL surpasses all open-source and proprietary models evaluated on ShotBench. The work therefore contributes both a specialized assessment and a training approach that substantially improves performance on that assessment.
summary.tldr: ShotBench exposes gaps in cinematic understanding, while the authors’ ShotVL model outperforms all evaluated competitors on the benchmark.

title: ShotBench: Expert-Level Cinematic Understanding in Vision-Language Models

abstract: Time series analysis provides essential insights for real-world system dynamics and informs downstream decision-making, yet most existing methods often overlook the rich contextual signals present in auxiliary modalities. To bridge this gap, we introduce TimeXL, a multi-modal prediction framework that integrates a prototype-based time series encoder with three collaborating Large Language Models (LLMs) to deliver more accurate predictions and interpretable explanations. First, a multi-modal prototype-based encoder processes both time series and textual inputs to generate preliminary forecasts alongside case-based rationales. These outputs then feed into a prediction LLM, which refines the forecasts by reasoning over the encoder's predictions and explanations. Next, a reflection LLM compares the predicted values against the ground truth, identifying textual inconsistencies or noise. Guided by this feedback, a refinement LLM iteratively enhances text quality and triggers encoder retraining. This closed-loop workflow---prediction, critique (reflect), and refinement---continuously boosts the framework's performance and interpretability. Empirical evaluations on four real-world datasets demonstrate that TimeXL achieves up to 8.9\% improvement in AUC and produces human-centric, multi-modal explanations, highlighting the power of LLM-driven reasoning for time series prediction.

paragraphs: Time series can be accompanied by text that helps explain the system being observed. TimeXL uses that context together with numerical observations to produce predictions and explanations. Its starting point is a prototype-based encoder that processes both modalities and generates preliminary forecasts with case-based rationales, connecting predictions to representative patterns.

Three language models then take distinct roles in a feedback loop. A prediction model reasons over the encoder's forecasts and explanations to refine the output. A reflection model compares predictions with ground truth and identifies inconsistent or noisy text. A refinement model uses that feedback to improve the text and trigger another round of encoder training.

Evaluations on four real-world datasets report improvements of up to 8.9% in AUC and explanations that combine temporal and textual information. The approach makes contextual text an input that can be revised through feedback, alongside refining predictions. Its stated gains support integrating prediction, critique, and text refinement within an explainable multimodal time-series framework.
summary.tldr: TimeXL combines prototype-based time-series modeling with three language models that refine forecasts, critique errors, and improve contextual text.

title: TimeXL: Explainable Multi-modal Time Series Prediction with LLM-in-the-Loop

abstract: Vision-language models have demonstrated impressive capabilities as computer-use agents (CUAs) capable of automating diverse computer tasks. As their commercial potential grows, critical details of the most capable CUA systems remain closed. As these agents will increasingly mediate digital interactions and execute consequential decisions on our behalf, the research community needs access to open CUA frameworks to study their capabilities, limitations, and risks. To bridge this gap, we propose OpenCUA, a comprehensive open-source framework for scaling CUA data and foundation models. Our framework consists of: (1) an annotation infrastructure that seamlessly captures human computer-use demonstrations; (2) AgentNet, the first large-scale computer-use task dataset spanning 3 operating systems and 200+ applications and websites; (3) a scalable pipeline that transforms demonstrations into state–action pairs with reflective long Chain-of-Thought reasoning that sustain robust performance gains as data scales. Our end-to-end agent models demonstrate strong performance across CUA benchmarks. In particular, OpenCUA-72B achieves an average success rate of 45.0% on OSWorld‑Verified, establishing a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) among open-source models. Further analysis confirms that our approach generalizes well across domains and benefits significantly from increased test-time computation. We release our annotation tool, datasets, code, and models to build open foundations for further CUA research.

OpenCUA addresses the research community's need to inspect and develop these systems by providing an open framework covering demonstration collection, training data, processing infrastructure, and agent models.

An annotation tool captures human computer-use demonstrations. The resulting AgentNet dataset spans three operating systems and more than 200 applications and websites. A scalable processing pipeline turns demonstrations into state-action pairs accompanied by reflective, extended reasoning. The authors report that this pipeline sustains performance gains as the amount of data increases, connecting the collection infrastructure with scalable model training.

OpenCUA-72B achieves an average success rate of 45.0% on OSWorld-Verified, which the authors report as a new best result among open-source models. Further analysis finds good cross-domain generalization and substantial benefits from additional computation at test time. Releasing the tools, data, code, and models provides a concrete foundation for studying computer-use capabilities, limitations, and risks.
summary.tldr: OpenCUA releases a full computer-use-agent framework, with its 72B model achieving 45.0% average success on OSWorld-Verified.

title: OpenCUA: Open Foundations for Computer-Use Agents

abstract: Physics‑Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) often exhibit “failure modes” in which the PDE residual loss converges while the solution error stays large, a phenomenon traditionally blamed on local optima separated from the true solution by steep loss barriers. We challenge this understanding by demonstrate that the real culprit is insufficient arithmetic precision: with standard FP32, the L‑BFGS optimizer prematurely satisfies its convergence test, freezing the network in a spurious failure phase. Simply upgrading to FP64 rescues optimization, enabling vanilla PINNs to solve PDEs without any failure modes. These results reframe PINN failure modes as precision‑induced stalls rather than inescapable local minima and expose a three‑stage training dynamic—un‑converged, failure, success—whose boundaries shift with numerical precision. Our findings emphasize that rigorous arithmetic precision is the key to dependable PDE solving with neural networks. Our code is available at Supplementary Material.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks can appear to finish optimizing their differential-equation residual loss while still producing an inaccurate solution. These failures have traditionally been attributed to local optima separated from the correct solution by steep barriers in the loss landscape. This paper challenges that explanation by examining arithmetic precision and the optimizer's stopping behavior.

The authors identify a mechanism in which standard FP32 arithmetic causes L-BFGS to satisfy its convergence test prematurely. Training then freezes in a misleading failure phase. Switching to FP64 restores optimization and allows vanilla PINNs to solve the studied differential-equation problems without the reported failure modes. The change concerns numerical precision rather than a redesigned network or training objective.

The analysis describes three training phases: unconverged, failure, and success. Their boundaries shift with numerical precision, supporting the interpretation that the apparent failures are precision-induced stalls. The findings make optimizer convergence checks central to understanding these results: a stopping signal can reflect numerical limitations even when the learned solution remains inaccurate.
summary.tldr: The paper attributes reported PINN failure modes to premature L-BFGS convergence under FP32 and shows that FP64 restores successful optimization.

title: FP64 is All You Need: Rethinking Failure Modes in Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Scaffolding Large Language Models (LLMs) into multi-agent systems often improves performance on complex tasks, but the safety impact of such scaffolds has not been thoroughly explored. We introduce AgentBreeder, a framework for multi-objective self-improving evolutionary search over scaffolds. We evaluate discovered scaffolds on widely recognized reasoning, mathematics, and safety benchmarks and compare them with popular baselines. In "blue" mode, we see a 79.4% average uplift in safety benchmark performance while maintaining or improving capability scores. In "red" mode, we find adversarially weak scaffolds emerging concurrently with capability optimization. Our work demonstrates the risks of multi-agent scaffolding and provides a framework for mitigating them. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/jrosseruk/AgentBreeder}.

paragraphs: Organizing language models into a multi-agent system can improve performance on complex tasks, but the surrounding organization can also affect safety. This paper studies that organization, called a scaffold, as something to optimize and evaluate in its own right. Its central concern is whether improvements in task capability come with improvements or weaknesses in safety.

AgentBreeder uses an evolutionary search that repeatedly develops and evaluates candidate scaffolds against multiple objectives. This makes the arrangement of agents part of the improvement process. The researchers assess the discovered systems on reasoning, mathematics, and safety benchmarks, comparing them with established baselines rather than evaluating capability alone.

In its blue mode, the framework produces a reported average safety benchmark uplift of 79.4% while preserving or improving capability scores. In red mode, adversarially weak scaffolds emerge alongside capability optimization. These findings show that scaffold design can influence both capability and safety in the evaluated settings, and that explicitly searching for safety improvements offers a way to address those risks.
summary.tldr: AgentBreeder searches for multi-agent designs that improve safety and capability while exposing safety weaknesses that can accompany capability optimization.

title: AgentBreeder: Mitigating the AI Safety Risks of Multi-Agent Scaffolds via Self-Improvement

abstract: Light field microscopy (LFM) has become an emerging tool in neuroscience for large-scale neural imaging in vivo, with XLFM (eXtended Light Field Microscopy) notable for its single-exposure volumetric imaging, broad field of view, and high temporal resolution. However, learning-based 3D reconstruction in XLFM remains underdeveloped due to two core challenges: the absence of standardized datasets and the lack of methods that can efficiently model its angular–spatial structure while remaining physically grounded. We address these challenges by introducing three key contributions. First, we construct the XLFM-Zebrafish benchmark, a large-scale dataset and evaluation suite for XLFM reconstruction. Second, we propose Masked View Modeling for Light Fields (MVM-LF), a self-supervised task that learns angular priors by predicting occluded views, improving data efficiency. Third, we formulate the Optical Rendering Consistency Loss (ORC Loss), a differentiable rendering constraint that enforces alignment between predicted volumes and their PSF-based forward projections. On the XLFM-Zebrafish benchmark, our method improves PSNR by 7.7\% over state-of-the-art baselines. Code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/hefengcs/XLFM-Former.

paragraphs: Extended light field microscopy can capture volumetric information in a single exposure over a broad field of view. Reconstructing a three-dimensional volume from those measurements requires using both spatial and angular information. This paper addresses two obstacles to learned reconstruction: a lack of standardized evaluation data and difficulty combining efficient representations with the microscope's imaging physics.

The authors introduce the XLFM-Zebrafish dataset and evaluation suite. They also propose Masked View Modeling for Light Fields, a self-supervised task that predicts hidden views to learn relationships across viewing angles. A separate optical rendering consistency loss ties the reconstructed volume to the measurement process by comparing its point-spread-function-based forward projections with the observed data.

These components connect learning from incomplete views with checking whether a predicted volume agrees with the optical formation process. On the XLFM-Zebrafish benchmark, the method improves PSNR by 7.7% over state-of-the-art baselines. The stated result supports the combination of angular representation learning and physical consistency for reconstruction, while the benchmark provides a common setting for evaluating such methods.
summary.tldr: A zebrafish microscopy benchmark, masked-view learning, and optical consistency constraints improve learned volumetric reconstruction.

title: From Pixels to Views: Learning Angular-Aware and Physics-Consistent Representations for Light Field Microscopy

abstract: While reinforcement learning (RL) over chains of thought has significantly advanced language models in tasks such as mathematics and coding, visual reasoning introduces added complexity by requiring models to direct visual attention, interpret perceptual inputs, and ground abstract reasoning in spatial evidence. We introduce ViGoRL (**Vi**sually **G**r**o**unded **R**einforcement **L**earning), a vision-language model trained with RL to explicitly anchor each reasoning step to specific visual coordinates. Inspired by human visual decision-making, ViGoRL learns to produce spatially grounded reasoning traces, guiding visual attention to task-relevant regions at each step. When fine-grained exploration is required, our novel multi-turn RL framework enables the model to dynamically zoom into predicted coordinates as reasoning unfolds. Across a diverse set of visual reasoning benchmarks—including SAT-2 and BLINK for spatial reasoning, V$^\*$bench for visual search, and ScreenSpot and VisualWebArena for web-based grounding—ViGoRL consistently outperforms both supervised fine-tuning and conventional RL baselines that lack explicit grounding mechanisms. Incorporating multi-turn RL with zoomed-in visual feedback significantly improves ViGoRL’s performance on localizing small GUI elements and visual search, achieving 86.4% on V$^\*$Bench. Additionally, we find that grounding amplifies other visual behaviors such as region exploration, grounded subgoal setting, and visual verification. Finally, human evaluations show that the model’s visual references are not only spatially accurate but also helpful for understanding model reasoning steps. Our results show that visually grounded RL is a strong paradigm for imbuing models with general-purpose visual reasoning.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning requires a model to connect its reasoning with relevant parts of an image. A verbal reasoning sequence alone does not establish where the supporting visual evidence lies. ViGoRL addresses this by using reinforcement learning to train a vision-language model to associate each reasoning step with specific image coordinates.

These spatial references guide attention as the model works through a task. When finer inspection is useful, a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework lets it zoom into predicted locations and continue reasoning with the resulting visual feedback. This makes region selection and closer inspection part of the learned reasoning process, including for small interface elements and visual search.

Human evaluations find the references spatially accurate and helpful for understanding the reasoning steps, linking improved performance with more interpretable visual evidence.
summary.tldr: ViGoRL learns to ground reasoning steps in image coordinates and zoom into relevant regions, improving visual reasoning performance.

title: Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Visual Reasoning

abstract: We study the dynamics of gradient flow with small weight decay on general training losses $F: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$. Under mild regularity assumptions and assuming convergence of the unregularised gradient flow, we show that the trajectory with weight decay $\lambda$ exhibits a two-phase behaviour as $\lambda \to 0$. During the initial fast phase, the trajectory follows the unregularised gradient flow and converges to a manifold of critical points of $F$. Then, at time of order $1/\lambda$, the trajectory enters a slow drift phase and follows a Riemannian gradient flow minimising the $\ell_2$-norm of the parameters. This purely optimisation-based phenomenon offers a natural explanation for the \textit{grokking} effect observed in deep learning, where the training loss rapidly reaches zero while the test loss plateaus for an extended period before suddenly improving. We argue that this generalisation jump can be attributed to the slow norm reduction induced by weight decay, as explained by our analysis. We validate this mechanism empirically on several synthetic regression tasks.
originalAbstract: We study the dynamics of gradient flow with small weight decay on general training losses $F: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$. Under mild regularity assumptions and assuming convergence of the unregularised gradient flow, we show that the trajectory with weight decay $\lambda$ exhibits a two-phase behaviour as $\lambda \to 0$. During the initial fast phase, the trajectory follows the unregularised gradient flow and converges to a manifold of critical points of $F$. Then, at time of order $1/\lambda$, the trajectory enters a slow drift phase and follows a Riemannian gradient flow minimising the $\ell_2$-norm of the parameters. This purely optimisation-based phenomenon offers a natural explanation for the \textit{grokking} effect observed in deep learning, where the training loss rapidly reaches zero while the test loss plateaus for an extended period before suddenly improving. We argue that this generalisation jump can be attributed to the slow norm reduction induced by weight decay, as explained by our analysis. We validate this mechanism empirically on several synthetic regression tasks.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a training pattern in which a model fits its training examples early but improves on test examples much later. This paper investigates whether optimization itself can explain that delay. It studies continuous-time gradient flow with small weight decay, which encourages parameters to have a smaller overall magnitude.

Under mild regularity assumptions and convergence of the unregularized gradient flow, the authors establish two phases as weight decay approaches zero. Initially, the parameters follow approximately the path they would take without weight decay, reaching a manifold of critical points of the training loss. On a timescale proportional to the inverse weight-decay strength, a slower motion then emerges.

That slow motion follows a Riemannian gradient flow that reduces parameter norm while respecting the geometry of the critical-point manifold. The authors argue that this delayed norm reduction can account for a later jump in generalization. Experiments on synthetic regression tasks support the proposed mechanism. The result offers an optimization-based explanation for grokking under the stated assumptions, rather than establishing that every observed grokking event has this cause.
summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, small weight decay produces a slow norm-reduction phase that offers an explanation for delayed generalization.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Grokking: Interpolation followed by Riemannian Norm Minimisation

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), as a thriving field, explores how multiple agents independently make decisions in a shared dynamic environment. Due to environmental uncertainties, policies in MARL must remain robust to tackle the sim-to-real gap. We focus on robust two-player zero-sum Markov games (TZMGs) in offline settings, specifically on tabular robust TZMGs (RTZMGs). We propose a model-based algorithm (*RTZ-VI-LCB*) for offline RTZMGs, which is optimistic robust value iteration combined with a data-driven Bernstein-style penalty term for robust value estimation. By accounting for distribution shifts in the historical dataset, the proposed algorithm establishes near-optimal sample complexity guarantees under partial coverage and environmental uncertainty. An information-theoretic lower bound is developed to confirm the tightness of our algorithm's sample complexity, which is optimal regarding both state and action spaces. To the best of our knowledge, RTZ-VI-LCB is the first to attain this optimality, sets a new benchmark for offline RTZMGs, and is validated experimentally.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning robust strategies for two-player zero-sum Markov games from historical data. The setting is tabular, meaning states and actions are represented explicitly, and offline, meaning learning relies on an existing dataset. Environmental uncertainty and distribution shifts make it necessary to reason about performance beyond the exact conditions represented in that dataset.

The proposed model-based algorithm, RTZ-VI-LCB, combines optimistic robust value iteration with a data-dependent Bernstein-style penalty for estimating robust values. Its analysis accounts for shifts in the historical data and establishes near-optimal sample complexity under partial coverage and environmental uncertainty. Sample complexity describes how much data is needed to achieve the learning guarantee.

The authors also derive an information-theoretic lower bound to assess how close the algorithm comes to the best possible data requirements. This establishes optimal dependence on the sizes of the state and action spaces. Experimental validation accompanies the theory. The result advances sample-efficient offline learning within the specified robust tabular game setting, with particularly strong guarantees about scaling in states and actions.
summary.tldr: RTZ-VI-LCB learns robust strategies from offline game data with near-optimal sample complexity and optimal state–action scaling.

title: Sample-Efficient Tabular Self-Play for Offline Robust Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the problem of structured output learning from a regression perspective. We first provide a general formulation of the kernel dependency estimation (KDE) approach to this problem using operator-valued kernels. Our formulation overcomes the two main limitations of the original KDE approach, namely the decoupling between outputs in the image space and the inability to use a joint feature space. We then propose a covariance-based operator-valued kernel that allows us to take into account the structure of the kernel feature space. This kernel operates on the output space and only encodes the interactions between the outputs without any reference to the input space. To address this issue, we introduce a variant of our KDE method based on the conditional covariance operator that in addition to the correlation between the outputs takes into account the effects of the input variables. Finally, we evaluate the performance of our KDE approach using both covariance and conditional covariance kernels on three structured output problems, and compare it to the state-of-the art kernel-based structured output regression methods.

paragraphs: Structured output learning predicts outputs whose parts have meaningful relationships. This paper approaches that problem through regression, extending kernel dependency estimation with operator-valued kernels. The formulation addresses two restrictions of the original approach: treating outputs separately in the transformed space and being unable to use a joint feature space.

The authors first construct a kernel using covariance, which describes how outputs vary together. This lets the method represent interactions within the output feature space. However, those interactions alone do not account for the inputs. A second construction uses conditional covariance to incorporate both relationships among outputs and the effects of input variables.

The distinction matters because output relationships and input-dependent relationships offer different information for prediction. The paper evaluates both constructions on three structured output problems and compares them with existing kernel-based regression methods. The abstract establishes the expanded modeling framework and the scope of evaluation, without claiming that either construction consistently wins.
summary.tldr: An expanded kernel regression framework models relationships among structured outputs and, through conditional covariance, their dependence on inputs.

title: A Generalized Kernel Approach to Structured Output Learning

abstract: We propose a method for producing ensembles of predictors based on holdout estimations of their generalization performances. This approach uses a prior directly on the performance of predictors taken from a finite set of candidates and attempts to infer which one is best. Using Bayesian inference, we can thus obtain a posterior that represents our uncertainty about that choice and construct a weighted ensemble of predictors accordingly. This approach has the advantage of not requiring that the predictors be probabilistic themselves, can deal with arbitrary measures of performance and does not assume that the data was actually generated from any of the predictors in the ensemble. Since the problem of finding the best (as opposed to the true) predictor among a class is known as agnostic PAC-learning, we refer to our method as agnostic Bayesian learning. We also propose a method to address the case where the performance estimate is obtained from k-fold cross validation. While being efficient and easily adjustable to any loss function, our experiments confirm that the agnostic Bayes approach is state of the art compared to common baselines such as model selection based on k-fold cross-validation or a linear combination of predictor outputs.
