This approach has the advantage of not requiring that the predictors be probabilistic themselves, can deal with arbitrary measures of performance and does not assume that the data was actually generated from any of the predictors in the ensemble. Since the problem of finding the best (as opposed to the true) predictor among a class is known as agnostic PAC-learning, we refer to our method as agnostic Bayesian learning. We also propose a method to address the case where the performance estimate is obtained from k-fold cross validation. While being efficient and easily adjustable to any loss function, our experiments confirm that the agnostic Bayes approach is state of the art compared to common baselines such as model selection based on k-fold cross-validation or a linear combination of predictor outputs.

paragraphs: Choosing a predictor from validation results involves uncertainty: measured performance does not identify the best candidate with certainty. This paper uses that uncertainty to construct an ensemble. Starting from a finite set of predictors, it places a prior on their performance and updates it using estimates from held-out data.

The resulting Bayesian posterior expresses uncertainty about which predictor is best. The method uses that posterior to form a weighted ensemble. Because the Bayesian reasoning concerns performance, the candidate predictors need not produce probabilities themselves. The approach also accommodates arbitrary performance measures and does not assume that any candidate generated the observed data.

The authors additionally address performance estimates obtained through k-fold cross-validation, connecting the approach to a common evaluation procedure. Their experiments report state-of-the-art performance against baselines including cross-validation-based model selection and linear combinations of predictor outputs. The contribution is a flexible way to turn evidence about predictive quality into ensemble weights, while explicitly retaining uncertainty about the choice of the best predictor.
summary.tldr: Agnostic Bayesian learning builds ensembles by modeling uncertainty about candidate predictors' generalization performance.

title: Agnostic Bayesian Learning of Ensembles

abstract: This paper introduces a new topic model based on an admixture of Poisson Markov Random Fields (APM), which can model dependencies between words as opposed to previous independent topic models such as PLSA (Hofmann, 1999), LDA (Blei et al., 2003) or SAM (Reisinger et al., 2010). We propose a class of admixture models that generalizes previous topic models and show an equivalence between the conditional distribution of LDA and independent Poissons—suggesting that APM subsumes the modeling power of LDA. We present a tractable method for estimating the parameters of an APM based on the pseudo log-likelihood and demonstrate the benefits of APM over previous models by preliminary qualitative and quantitative experiments.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces a new topic model based on an admixture of Poisson Markov Random Fields (APM), which can model dependencies between words as opposed to previous independent topic models such as PLSA (Hofmann, 1999), LDA (Blei et al., 2003) or SAM (Reisinger et al., 2010). We propose a class of admixture models that generalizes previous topic models and show an equivalence between the conditional distribution of LDA and independent Poissons—suggesting that APM subsumes the modeling power of LDA. We present a tractable method for estimating the parameters of an APM based on the pseudo log-likelihood and demonstrate the benefits of APM over previous models by preliminary qualitative and quantitative experiments.

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents through mixtures of underlying topics. This paper introduces an admixture of Poisson Markov Random Fields, called APM, that can represent dependencies between words. The motivation is to make relationships among words part of the model, extending beyond the independent topic models identified in the abstract.

The authors develop a broader class of admixture models that generalizes earlier approaches. They also establish an equivalence between LDA's conditional distribution and independent Poisson distributions. This connection suggests that APM subsumes LDA's modeling power: the proposed framework has a mathematical link to an established topic model while allowing word dependencies to enter the representation.

To make parameter estimation tractable, the paper uses a pseudo log-likelihood objective. This provides a concrete estimation method alongside the more expressive model. Preliminary qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate benefits over previous models. These results support the usefulness of modeling word relationships, while their explicitly preliminary status keeps the empirical conclusion narrower than a general claim of superiority across document collections.
summary.tldr: APM extends topic modeling to capture word dependencies, with tractable estimation and preliminary evidence of benefits over earlier models.

title: Admixture of Poisson MRFs: A Topic Model with Word Dependencies

abstract: We present a new probabilistic model of compact commutative Lie groups that produces invariant-equivariant and disentangled representations of data. To define the notion of disentangling, we borrow a fundamental principle from physics that is used to derive the elementary particles of a system from its symmetries. Our model employs a newfound Bayesian conjugacy relation that enables fully tractable probabilistic inference over compact commutative Lie groups – a class that includes the groups that describe the rotation and cyclic translation of images. We train the model on pairs of transformed image patches, and show that the learned invariant representation is highly effective for classification.

To define the notion of disentangling, we borrow a fundamental principle from physics that is used to derive the elementary particles of a system from its symmetries. Our model employs a newfound Bayesian conjugacy relation that enables fully tractable probabilistic inference over compact commutative Lie groups – a class that includes the groups that describe the rotation and cyclic translation of images. We train the model on pairs of transformed image patches, and show that the learned invariant representation is highly effective for classification.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic model for learning representations organized around transformations of data. It targets compact commutative Lie groups, a class that includes image rotations and cyclic translations. The model produces invariant, equivariant, and disentangled representations, connecting how data change under transformations with how their representations are structured.

The authors define disentangling using a symmetry-based principle borrowed from physics, where a system's elementary components are understood through its symmetries. A newly identified Bayesian conjugacy relation makes probabilistic inference fully tractable over the supported group class. That tractability is central: the model can reason probabilistically about these transformations without leaving the mathematical setting in which inference is manageable.

Training uses pairs of image patches related by transformations. The authors show that the learned invariant representation is highly effective for classification. This gives an application-level result for the symmetry-based construction: a representation designed to remain stable under the modeled transformations can also be useful for recognizing classes. The tractability claim is specifically tied to compact commutative Lie groups, rather than arbitrary transformation families.
summary.tldr: A tractable probabilistic model of compact commutative Lie groups learns symmetry-based representations that are effective for image-patch classification.

title: Learning the Irreducible Representations of Commutative Lie Groups

abstract: An important question in feature selection is whether a selection strategy recovers the “true” set of features, given enough data. We study this question in the context of the popular Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso) feature selection strategy. In particular, we consider the scenario when the model is misspecified so that the learned model is linear while the underlying real target is nonlinear. Surprisingly, we prove that under certain conditions, Lasso is still able to recover the correct features in this case. We also carry out numerical studies to empirically verify the theoretical results and explore the necessity of the conditions under which the proof holds.
originalAbstract: An important question in feature selection is whether a selection strategy recovers the “true” set of features, given enough data. We study this question in the context of the popular Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (Lasso) feature selection strategy. In particular, we consider the scenario when the model is misspecified so that the learned model is linear while the underlying real target is nonlinear. Surprisingly, we prove that under certain conditions, Lasso is still able to recover the correct features in this case. We also carry out numerical studies to empirically verify the theoretical results and explore the necessity of the conditions under which the proof holds.

paragraphs: Feature selection asks which input variables truly matter for a target. This paper studies whether Lasso can recover that set when given enough data, even when its fitted linear model does not match the target’s nonlinear form. The question separates identifying relevant variables from correctly representing the full relationship between inputs and outputs.

The authors prove that, under certain conditions, Lasso can still recover the correct features despite this mismatch. The result matters because fitting an incorrect functional form does not automatically prevent useful variable identification. At the same time, the claim is conditional: it does not establish that arbitrary nonlinear targets are suitable for feature recovery using a linear Lasso model.

Numerical studies serve two purposes. They check the theoretical result empirically and investigate whether the conditions used in the proof are necessary. This combines a positive recovery result with exploration of its scope. The central finding is that feature-selection consistency can survive some forms of model misspecification, provided the conditions supporting the result hold.
summary.tldr: Under certain conditions, Lasso can consistently identify the correct features even when the true target is nonlinear.

title: On the Consistency of Feature Selection With Lasso for Non-linear Targets

abstract: We study an online learning framework introduced by Mannor and Shamir (2011) in which the feedback is specified by a graph, in a setting where the graph may vary from round to round and is \emphnever fully revealed to the learner. We show a large gap between the adversarial and the stochastic cases. In the adversarial case, we prove that even for dense feedback graphs, the learner cannot improve upon a trivial regret bound obtained by ignoring any additional feedback besides her own loss. In contrast, in the stochastic case we give an algorithm that achieves \widetildeΘ(\sqrtαT) regret over T rounds, provided that the independence numbers of the hidden feedback graphs are at most α. We also extend our results to a more general feedback model, in which the learner does not necessarily observe her own loss, and show that, even in simple cases, concealing the feedback graphs might render the problem unlearnable.
originalAbstract: We study an online learning framework introduced by Mannor and Shamir (2011) in which the feedback is specified by a graph, in a setting where the graph may vary from round to round and is \emphnever fully revealed to the learner. We show a large gap between the adversarial and the stochastic cases. In the adversarial case, we prove that even for dense feedback graphs, the learner cannot improve upon a trivial regret bound obtained by ignoring any additional feedback besides her own loss. In contrast, in the stochastic case we give an algorithm that achieves \widetildeΘ(\sqrtαT) regret over T rounds, provided that the independence numbers of the hidden feedback graphs are at most α. We also extend our results to a more general feedback model, in which the learner does not necessarily observe her own loss, and show that, even in simple cases, concealing the feedback graphs might render the problem unlearnable.

paragraphs: Feedback graphs describe which losses a learner can observe after taking an action. This paper studies online learning when those graphs can change each round and are never fully disclosed. The learner receives feedback without complete knowledge of the structure governing which observations become available.

The authors prove a sharp distinction between adversarial and stochastic settings. In the adversarial case, even dense graphs cannot improve the guaranteed regret beyond the trivial bound obtained by using only the learner's own loss. In the stochastic case, their algorithm achieves regret of order √(αT), up to logarithmic factors, when every hidden graph has independence number at most α.

The paper also considers a more general setting where an action need not reveal its own loss. There, hiding the graph can make learning impossible even in simple cases. These results show that the usefulness of additional feedback depends on both the process generating losses and knowledge of the observation structure, rather than solely on how many observations might be available.
summary.tldr: Hidden feedback graphs permit strong stochastic regret guarantees but can eliminate the benefits of extra feedback in adversarial settings.

title: Online Learning with Feedback Graphs Without the Graphs

abstract: Successfully recommending personalized course schedules is a difficult problem given the diversity of students knowledge, learning behaviour, and goals. This paper presents personalized course recommendation and curriculum design algorithms that exploit logged student data. The algorithms are based on the regression estimator for contextual multi-armed bandits with a penalized variance term. Guarantees on the predictive performance of the algorithms are provided using empirical Bernstein bounds. We also provide guidelines for including expert domain knowledge into the recommendations. Using undergraduate engineering logged data from a post-secondary institution we illustrate the performance of these algorithms.

Guarantees on the predictive performance of the algorithms are provided using empirical Bernstein bounds. We also provide guidelines for including expert domain knowledge into the recommendations. Using undergraduate engineering logged data from a post-secondary institution we illustrate the performance of these algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper develops algorithms for personalized course recommendations and curriculum design using logged student data. Personalization is challenging because students differ in their knowledge, learning behavior, and goals. The proposed approach uses historical observations to inform recommendations while explicitly addressing the reliability of the predictions used to make them.

The algorithms build on a regression estimator for contextual multi-armed bandits and add a variance penalty. This connects recommendation to a framework in which the usefulness of a choice depends on the student’s context. The variance term makes variability part of the recommendation criterion. The authors provide predictive-performance guarantees using empirical Bernstein bounds, giving the approach a statistical basis for assessing its predictions.

The paper also provides guidance for incorporating expert domain knowledge into recommendations. Its empirical illustration uses logged data from undergraduate engineering students at a post-secondary institution. Together, these contributions combine historical-data modeling, uncertainty-sensitive evaluation, and expert input in an approach to educational recommendations and curriculum design.
summary.tldr: Course recommendation algorithms combine logged student data, variance-penalized prediction, statistical guarantees, and guidance for incorporating expert knowledge.

title: Bounded Off-Policy Evaluation with Missing Data for Course Recommendation and Curriculum Design

abstract: Causal inference among high-dimensional time series data proves an important research problem in many fields. While in the classical regime one often establishes causality among time series via a concept known as “Granger causality,” existing approaches for Granger causal inference in high-dimensional data lack the means to characterize the uncertainty associated with Granger causality estimates (e.g., p-values and confidence intervals). We make two contributions in this work. First, we introduce a novel asymptotically unbiased Granger causality estimator with corresponding test statistics and confidence intervals to allow, for the first time, uncertainty characterization in high-dimensional Granger causal inference. Second, we introduce a novel method for false discovery rate control that achieves higher power in multiple testing than existing techniques and that can cope with dependent test statistics and dependent observations. We corroborate our theoretical results with experiments on both synthetic data and real-world climatological data.

We make two contributions in this work. First, we introduce a novel asymptotically unbiased Granger causality estimator with corresponding test statistics and confidence intervals to allow, for the first time, uncertainty characterization in high-dimensional Granger causal inference. Second, we introduce a novel method for false discovery rate control that achieves higher power in multiple testing than existing techniques and that can cope with dependent test statistics and dependent observations. We corroborate our theoretical results with experiments on both synthetic data and real-world climatological data.

paragraphs: Finding Granger-causal relationships among many time series requires more than estimating which relationships are present. Researchers also need to assess the uncertainty of those estimates and manage false discoveries across many tests. This paper addresses both needs in the high-dimensional setting, where existing approaches lacked the stated uncertainty tools.

The first contribution is an asymptotically unbiased estimator of Granger causality, accompanied by test statistics and confidence intervals. Asymptotic unbiasedness describes behavior as the amount of data grows. The associated inferential tools make it possible to attach uncertainty assessments to estimates rather than report only estimated relationships.

The second contribution is a false discovery rate control method that accommodates dependence among both test statistics and observations. The authors report higher multiple-testing power than existing techniques. Experiments on synthetic and climatological data corroborate the theoretical results. Together, the contributions support evaluating individual relationships while also controlling false discoveries across the larger collection of tested relationships.
summary.tldr: A new Granger-causality estimator supplies uncertainty assessments, alongside higher-power false discovery control that accommodates dependent data and tests.

title: Uncertainty Assessment and False Discovery Rate Control in High-Dimensional Granger Causal Inference

abstract: Quantile regression aims at modeling the conditional median and quantiles of a response variable given certain predictor variables. In this work we consider the problem of linear quantile regression in high dimensions where the number of predictor variables is much higher than the number of samples available for parameter estimation. We assume the true parameter to have some structure characterized as having a small value according to some atomic norm R(.) and consider the norm regularized quantile regression estimator. We characterize the sample complexity for consistent recovery and give non-asymptotic bounds on the estimation error. While this problem has been previously considered, our analysis reveals geometric and statistical characteristics of the problem not available in prior literature. We perform experiments on synthetic data which support the theoretical results.
originalAbstract: Quantile regression aims at modeling the conditional median and quantiles of a response variable given certain predictor variables. In this work we consider the problem of linear quantile regression in high dimensions where the number of predictor variables is much higher than the number of samples available for parameter estimation. We assume the true parameter to have some structure characterized as having a small value according to some atomic norm R(.) and consider the norm regularized quantile regression estimator. We characterize the sample complexity for consistent recovery and give non-asymptotic bounds on the estimation error. While this problem has been previously considered, our analysis reveals geometric and statistical characteristics of the problem not available in prior literature. We perform experiments on synthetic data which support the theoretical results.

paragraphs: Quantile regression models features of a response distribution such as its median rather than only its mean. Estimating a linear quantile model becomes difficult when the number of predictors greatly exceeds the number of observations. This paper studies how structural knowledge about the unknown coefficients can make that high-dimensional estimation problem manageable.

The authors assume that the true parameter has a small value under an atomic norm, a mathematical way of representing low-complexity structure. They incorporate that norm as a regularizer in the quantile regression estimator. The analysis then connects recovery behavior to the geometry of the assumed structure and to statistical properties of the estimation problem.

The paper gives sample-complexity conditions for consistent recovery and finite-sample bounds on estimation error. Synthetic experiments support the theoretical conclusions. Its main contribution is an account of which structural and statistical features govern estimation accuracy; the reported evidence does not establish performance on a particular real-world application.
summary.tldr: Atomic-norm regularization gives structured high-dimensional quantile regression explicit sample and error guarantees.

title: High-Dimensional Structured Quantile Regression

abstract: The explosion in workload complexity and the recent slow-down in Moore’s law scaling call for new approaches towards efficient computing. Researchers are now beginning to use recent advances in machine learning in software optimizations; augmenting or replacing traditional heuristics and data structures. However, the space of machine learning for computer hardware architecture is only lightly explored. In this paper, we demonstrate the potential of deep learning to address the von Neumann bottleneck of memory performance. We focus on the critical problem of learning memory access patterns, with the goal of constructing accurate and efficient memory prefetchers. We relate contemporary prefetching strategies to n-gram models in natural language processing, and show how recurrent neural networks can serve as a drop-in replacement. On a suite of challenging benchmark datasets, we find that neural networks consistently demonstrate superior performance in terms of precision and recall. This work represents the first step towards practical neural-network based prefetching, and opens a wide range of exciting directions for machine learning in computer architecture research.
originalAbstract: The explosion in workload complexity and the recent slow-down in Moore’s law scaling call for new approaches towards efficient computing. Researchers are now beginning to use recent advances in machine learning in software optimizations; augmenting or replacing traditional heuristics and data structures. However, the space of machine learning for computer hardware architecture is only lightly explored. We focus on the critical problem of learning memory access patterns, with the goal of constructing accurate and efficient memory prefetchers. On a suite of challenging benchmark datasets, we find that neural networks consistently demonstrate superior performance in terms of precision and recall. This work represents the first step towards practical neural-network based prefetching, and opens a wide range of exciting directions for machine learning in computer architecture research.

paragraphs: Memory performance can limit computing even when substantial processing capability is available. This paper explores learning the patterns of memory accesses as a step toward better prefetchers: systems intended to anticipate which memory will be needed. The objective is to use deep learning to improve the accuracy and efficiency of that anticipation.

The authors connect contemporary prefetching strategies to n-gram models from natural language processing. This frames memory accesses as a sequence-prediction problem and motivates recurrent neural networks as a replacement for the existing prediction mechanism. The connection gives a concrete role to sequence learning within computer hardware architecture rather than treating machine learning as a general-purpose optimization suggestion.

Across a suite of challenging benchmark datasets, neural networks consistently achieve better precision and recall. These findings support their ability to predict memory-access patterns in the evaluated workloads. The authors position the work as an initial step toward practical neural prefetching, so the reported prediction improvements establish potential for that direction rather than a completed demonstration of practical hardware deployment.
summary.tldr: Recurrent neural networks improve memory-access prediction on benchmark datasets, supporting further development of neural memory prefetchers.

title: Learning Memory Access Patterns

abstract: Consider a large social network with possibly severe degree heterogeneity and mixed-memberships. We are interested in testing whether the network has only one community or there are more than one communities. The problem is known to be non-trivial, partially due to the presence of severe degree heterogeneity. We construct a class of test statistics using the numbers of short paths and short cycles, and the key to our approach is a general framework for canceling the effects of degree heterogeneity. The tests compare favorably with existing methods. We support our methods with careful analysis and numerical study with simulated data and a real data example.
originalAbstract: Consider a large social network with possibly severe degree heterogeneity and mixed-memberships. We are interested in testing whether the network has only one community or there are more than one communities. The problem is known to be non-trivial, partially due to the presence of severe degree heterogeneity. We construct a class of test statistics using the numbers of short paths and short cycles, and the key to our approach is a general framework for canceling the effects of degree heterogeneity. The tests compare favorably with existing methods. We support our methods with careful analysis and numerical study with simulated data and a real data example.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a large network contains a single community or multiple communities. This is a global testing question about the network's structure. It becomes difficult when nodes have very different numbers of connections, because those degree differences can complicate the evidence for community structure. The setting also allows mixed community memberships.

The authors construct test statistics from counts of short paths and short cycles. These small graph patterns provide information that can be aggregated across the network. The central contribution is a general framework for canceling the effects of degree heterogeneity, so the statistics can address community structure while accounting for large differences in node connectivity.

The proposed tests compare favorably with existing methods, supported by theoretical analysis, simulated networks, and a real-data example. The work shows how counts of small patterns can support a network-wide statistical decision. Its significance lies in combining these accessible structural summaries with a mechanism designed to address a major source of difficulty in heterogeneous networks.
summary.tldr: Tests based on short paths and cycles assess whether a network has multiple communities while canceling effects of degree heterogeneity.

title: Network Global Testing by Counting Graphlets

abstract: A new generative adversarial network is developed for joint distribution matching.Distinct from most existing approaches, that only learn conditional distributions, the proposed model aims to learn a joint distribution of multiple random variables (domains). This is achieved by learning to sample from conditional distributions between the domains, while simultaneously learning to sample from the marginals of each individual domain.The proposed framework consists of multiple generators and a single softmax-based critic, all jointly trained via adversarial learning.From a simple noise source, the proposed framework allows synthesis of draws from the marginals, conditional draws given observations from a subset of random variables, or complete draws from the full joint distribution. Most examples considered are for joint analysis of two domains, with examples for three domains also presented.

This is achieved by learning to sample from conditional distributions between the domains, while simultaneously learning to sample from the marginals of each individual domain.The proposed framework consists of multiple generators and a single softmax-based critic, all jointly trained via adversarial learning.From a simple noise source, the proposed framework allows synthesis of draws from the marginals, conditional draws given observations from a subset of random variables, or complete draws from the full joint distribution. Most examples considered are for joint analysis of two domains, with examples for three domains also presented.

paragraphs: JointGAN aims to learn the joint distribution of several domains: how their variables behave individually and together. A conditional distribution describes one domain given information about another, while a joint distribution describes their combined behavior. The paper develops an adversarial framework that targets this broader object by learning both conditional relationships and individual domain distributions.

The architecture contains multiple generators and one softmax-based critic, trained together through adversarial learning. The generators learn to sample between domains conditionally and from each domain’s marginal distribution. Training these components together is the mechanism used to support joint distribution matching across the participating domains.

Starting from a simple noise source, the framework can generate samples from one domain, generate conditionally when some variables are observed, or generate complete samples spanning the joint distribution. These capabilities allow several kinds of generation within the same framework. Most presented examples involve two domains, and the authors also include three-domain examples to illustrate a broader setting.
summary.tldr: JointGAN jointly learns marginal and conditional generators to support sampling from individual domains or their full joint distribution.

title: JointGAN: Multi-Domain Joint Distribution Learning with Generative Adversarial Nets

abstract: Recent studies on the adversarial vulnerability of neural networks have shown that models trained to be more robust to adversarial attacks exhibit more interpretable saliency maps than their non-robust counterparts. We aim to quantify this behaviour by considering the alignment between input image and saliency map. We hypothesize that as the distance to the decision boundary grows, so does the alignment. This connection is strictly true in the case of linear models. We confirm these theoretical findings with experiments based on models trained with a local Lipschitz regularization and identify where the nonlinear nature of neural networks weakens the relation.

paragraphs: Models trained for greater adversarial robustness have been observed to produce more interpretable saliency maps. This paper seeks to quantify that relationship by measuring alignment between an input image and its saliency map. Alignment supplies a concrete property to study, giving mathematical form to part of the observed connection between robustness and explanations.

The authors hypothesize that alignment increases as an input’s distance from the decision boundary grows. They establish this relationship strictly for linear models. In that setting, the proposed connection has a theoretical foundation linking the separation from a classification boundary with the structure of the saliency map.

Experiments use models trained with local Lipschitz regularization to examine the theoretical findings. The authors also identify where neural-network nonlinearity weakens the relationship. The result is a qualified account of why robustness and saliency interpretability may move together: the relationship is exact in the stated linear case, while nonlinear behavior complicates its extension to neural networks.
summary.tldr: The paper links decision-boundary distance to saliency alignment exactly for linear models and investigates how neural-network nonlinearity weakens that relationship.

title: On the Connection Between Adversarial Robustness and Saliency Map Interpretability

abstract: Domain adaptation addresses the common situation in which the target distribution generating our test data differs from the source distribution generating our training data. While absent assumptions, domain adaptation is impossible, strict conditions, e.g. covariate or label shift, enable principled algorithms. Recently-proposed domain-adversarial approaches consist of aligning source and target encodings, an approach often motivated as minimizing two (of three) terms in a theoretical bound on target error. Unfortunately, this minimization can cause arbitrary increases in the third term, a problem guaranteed to arise under shifting label distributions. We propose asymmetrically-relaxed distribution alignment, a new approach that overcomes some limitations of standard domain-adversarial algorithms. Moreover, we characterize precise assumptions under which our algorithm is theoretically principled and demonstrate empirical benefits on both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation tries to make a model work when its test data follow a different distribution from its training data. The paper examines approaches that align representations of the source and target domains. Although this strategy can make the domains look similar, that similarity alone does not establish good target predictions.

A common justification uses a target-error bound with three terms, while the training procedure reduces two of them. The authors show that this reduction can cause arbitrarily large increases in the remaining term. They identify changing label distributions as a situation in which the problem is guaranteed to arise, exposing a weakness in the usual alignment argument.

The proposed alternative relaxes distribution alignment asymmetrically and overcomes some limitations of standard domain-adversarial methods. The authors specify assumptions under which their algorithm has a principled theoretical basis and report benefits on synthetic and real datasets. The contribution combines a diagnosis of why alignment can fail with an alternative whose justification explicitly depends on assumptions about the adaptation problem.
summary.tldr: Asymmetrically relaxed alignment addresses some failures of domain-adversarial adaptation, with theoretical support under explicit assumptions and empirical benefits.

title: Domain Adaptation with Asymmetrically-Relaxed Distribution Alignment

abstract: We develop a novel method, called PoWER-BERT, for improving the inference time of the popular BERT model, while maintaining the accuracy. It works by: a) exploiting redundancy pertaining to word-vectors (intermediate transformer block outputs) and eliminating the redundant vectors. b) determining which word-vectors to eliminate by developing a strategy for measuring their significance, based on the self-attention mechanism. c) learning how many word-vectors to eliminate by augmenting the BERT model and the loss function. Experiments on the standard GLUE benchmark shows that PoWER-BERT achieves up to 4.5x reduction in inference time over BERT with < 1% loss in accuracy. We show that PoWER-BERT offers significantly better trade-off between accuracy and inference time compared to prior methods. We demonstrate that our method attains up to 6.8x reduction in inference time with < 1% loss in accuracy when applied over ALBERT, a highly compressed version of BERT. The code for PoWER-BERT is publicly available at https://github.com/IBM/PoWER-BERT.

paragraphs: PoWER-BERT speeds up BERT inference by removing redundant word vectors from intermediate transformer outputs. The central idea is that carrying every intermediate vector through the model can involve unnecessary computation. Progressively eliminating less significant vectors offers a way to reduce inference time while largely preserving predictive accuracy.

The method uses self-attention to measure the significance of word vectors and decide which ones to remove. It also augments the model and its loss function to learn how many vectors should be eliminated. These two decisions address both the identity of the retained information and the amount of computation reduced.

On GLUE, the authors report inference-time reductions of up to 4.5 times relative to BERT with less than 1% accuracy loss, alongside a better accuracy-time tradeoff than prior methods. Applied to ALBERT, the method reaches reductions of up to 6.8 times with less than 1% accuracy loss. These reported maxima show that intermediate-vector reduction can also benefit an already compressed model.
summary.tldr: PoWER-BERT learns to remove intermediate word vectors, reporting up to 4.5-fold faster BERT inference with less than 1% accuracy loss.

title: PoWER-BERT: Accelerating BERT Inference via Progressive Word-vector Elimination

abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning is known to be memory and computation efficient and more amendable to large scale problems. In this paper, two model-free algorithms are introduced for learning infinite-horizon average-reward Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). The first algorithm reduces the problem to the discounted-reward version and achieves $\mathcal{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret after $T$ steps, under the minimal assumption of weakly communicating MDPs. To our knowledge, this is the first model-free algorithm for general MDPs in this setting. The second algorithm makes use of recent advances in adaptive algorithms for adversarial multi-armed bandits and improves the regret to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$, albeit with a stronger ergodic assumption. This result significantly improves over the $\mathcal{O}(T^{3/4})$ regret achieved by the only existing model-free algorithm by Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2019) for ergodic MDPs in the infinite-horizon average-reward setting.

paragraphs: This paper develops model-free reinforcement learning algorithms for continuing decision problems evaluated by average reward. The infinite-horizon setting has no fixed final step, so the objective concerns sustained performance. The authors seek algorithms that retain the memory and computational advantages associated with model-free learning while providing theoretical regret guarantees.

The first algorithm converts the average-reward problem into a discounted-reward problem. Under the assumption that the Markov decision process is weakly communicating, it achieves regret of order T^(2/3) after T steps. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first model-free algorithm for general Markov decision processes in this setting.

The second algorithm draws on adaptive methods for adversarial multi-armed bandits and improves the regret rate to order sqrt(T). That stronger rate requires the stronger assumption of ergodicity. It improves on the previously available model-free rate of order T^(3/4) for the ergodic setting. The two results therefore offer different combinations of assumptions and guarantees, rather than a single bound that applies equally broadly.
summary.tldr: Two model-free algorithms achieve sublinear regret for average-reward learning, with a stronger rate available under a stronger ergodic assumption.

title: Model-free Reinforcement Learning in Infinite-horizon Average-reward Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are non-parametric, flexible, models that work well in many tasks. Combining GPs with deep learning methods via deep kernel learning (DKL) is especially compelling due to the strong representational power induced by the network. However, inference in GPs, whether with or without DKL, can be computationally challenging on large datasets. Here, we propose GP-Tree, a novel method for multi-class classification with Gaussian processes and DKL. We develop a tree-based hierarchical model in which each internal node of the tree fits a GP to the data using the P{ó}lya-Gamma augmentation scheme. As a result, our method scales well with both the number of classes and data size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method against other Gaussian process training baselines, and we show how our general GP approach achieves improved accuracy on standard incremental few-shot learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes provide flexible models, and deep kernel learning combines them with the representational power of neural networks. However, inference can become computationally difficult as datasets grow. GP-Tree addresses this problem for multiclass classification, including the incremental few-shot learning setting in which the paper evaluates its predictive performance.

The method organizes classification as a tree-based hierarchy. Each internal node fits a Gaussian process using Pólya-Gamma augmentation. This structure supplies a way to distribute the multiclass modeling problem across the hierarchy. The authors report that the resulting approach scales well with both dataset size and the number of classes, addressing two sources of computational growth.

Evaluations compare GP-Tree with other Gaussian process training approaches and demonstrate its effectiveness. On standard incremental few-shot benchmarks, the method also achieves improved accuracy. These findings connect the computational organization of the model to its practical classification performance. The contribution is a general Gaussian process approach that supports deep kernel learning while making larger multiclass problems more manageable in the settings studied.
summary.tldr: GP-Tree organizes Gaussian process classifiers into a hierarchy that scales with data and classes and improves accuracy on incremental few-shot benchmarks.

title: GP-Tree: A Gaussian Process Classifier for Few-Shot Incremental Learning

abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of sample-efficient learning of decision-making policies by leveraging past experience. However, in the offline RL setting – where a fixed collection of interactions are provided and no further interactions are allowed – it has been shown that standard off-policy RL methods can significantly underperform. In this work, we closely investigate an important simplification of BCQ (Fujimoto et al., 2018) – a prior approach for offline RL – removing a heuristic design choice. Importantly, in contrast to their original theoretical considerations, we derive this simplified algorithm through the introduction of a novel backup operator, Expected-Max Q-Learning (EMaQ), which is more closely related to the resulting practical algorithm. Specifically, in addition to the distribution support, EMaQ explicitly considers the number of samples and the proposal distribution, allowing us to derive new sub-optimality bounds. In the offline RL setting – the main focus of this work – EMaQ matches and outperforms prior state-of-the-art in the D4RL benchmarks (Fu et al., 2020). In the online RL setting, we demonstrate that EMaQ is competitive with Soft Actor Critic (SAC). The key contributions of our empirical findings are demonstrating the importance of careful generative model design for estimating behavior policies, and an intuitive notion of complexity for offline RL problems. With its simple interpretation and fewer moving parts, such as no explicit function approximator representing the policy, EMaQ serves as a strong yet easy to implement baseline for future work.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from a fixed collection of interactions without gathering further experience. Standard off-policy methods can perform poorly in this setting. The paper investigates a simplified version of BCQ that removes a heuristic design choice, then develops a theoretical account more closely aligned with the resulting practical algorithm.

That account centers on the Expected-Max Q-Learning operator, or EMaQ. Beyond considering which actions a distribution supports, the operator explicitly incorporates the proposal distribution and the number of samples. These ingredients let the authors derive new bounds on suboptimality. The formulation connects the way candidate actions are generated to the quality of the resulting decision process.

On D4RL offline benchmarks, EMaQ matches or exceeds prior state-of-the-art performance; in online experiments, it is competitive with Soft Actor Critic. The findings emphasize careful generative modeling of behavior policies and introduce an intuitive view of offline problem complexity. With fewer components, including no explicit policy function approximator, the method also provides a comparatively simple baseline for further research.
summary.tldr: EMaQ connects a simplified offline RL algorithm to a backup operator that accounts for action proposals and sample counts, with strong reported benchmark performance.

title: EMaQ: Expected-Max Q-Learning Operator for Simple Yet Effective Offline and Online RL

abstract: We present several classes of reinforcement learning algorithms that safely generalize to Markov decision processes (MDPs) not seen during training. Specifically, we study the setting in which some set of MDPs is accessible for training. The goal is to generalize safely to MDPs that are sampled from the same distribution, but which may not be in the set accessible for training. For various definitions of safety, our algorithms give probabilistic guarantees that agents can safely generalize to MDPs that are sampled from the same distribution but are not necessarily in the training set. These algorithms are a type of Seldonian algorithm (Thomas et al., 2019), which is a class of machine learning algorithms that return models with probabilistic safety guarantees for user-specified definitions of safety.
originalAbstract: We present several classes of reinforcement learning algorithms that safely generalize to Markov decision processes (MDPs) not seen during training. Specifically, we study the setting in which some set of MDPs is accessible for training. The goal is to generalize safely to MDPs that are sampled from the same distribution, but which may not be in the set accessible for training. For various definitions of safety, our algorithms give probabilistic guarantees that agents can safely generalize to MDPs that are sampled from the same distribution but are not necessarily in the training set. These algorithms are a type of Seldonian algorithm (Thomas et al., 2019), which is a class of machine learning algorithms that return models with probabilistic safety guarantees for user-specified definitions of safety.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents may encounter environments that were unavailable during training. This paper asks how to give meaningful safety assurances for that situation. It considers a collection of Markov decision processes available for training and new processes sampled from the same underlying distribution. A new environment can therefore differ from every training environment while still belonging to the distribution covered by the analysis.

The authors present several classes of algorithms with probabilistic guarantees of safe generalization. Safety is not restricted to one fixed definition: the work considers multiple definitions and allows users to specify the safety requirements of interest. The guarantees concern satisfying those requirements when transferring to environments sampled in the stated way.

These methods belong to the Seldonian family of learning algorithms, which return models with probabilistic safety assurances. The contribution connects that approach to reinforcement learning across environments. Its scope depends on both the chosen safety definition and the shared-distribution assumption; it does not turn safety on unseen environments into an unconditional or certain property.
summary.tldr: The paper develops reinforcement-learning algorithms with probabilistic safety guarantees for unseen environments sampled from the same distribution as training environments.

title: High Confidence Generalization for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce a new balanced assignment of experts (BASE) layer for large language models that greatly simplifies existing high capacity sparse layers. Sparse layers can dramatically improve the efficiency of training and inference by routing each token to specialized expert modules that contain only a small fraction of the model parameters. However, it can be difficult to learn balanced routing functions that make full use of the available experts; existing approaches typically use routing heuristics or auxiliary expert-balancing loss functions. In contrast, we formulate token-to-expert allocation as a linear assignment problem, allowing an optimal assignment in which each expert receives an equal number of tokens. This optimal assignment scheme improves efficiency by guaranteeing balanced compute loads, and also simplifies training by not requiring any new hyperparameters or auxiliary losses. Code is publicly released.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new balanced assignment of experts (BASE) layer for large language models that greatly simplifies existing high capacity sparse layers. Sparse layers can dramatically improve the efficiency of training and inference by routing each token to specialized expert modules that contain only a small fraction of the model parameters. However, it can be difficult to learn balanced routing functions that make full use of the available experts; existing approaches typically use routing heuristics or auxiliary expert-balancing loss functions. In contrast, we formulate token-to-expert allocation as a linear assignment problem, allowing an optimal assignment in which each expert receives an equal number of tokens. Code is publicly released.

paragraphs: Sparse language models can hold many parameters while using only a small fraction for each token. They do this by sending tokens to specialized expert modules. The challenge is routing: an allocation that leaves some experts underused and others overloaded fails to make balanced use of the available computation.

BASE layers address this by formulating token-to-expert routing as a linear assignment problem. The assignment is optimized subject to each expert receiving an equal number of tokens. Balance is therefore built into the allocation itself. This differs from approaches that try to obtain balanced behavior through routing heuristics or additional expert-balancing terms in the training loss.

The resulting scheme guarantees balanced compute loads and requires neither new hyperparameters nor auxiliary losses for balancing. Its significance is that a central operational requirement of sparse models becomes part of a directly solved optimization problem. The paper presents this as a way to improve efficiency and simplify training while retaining the high-capacity structure provided by specialized experts.
summary.tldr: BASE layers optimize token-to-expert assignments with equal expert workloads, simplifying sparse language-model training without auxiliary balancing losses.

title: BASE Layers: Simplifying Training of Large, Sparse Models

abstract: The time and effort involved in hand-designing deep neural networks is immense. This has prompted the development of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) techniques to automate this design. However, NAS algorithms tend to be slow and expensive; they need to train vast numbers of candidate networks to inform the search process. This could be alleviated if we could partially predict a network’s trained accuracy from its initial state. In this work, we examine the overlap of activations between datapoints in untrained networks and motivate how this can give a measure which is usefully indicative of a network’s trained performance. We incorporate this measure into a simple algorithm that allows us to search for powerful networks without any training in a matter of seconds on a single GPU, and verify its effectiveness on NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NATS-Bench, and Network Design Spaces. Our approach can be readily combined with more expensive search methods; we examine a simple adaptation of regularised evolutionary search. Code for reproducing our experiments is available at https://github.com/BayesWatch/nas-without-training.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can be expensive because it commonly trains many candidate networks to judge their quality. This paper investigates whether an untrained network already contains a useful signal about its eventual trained accuracy. Such a signal could make it much cheaper to choose promising architectures during search.

The authors examine how activations overlap across data points in networks before training. They motivate a measure based on that overlap that is usefully indicative of trained performance. A simple search algorithm uses the measure to find powerful networks in seconds on a single GPU, without training the candidates during the search process.

The approach is evaluated on NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NATS-Bench, and Network Design Spaces. The authors also examine combining it with a more expensive method through an adaptation of regularized evolutionary search. The contribution is a fast architecture-selection signal that partially anticipates trained performance, making both standalone search and integration with existing search procedures possible.
summary.tldr: Activation overlap in untrained networks provides a useful performance signal for architecture search in seconds on one GPU.

title: Neural Architecture Search without Training

abstract: Reconstruction-based Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) agents, such as Dreamer, often fail to discard task-irrelevant visual distractions that are prevalent in natural scenes. In this paper, we propose a reconstruction-free MBRL agent, called DreamerPro, that can enhance robustness to distractions. Motivated by the recent success of prototypical representations, a non-contrastive self-supervised learning approach in computer vision, DreamerPro combines Dreamer with prototypes. In order for the prototypes to benefit temporal dynamics learning in MBRL, we propose to additionally learn the prototypes from the recurrent states of the world model, thereby distilling temporal structures from past observations and actions into the prototypes. Experiments on the DeepMind Control suite show that DreamerPro achieves better overall performance than state-of-the-art contrastive MBRL agents when there are complex background distractions, and maintains similar performance as Dreamer in standard tasks where contrastive MBRL agents can perform much worse.

paragraphs: Agents that learn a model of their visual environment through image reconstruction can retain distracting details unrelated to their task. DreamerPro addresses this problem by removing the reconstruction requirement from a Dreamer-based agent. It uses prototypical representations, a form of non-contrastive self-supervised learning, to improve robustness to visual distractions.

The method combines Dreamer with learned prototypes and also learns those prototypes from the world model's recurrent states. These states incorporate past observations and actions. Learning from them lets the prototypes capture temporal structure, connecting the representation-learning objective to the dynamics that a model-based reinforcement-learning agent needs to understand.

On the DeepMind Control suite, DreamerPro achieves better overall performance than state-of-the-art contrastive model-based agents when backgrounds contain complex distractions. On standard tasks, it maintains performance similar to Dreamer, where contrastive alternatives can perform much worse. The results support prototypes as a way to improve distraction resistance while retaining the performance of the underlying agent in the standard evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: DreamerPro learns temporally informed prototypes instead of reconstructing images, improving performance with distracting backgrounds.

title: DreamerPro: Reconstruction-Free Model-Based Reinforcement Learning with Prototypical Representations

abstract: We introduce a new algorithm for numerical composition of privacy random variables, useful for computing the accurate differential privacy parameters for compositions of mechanisms. Our algorithm achieves a running time and memory usage of $polylog(k)$ for the task of self-composing a mechanism, from a broad class of mechanisms, $k$ times; this class, e.g., includes the sub-sampled Gaussian mechanism, that appears in the analysis of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). By comparison, recent work by Gopi et al. (NeurIPS 2021) has obtained a running time of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k})$ for the same task. Our approach extends to the case of composing $k$ different mechanisms in the same class, improving upon the running time and memory usage in their work from $\widetilde{O}(k^{1.5})$ to $\wtilde{O}(k)$.

Our algorithm achieves a running time and memory usage of $polylog(k)$ for the task of self-composing a mechanism, from a broad class of mechanisms, $k$ times; this class, e.g., includes the sub-sampled Gaussian mechanism, that appears in the analysis of differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). paragraphs: Privacy accounting computes the privacy parameters that result when mechanisms are used together or repeatedly. This paper introduces a numerical algorithm for composing privacy random variables, with the goal of calculating accurate differential privacy parameters efficiently. Its contribution concerns the computational resources needed for this accounting task.

For repeating the same mechanism k times, the algorithm requires time and memory that grow polylogarithmically in k. The guarantee applies to a broad class of mechanisms, including the subsampled Gaussian mechanism used in analyses of differentially private stochastic gradient descent. The cited previous approach required roughly square-root growth in running time for this repeated-mechanism task, up to logarithmic factors.

The approach also handles compositions of k different mechanisms from the same class. In that case, it improves the stated time and memory dependence from approximately k to the power 1.5 to approximately linear in k, again suppressing logarithmic factors. These results make accurate numerical accounting more computationally efficient for both repeated and varied mechanisms, with the strongest improvement applying to self-composition.
summary.tldr: A numerical privacy-accounting algorithm achieves polylogarithmic time and memory for repeated composition of mechanisms from a broad class.

title: Faster Privacy Accounting via Evolving Discretization

abstract: Real-world data is high-dimensional: a book, image, or musical performance can easily contain hundreds of thousands of elements even after compression. However, the most commonly used autoregressive models, Transformers, are prohibitively expensive to scale to the number of inputs and layers needed to capture this long-range structure. We develop Perceiver AR, an autoregressive, modality-agnostic architecture which uses cross-attention to map long-range inputs to a small number of latents while also maintaining end-to-end causal masking. Perceiver AR can directly attend to over a hundred thousand tokens, enabling practical long-context density estimation without the need for hand-crafted sparsity patterns or memory mechanisms. When trained on images or music, Perceiver AR generates outputs with clear long-term coherence and structure. Our architecture also obtains state-of-the-art likelihood on long-sequence benchmarks, including 64x64 ImageNet images and PG-19 books.

Perceiver AR addresses this computational problem with an architecture intended to work across modalities. Its aim is to make long-context probability modeling practical while retaining the ordering required for autoregressive generation.

The architecture uses cross-attention to map a long input sequence into a smaller collection of latent representations. It maintains causal masking throughout, so predictions respect which inputs are available at each position. This design allows direct attention to more than one hundred thousand tokens without requiring manually designed sparse attention patterns or separate memory mechanisms.

When trained on images and music, Perceiver AR produces samples with clear long-term structure and coherence. It also achieves state-of-the-art likelihood on the reported long-sequence benchmarks, including 64-by-64 ImageNet images and PG-19 books. These findings support the architectural idea that a compact latent representation can make very long input contexts useful for both probability estimation and structured generation.
summary.tldr: Perceiver AR uses cross-attention and compact latents to model long sequences while preserving causal autoregressive prediction.

title: General-purpose, long-context autoregressive modeling with Perceiver AR

abstract: We develop fast algorithms and robust software for convex optimization of two-layer neural networks with ReLU activation functions. Our work leverages a convex re-formulation of the standard weight-decay penalized training problem as a set of group-l1-regularized data-local models, where locality is enforced by polyhedral cone constraints. In the special case of zero-regularization, we show that this problem is exactly equivalent to unconstrained optimization of a convex "gated ReLU" network. For problems with non-zero regularization, we show that convex gated ReLU models obtain data-dependent approximation bounds for the ReLU training problem. To optimize the convex re-formulations, we develop an accelerated proximal gradient method and a practical augmented Lagrangian solver. We show that these approaches are faster than standard training heuristics for the non-convex problem, such as SGD, and outperform commercial interior-point solvers. Experimentally, we verify our theoretical results, explore the group-l1 regularization path, and scale convex optimization for neural networks to image classification on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: Training a two-layer ReLU network is usually approached as a nonconvex optimization problem. This paper develops algorithms and software around a convex reformulation of training with weight decay. The reformulation uses groups of models associated with portions of the data, with group regularization and polyhedral cone constraints defining their structure.

The authors clarify when a simpler convex model can represent the training problem. With zero regularization, they establish exact equivalence to unconstrained optimization of a convex gated ReLU network. With nonzero regularization, gated ReLU models instead provide approximation bounds that depend on the data. This distinction separates an exact reformulation from a controlled approximation.

To solve these problems, the paper develops an accelerated proximal gradient method and a practical augmented Lagrangian solver. The reported comparisons show faster optimization than standard nonconvex training heuristics such as SGD and better performance than commercial interior-point solvers. Experiments also examine the regularization path and demonstrate image classification on MNIST and CIFAR-10, connecting the theoretical formulations to usable training procedures.
summary.tldr: Convex reformulations and specialized solvers make two-layer ReLU training faster in the reported comparisons, with exact or approximate relationships depending on regularization.

title: Fast Convex Optimization for Two-Layer ReLU Networks: Equivalent Model Classes and Cone Decompositions

abstract: Distributed Mean Estimation (DME) is a central building block in federated learning, where clients send local gradients to a parameter server for averaging and updating the model. Due to communication constraints, clients often use lossy compression techniques to compress the gradients, resulting in estimation inaccuracies. DME is more challenging when clients have diverse network conditions, such as constrained communication budgets and packet losses. In such settings, DME techniques often incur a significant increase in the estimation error leading to degraded learning performance. In this work, we propose a robust DME technique named EDEN that naturally handles heterogeneous communication budgets and packet losses. We derive appealing theoretical guarantees for EDEN and evaluate it empirically. Our results demonstrate that EDEN consistently improves over state-of-the-art DME techniques.

paragraphs: Federated learning often requires a server to average gradients computed by many clients. Sending those gradients can be expensive, so clients compress them before transmission. Because compression loses information, the server’s estimate of the average becomes less accurate. Different communication budgets and missing packets make this estimation problem harder.

EDEN is a distributed mean-estimation technique designed to handle both unequal communication budgets and packet loss. These conditions matter together because participating clients may differ substantially in how much information they can send and how reliably it arrives. A useful averaging method must accommodate that variation while controlling the inaccuracies introduced by communication constraints.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for EDEN and evaluates it empirically. The reported results consistently improve on leading distributed mean-estimation techniques in the evaluations. The contribution concerns a central operation within federated learning: obtaining a useful aggregate from compressed, unevenly delivered client information. Improving that operation addresses a source of estimation error that can otherwise degrade the learning process.
summary.tldr: EDEN improves distributed mean estimation while accommodating differing client communication budgets and packet loss.

title: EDEN: Communication-Efficient and Robust Distributed Mean Estimation for Federated Learning

abstract: Label smoothing (LS) is an arising learning paradigm that uses the positively weighted average of both the hard training labels and uniformly distributed soft labels. It was shown that LS serves as a regularizer for training data with hard labels and therefore improves the generalization of the model. Later it was reported LS even helps with improving robustness when learning with noisy labels. However, we observed that the advantage of LS vanishes when we operate in a high label noise regime. Intuitively speaking, this is due to the increased entropy of P(noisy label|X) when the noise rate is high, in which case, further applying LS tends to “over-smooth” the estimated posterior. We proceeded to discover that several learning-with-noisy-labels solutions in the literature instead relate more closely to negative/not label smoothing (NLS), which acts counter to LS and defines as using a negative weight to combine the hard and soft labels! We provide understandings for the properties of LS and NLS when learning with noisy labels. Among other established properties, we theoretically show NLS is considered more beneficial when the label noise rates are high. We provide extensive experimental results on multiple benchmarks to support our findings too. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/UCSC-REAL/negative-label-smoothing.

paragraphs: Label smoothing mixes a hard training label with a uniform soft target, reducing how sharply the target favors one class. It can regularize learning and has also been reported to help with noisy labels. This paper finds that its advantage disappears when label noise becomes high, questioning whether more smoothing remains useful in that regime.

The proposed explanation is that high noise already makes the label distribution conditional on the input more uncertain. Additional smoothing can then make the estimated distribution excessively diffuse. The authors examine negative label smoothing, which reverses the direction of ordinary smoothing by using a negative weight in the hard-and-soft-label combination. They also connect several existing noisy-label learning methods to this formulation.

The paper analyzes properties of both positive and negative smoothing and theoretically shows that negative smoothing is more beneficial at high label-noise rates. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks support the findings. The result motivates choosing the direction of smoothing according to the noise regime, rather than assuming that the regularization benefits observed with cleaner labels carry over unchanged to heavily corrupted labels.
summary.tldr: At high label-noise rates, ordinary smoothing can over-smooth targets, while negative label smoothing can be more beneficial.

title: To Smooth or Not? When Label Smoothing Meets Noisy Labels

abstract: Guided sampling is a vital approach for applying diffusion models in real-world tasks that embeds human-defined guidance during the sampling procedure. This paper considers a general setting where the guidance is defined by an (unnormalized) energy function. The main challenge for this setting is that the intermediate guidance during the diffusion sampling procedure, which is jointly defined by the sampling distribution and the energy function, is unknown and is hard to estimate. To address this challenge, we propose an exact formulation of the intermediate guidance as well as a novel training objective named contrastive energy prediction (CEP) to learn the exact guidance. Our method is guaranteed to converge to the exact guidance under unlimited model capacity and data samples, while previous methods can not. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to offline reinforcement learning (RL). Extensive experiments on D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms. We also provide some examples of applying CEP for image synthesis to demonstrate the scalability of CEP on high-dimensional data.

paragraphs: Guided diffusion sampling steers generated outputs according to a desired preference. This paper considers preferences expressed by an unnormalized energy function. The difficulty is that the guidance needed at intermediate sampling steps depends jointly on this energy and the sampling distribution, making it unknown and difficult to estimate directly.

The authors derive an exact expression for that intermediate guidance and introduce contrastive energy prediction, or CEP, as a training objective for learning it. Their convergence guarantee requires unlimited model capacity and data samples. Under those conditions, CEP converges to the exact guidance, a property the abstract states previous methods do not provide.

The main application is offline reinforcement learning, where the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in experiments on D4RL benchmarks. Image synthesis examples additionally demonstrate its applicability to high-dimensional data. Together, these results connect a theoretical formulation of guidance with practical sampling tasks. The exactness guarantee belongs to the stated unlimited-capacity and unlimited-data setting, while the benchmark improvements provide separate empirical evidence of effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Contrastive energy prediction learns diffusion guidance with an idealized exactness guarantee and improves reported offline reinforcement learning results.

title: Contrastive Energy Prediction for Exact Energy-Guided Diffusion Sampling in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A major challenge to out-of-distribution generalization is reliance on spurious features — patterns that are predictive of the class label in the training data distribution, but not causally related to the target. Standard methods for reducing the reliance on spurious features typically assume that we know what the spurious feature is, which is rarely true in the real world. Methods that attempt to alleviate this limitation are complex, hard to tune, and lead to a significant computational overhead compared to standard training. In this paper, we propose Automatic Feature Reweighting (AFR), an extremely simple and fast method for updating the model to reduce the reliance on spurious features. AFR retrains the last layer of a standard ERM-trained base model with a weighted loss that emphasizes the examples where the ERM model predicts poorly, automatically upweighting the minority group without group labels. With this simple procedure, we improve upon the best reported results among competing methods trained without spurious attributes on several vision and natural language classification benchmarks, using only a fraction of their compute.

paragraphs: A classifier can rely on patterns that predict labels in its training data but have no causal connection to the target. When those patterns change, performance can deteriorate. Many approaches to this problem require knowing the spurious attribute in advance, while alternatives can add substantial complexity and computation. Automatic Feature Reweighting offers a simpler update procedure.

AFR starts with a model trained using standard empirical risk minimization and retrains its final layer. The new loss gives more weight to examples on which the original model predicts poorly. In the proposed procedure, this automatically increases the emphasis on minority-group examples without requiring group labels, changing how the existing features contribute to the final prediction.

On several vision and natural-language classification benchmarks, AFR improves on the best reported results among competing methods trained without spurious-attribute information. It uses only a fraction of their computation. The results show that a targeted final-layer update can provide strong group robustness in these evaluations without the more elaborate training procedures used by competing approaches.
summary.tldr: AFR improves group robustness efficiently by retraining a model’s final layer with extra weight on poorly predicted examples.

title: Simple and Fast Group Robustness by Automatic Feature Reweighting

abstract: In this paper, we study the predict-then-optimize problem where the output of a machine learning prediction task is used as the input of some downstream optimization problem, say, the objective coefficient vector of a linear program. The problem is also known as predictive analytics or contextual linear programming. The existing approaches largely suffer from either (i) optimization intractability (a non-convex objective function)/statistical inefficiency (a suboptimal generalization bound) or (ii) requiring strong condition(s) such as no constraint or loss calibration. We develop a new approach to the problem called maximum optimality margin which designs the machine learning loss function by the optimality condition of the downstream optimization. The max-margin formulation enjoys both computational efficiency and good theoretical properties for the learning procedure. More importantly, our new approach only needs the observations of the optimal solution in the training data rather than the objective function, which makes it a new and natural approach to the inverse linear programming problem under both contextual and context-free settings; we also analyze the proposed method under both offline and online settings, and demonstrate its performance using numerical experiments.
